title: Complex Variables, Fourier & Laplace Transforms (Math III)

lessons.title: Complex Numbers from Scratch
lessons.content:
Imagine you are standing at Shahbag and someone asks you, "Where is Dhanmondi?" You could say "about 3 km away". That is one number, but it is not enough. You also need a direction: south-west. The moment you need two pieces of information to describe one thing, a single ordinary number stops being enough. Complex numbers are exactly this: one number made of two parts, so it can describe a point on a flat map instead of a point on a line. This whole course, Math III, is built on top of that one small idea, so let us take it slowly and get it really solid.

Welcome to Math III: This course has three big parts. First, complex variables: numbers like 3 + 4i and functions of them, including a beautiful kind of integration done along paths in a plane. Second, Fourier analysis: breaking any repeating signal, like a sound wave, into simple sine and cosine waves. Third, the Laplace transform: a magic trick that turns hard differential equations into easy algebra. Engineers use all three every day in signal processing, communication, control systems and image processing. Today we start at the very bottom: what a complex number is and how to do arithmetic with it.

The problem that started it all: Try solving x² + 1 = 0. You need a number whose square is -1. On the ordinary number line, every number squared is zero or positive: 2² = 4, (-2)² = 4, 0² = 0. No real number squared gives -1. For centuries mathematicians said "no solution" and moved on. But when Italian mathematicians in the 1500s solved cubic equations, they found that their formulas sometimes passed through square roots of negative numbers on the way to a perfectly real answer. So these "impossible" numbers were useful even if they looked strange. Eventually people accepted them as real tools.

The imaginary unit i: We simply define a new number i with the rule i² = -1. That is all. Engineers often write j instead of i, because in electrical engineering i is already used for current. You will see both in your books, so do not get confused: j and i mean the same thing. With i in hand, the square root of -9 is 3i, because (3i)² = 9 × i² = 9 × (-1) = -9. And x² + 1 = 0 now has two solutions: x = i and x = -i.

Powers of i go in a circle: Watch what happens when you keep multiplying by i. i¹ = i. i² = -1. i³ = i² × i = -i. i⁴ = i² × i² = (-1)(-1) = 1. Then i⁵ = i again, and the pattern repeats every four steps. So to find a big power like i²⁰²⁶, divide the power by 4 and look at the remainder. 2026 = 4 × 506 + 2, so the remainder is 2 and i²⁰²⁶ = i² = -1. Exams love this question because it looks scary but takes ten seconds once you know the cycle.

What a complex number is: A complex number is z = x + iy, where x and y are ordinary real numbers. The x is called the real part, written Re(z), and the y is called the imaginary part, written Im(z). Careful: the imaginary part is y, not iy. So for z = 3 + 4i, Re(z) = 3 and Im(z) = 4. If y = 0, the number is just a real number, like 5. If x = 0 and y is not zero, it is called purely imaginary, like 7i. So real numbers live inside the complex numbers as a special case.

When are two complex numbers equal? Two complex numbers are equal only when both parts match: a + ib = c + id means a = c and b = d. This gives you two real equations from one complex equation, which is a powerful trick. For example, if x + iy = 5 - 2i, then x = 5 and y = -2 straight away. Another warning: complex numbers have no "greater than" or "less than". You can't say 3 + i is bigger than 1 + 2i. You can only compare their sizes, which we meet in the next lesson.

Addition and subtraction: Add the real parts together and the imaginary parts together, like adding apples with apples and oranges with oranges. (3 + 4i) + (1 - 2i) = (3 + 1) + (4 - 2)i = 4 + 2i. Subtraction is the same: (3 + 4i) - (1 - 2i) = 2 + 6i. Notice the sign: minus a minus becomes plus, so 4 - (-2) = 6.

Multiplication: Multiply like ordinary brackets, then replace i² with -1. (3 + 4i)(1 - 2i) = 3 - 6i + 4i - 8i². Now -8i² = -8(-1) = +8. So the total is 3 + 8 - 2i = 11 - 2i. A handy general formula: (a + ib)(c + id) = (ac - bd) + i(ad + bc). You do not need to memorise it if you just expand carefully, but it is nice for checking.

The conjugate: The conjugate of z = x + iy is z̄ = x - iy. You just flip the sign of the imaginary part. The conjugate of 3 + 4i is 3 - 4i. Here is the magic: z times z̄ is always a real number, and never negative. (3 + 4i)(3 - 4i) = 9 - 12i + 12i - 16i² = 9 + 16 = 25. In general, (x + iy)(x - iy) = x² + y². Also, z + z̄ = 2x and z - z̄ = 2iy, so Re(z) = (z + z̄)/2 and Im(z) = (z - z̄)/(2i). These formulas show up again when we study analytic functions.

Rules of the conjugate: The conjugate of a sum is the sum of the conjugates, and the conjugate of a product is the product of the conjugates. Conjugating twice gives back the original number. And a number equals its own conjugate exactly when it is real. These small rules make many proofs one line long.

Division: To divide, multiply the top and the bottom by the conjugate of the bottom. This makes the bottom real. Example: (3 + 4i)/(1 - 2i). Multiply top and bottom by (1 + 2i). Bottom: (1 - 2i)(1 + 2i) = 1 + 4 = 5. Top: (3 + 4i)(1 + 2i) = 3 + 6i + 4i + 8i² = 3 - 8 + 10i = -5 + 10i. So the answer is (-5 + 10i)/5 = -1 + 2i. Check: (-1 + 2i)(1 - 2i) = -1 + 2i + 2i - 4i² = -1 + 4 + 4i = 3 + 4i. Correct! Always check division by multiplying back; it catches silly sign mistakes.

The reciprocal: A special case of division is 1/z. Using the same trick, 1/(x + iy) = (x - iy)/(x² + y²). For example, 1/i = -i, because i × (-i) = -i² = 1. This little fact, 1/i = -i, appears again and again, so remember it.

The Argand plane: Now the best part. Since a complex number has two parts, we can draw it as a point (x, y) on a flat plane. The horizontal axis is the real axis and the vertical axis is the imaginary axis. This picture is called the complex plane or the Argand plane (also Argand diagram). So 3 + 4i is the point 3 steps right and 4 steps up. The number -2 sits on the real axis to the left. The number 5i sits on the imaginary axis, 5 steps up. Suddenly numbers are not on a line any more; they live on a whole sheet of paper.

Pictures of arithmetic: Addition in the plane is the same as adding arrows (vectors) head to tail, the parallelogram rule from physics. If you draw 3 + 4i and 1 - 2i as arrows from the origin, their sum 4 + 2i is the diagonal of the parallelogram. Subtraction z₁ - z₂ is the arrow from z₂ to z₁, so its length is the distance between the two points. The conjugate is a mirror reflection in the real axis: 3 + 4i reflects to 3 - 4i. Multiplication by i rotates a point 90 degrees anticlockwise: i(3 + 4i) = 3i + 4i² = -4 + 3i. Point (3, 4) has turned into (-4, 3), a quarter turn. This geometric meaning of multiplication is so important it gets its own lesson next.

Real life example 1, a mobile tower signal: Grameenphone engineers deal with radio waves. A wave at a fixed frequency is fully described by two numbers: how strong it is (amplitude) and where in its cycle it is (phase). Engineers pack these two numbers into one complex number called a phasor. When two signals from two antennas meet at your phone, their phasors simply add, like we added 3 + 4i and 1 - 2i. If they point in similar directions, the signal gets stronger. If they point in opposite directions, they cancel and you get a dead spot in your room. Complex addition is literally how engineers predict where you get good network.

Real life example 2, electric circuits: In AC circuits, like the electricity in your home at 50 Hz in Bangladesh, a resistor, a coil and a capacitor all resist current in different ways. A resistor's resistance is real, say 4 ohms. A coil's effect (reactance) is written as an imaginary number, say 3j ohms. The total impedance is Z = 4 + 3j ohms, a complex number. Its size, which you will learn to calculate next lesson, is 5 ohms. Using complex numbers, circuit problems that would need messy trigonometry become simple arithmetic like the examples above.

Real life example 3, computer graphics: Because multiplying by a complex number rotates points, some graphics and game programs use complex numbers for 2D rotation. To turn a character in a mobile game by 90 degrees, multiply its position by i. There is a 3D cousin of complex numbers called quaternions, used in game engines and drones to handle rotation smoothly. So the idea you learned today travels all the way to Unity and drone flight controllers.

Where students go wrong: The most common mistake is forgetting that i² = -1 while multiplying, so they write 3 - 6i + 4i - 8i² = 3 - 2i - 8 instead of 3 - 2i + 8. Second, saying Im(3 + 4i) = 4i, when it is just 4. Third, dividing by multiplying with the conjugate of the top instead of the bottom. Fourth, trying to say one complex number is "greater" than another. Fifth, writing √(-4) × √(-9) = √36 = 6. That rule does not work for negatives! Correct is 2i × 3i = 6i² = -6.

What exams ask: Typical questions are: simplify (2 + 3i)/(1 - i) into the form a + ib; find the real and imaginary parts of an expression; find i raised to a large power; solve for real x and y when x + iy = some expression, by comparing parts; plot given numbers on the Argand plane and describe the conjugate or rotation by i. Practise each type once and you are already ahead.

Quick recap: We invented i with i² = -1 so that equations like x² + 1 = 0 have solutions. A complex number z = x + iy has a real part x and an imaginary part y. We add part by part, multiply by expanding and using i² = -1, and divide by multiplying top and bottom with the conjugate of the bottom. The conjugate flips the sign of the imaginary part, and z z̄ = x² + y² is real. Every complex number is a point on the Argand plane, where addition is adding arrows, the conjugate is a mirror image, and multiplication by i is a quarter turn. Next lesson we describe points using distance and angle, which unlocks Euler's famous formula.
key_points: i is defined by i² = -1; engineers often write j instead of i.
Powers of i repeat every 4: i, -1, -i, 1.
z = x + iy has real part x and imaginary part y (not iy).
Add part by part; multiply by expanding and replacing i² with -1.
Divide by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate of the bottom.
The conjugate z̄ = x - iy, and z z̄ = x² + y² is always real and non-negative.
On the Argand plane, z is the point (x, y); multiplying by i rotates it 90 degrees anticlockwise.
lessons.tip: After every division, multiply your answer back by the denominator. If you get the original top, you're right. This one habit saves marks in every exam.
lessons.task: On graph paper, plot z = 2 + i. Then plot iz, i²z and i³z. Join the four points. What shape do you get, and why?

quiz.q: What is i²⁰²⁶?
quiz.explain: 2026 leaves remainder 2 when divided by 4, so i²⁰²⁶ = i² = -1.

quiz.q: What is Im(3 + 4i)?
quiz.explain: The imaginary part is the real number y in x + iy, so it is 4, not 4i.

quiz.q: What is (3 + 4i)/(1 - 2i)?
quiz.explain: Multiply top and bottom by 1 + 2i: (-5 + 10i)/5 = -1 + 2i.

quiz.q: What does multiplying a complex number by i do on the Argand plane?
options: Reflects it in the real axis
quiz.explain: For example i(3 + 4i) = -4 + 3i, which is (3, 4) turned a quarter turn.

quiz.q: What is (3 + 4i)(3 - 4i)?
quiz.explain: z z̄ = x² + y² = 9 + 16 = 25, a real number.

lessons.title: Polar Form, Euler's Formula and De Moivre
lessons.content:
Think about how a ship's captain or a pilot gives a position. They rarely say "go 3 km east and 4 km north". They say "go 5 km on a bearing of so many degrees". Distance plus direction. Last lesson we described a complex number like a city grid: x steps right and y steps up. Today we describe the very same point like a pilot: how far it is from the centre, and at what angle. This second description, called the polar form, turns multiplication into something so easy it feels like cheating.

Modulus, the distance: The modulus of z = x + iy is its distance from the origin, written |z|. By Pythagoras, |z| = √(x² + y²). For z = 3 + 4i, |z| = √(9 + 16) = 5. For z = 1 + i, |z| = √2. For z = -5, |z| = 5, the same as the absolute value you already know. Notice that |z|² = x² + y² = z z̄, which connects modulus to the conjugate from lesson 1. That is the "size" of a complex number, and sizes are the only things we can compare. So |3 + 4i| = 5 is bigger than |1 + 2i| = √5.

Useful modulus rules: The modulus of a product is the product of moduli: |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂|. Same for quotients: |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂|. So |(3 + 4i)(1 + i)| = 5 × √2 without multiplying anything out. For sums there is only an inequality, the triangle inequality: |z₁ + z₂| ≤ |z₁| + |z₂|. In words, going straight is never longer than taking a detour. This inequality is a workhorse in later lessons when we estimate integrals.

Distance between two points: |z₁ - z₂| is the distance between the points z₁ and z₂. For example, the distance between 1 + 2i and 4 + 6i is |(4 + 6i) - (1 + 2i)| = |3 + 4i| = 5. This tiny fact lets us describe circles: all points z with |z - 2| = 3 form the circle of radius 3 centred at 2. We will use that heavily in the next lesson.

Argument, the angle: The argument of z, written arg z, is the angle the arrow from 0 to z makes with the positive real axis, measured anticlockwise, usually in radians. For z = 1 + i, the arrow points exactly halfway between the axes, so arg z = π/4 (45 degrees). For z = i, arg z = π/2. For z = -1, arg z = π. Because turning a full circle (2π) brings you back to the same direction, the argument is not unique: π/4, π/4 + 2π, π/4 - 2π all describe the same direction.

Principal argument: To have one standard answer, we pick the principal argument, written Arg z with a capital A, in the range -π < Arg z ≤ π. Some books use 0 ≤ arg < 2π, so check what your teacher uses, but -π to π is the most common convention. The number 0 has no argument at all, because the zero arrow points nowhere.

Finding the argument without mistakes: The formula tan θ = y/x is tempting but dangerous, because tan repeats every π, so it cannot tell 1 + i from -1 - i (both give y/x = 1). The safe method: first find the reference angle α = tan⁻¹(|y|/|x|), then look at the quadrant. First quadrant (x > 0, y > 0): θ = α. Second quadrant (x < 0, y > 0): θ = π - α. Third quadrant (x < 0, y < 0): θ = -(π - α). Fourth quadrant (x > 0, y < 0): θ = -α. Example: z = -1 + √3 i. Reference angle tan⁻¹(√3) = π/3. Second quadrant, so Arg z = π - π/3 = 2π/3. Example: z = -1 - i. Reference angle π/4, third quadrant, so Arg z = -3π/4. Programmers know this as atan2(y, x), a function that does the quadrant check for you.

Polar form: If r = |z| and θ = arg z, then x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ, so z = r(cos θ + i sin θ). Some books shorten cos θ + i sin θ to cis θ. For example 1 + i = √2 (cos π/4 + i sin π/4). And -2 = 2(cos π + i sin π). Converting back is easy: 4(cos π/3 + i sin π/3) = 4(1/2 + i √3/2) = 2 + 2√3 i.

Euler's formula: Here comes the most famous formula in this course: e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ. It was published by Leonhard Euler in the 1700s. One way to see why it is true is power series: e^x = 1 + x + x²/2! + x³/3! + ..., and if you put x = iθ and use the powers of i cycle from lesson 1, the even terms collect into the series for cos θ and the odd terms collect into i times the series for sin θ. So the polar form can be written very compactly as z = r e^(iθ). The number 1 + i becomes √2 e^(iπ/4).

The famous special case: Put θ = π: e^(iπ) = cos π + i sin π = -1 + 0 = -1. So e^(iπ) + 1 = 0, often called Euler's identity. It links five of the most important numbers in mathematics: 0, 1, e, i and π. Also, e^(iπ/2) = i and e^(2πi) = 1. Every number of the form e^(iθ) has modulus 1, so it lies on the unit circle. As θ grows, e^(iθ) runs around that circle anticlockwise like the tip of a clock hand moving backwards.

Multiplication becomes easy: Now the payoff. Multiply z₁ = r₁e^(iθ₁) and z₂ = r₂e^(iθ₂). Using the ordinary rule of exponents, z₁z₂ = r₁r₂ e^(i(θ₁ + θ₂)). In words: multiply the lengths and add the angles. That is why multiplying by i (length 1, angle π/2) is a pure 90 degree rotation. Multiplying by 2i doubles the length and rotates 90 degrees. Example: (1 + i)(1 + √3 i) = √2 e^(iπ/4) × 2 e^(iπ/3) = 2√2 e^(i7π/12). One warning: the sum of two principal arguments might go outside -π to π, so you may need to add or subtract 2π to get the principal value again.

Division: For division you divide the lengths and subtract the angles: z₁/z₂ = (r₁/r₂) e^(i(θ₁ - θ₂)). The conjugate in polar form is r e^(-iθ): same length, opposite angle, which is the mirror image we saw before. And 1/z = (1/r) e^(-iθ).

De Moivre's theorem: Multiply z by itself n times and you multiply the length n times and add the angle n times: (r e^(iθ))ⁿ = rⁿ e^(inθ). With r = 1 this gives De Moivre's theorem: (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ, true for every integer n. This turns horrible powers into easy ones. Example: find (1 + i)¹⁰. In polar form 1 + i = √2 e^(iπ/4). So (1 + i)¹⁰ = (√2)¹⁰ e^(i10π/4) = 32 e^(i5π/2). Now 5π/2 = 2π + π/2, so e^(i5π/2) = e^(iπ/2) = i. Answer: 32i. Try expanding (1 + i)¹⁰ with brackets and you will appreciate the shortcut.

Trig identities for free: De Moivre's theorem also produces trigonometry formulas. Take n = 2: (cos θ + i sin θ)² = cos 2θ + i sin 2θ. Expanding the left side gives cos²θ - sin²θ + 2i sin θ cos θ. Comparing real and imaginary parts: cos 2θ = cos²θ - sin²θ and sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ. The same trick with n = 3 gives the triple angle formulas, which are a classic exam question.

Cos and sin from exponentials: Add e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ and e^(-iθ) = cos θ - i sin θ, and you get cos θ = (e^(iθ) + e^(-iθ))/2. Subtract them and you get sin θ = (e^(iθ) - e^(-iθ))/(2i). These two formulas are the bridge to Fourier series later in the course, where every sine and cosine wave gets rewritten as exponentials because exponentials are easier to multiply, differentiate and integrate.

Real life example 1, the electricity in your house: The AC voltage in a Bangladeshi home goes up and down 50 times a second. It can be written as v(t) = V cos(ωt + φ), where ω = 2π × 50. Engineers write this as the real part of V e^(iφ) e^(iωt). The part V e^(iφ) is the phasor: a complex number in polar form whose length is the amplitude and whose angle is the phase. In the impedance example from lesson 1, Z = 4 + 3j has modulus 5 and argument tan⁻¹(3/4), about 36.9 degrees. So if 230 V is applied, the current has size 230/5 = 46 A and lags the voltage by about 36.9 degrees. Division of complex numbers in polar form did all the work.

Real life example 2, a game spinner: Suppose a Ludo app wants to animate a spinner arrow that turns 10 degrees every frame. Store the arrow tip as a complex number z and multiply by w = e^(i × 10°) every frame. After 36 frames, wⁿ = e^(i × 360°) = 1, so the arrow is back where it started, exactly as De Moivre predicts. Because |w| = 1, the arrow never grows or shrinks. In real code, tiny rounding errors can make the length drift, so programmers renormalise now and then, but the idea is pure complex multiplication.

Where students go wrong: Using θ = tan⁻¹(y/x) without checking the quadrant is the number one mistake; it gives the same angle for 1 + i and -1 - i. Second, forgetting to bring the final angle back into -π to π when a principal value is asked. Third, writing |z₁ + z₂| = |z₁| + |z₂|, which is only an inequality. Fourth, computing (√2)¹⁰ wrongly; remember (√2)¹⁰ = 2⁵ = 32. Fifth, mixing degrees and radians in the same line.

What exams ask: Express a number like -1 + √3 i or (1 + i)/(1 - i) in polar and exponential form; find modulus and principal argument; use De Moivre to compute a power such as (1 + i√3)⁸ or (√3 + i)⁶; derive cos 3θ and sin 3θ in terms of cos θ and sin θ; prove simple results with |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂| or the triangle inequality; and show e^(iπ) = -1.

Quick recap: The modulus |z| = √(x² + y²) is distance from the origin, and |z₁ - z₂| is the distance between two points. The argument is the angle with the positive real axis; the principal value lies in -π to π, and you must check the quadrant. Polar form z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r e^(iθ) comes from Euler's formula. Multiplying means multiply lengths and add angles; dividing means divide lengths and subtract angles. De Moivre's theorem turns big powers into easy work and also produces trig identities. Next lesson we run De Moivre backwards to find roots, and we learn to describe whole regions of the plane.
key_points: |z| = √(x² + y²) is the distance from 0, and |z₁ - z₂| is the distance between two points.
|z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂|, but for sums only the triangle inequality |z₁ + z₂| ≤ |z₁| + |z₂| holds.
The principal argument Arg z lies in -π < θ ≤ π; always check the quadrant.
Euler's formula: e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ, so z = r e^(iθ) and e^(iπ) = -1.
Multiply: multiply lengths, add angles. Divide: divide lengths, subtract angles.
De Moivre: (cos θ + i sin θ)ⁿ = cos nθ + i sin nθ for every integer n.
cos θ = (e^(iθ) + e^(-iθ))/2 and sin θ = (e^(iθ) - e^(-iθ))/(2i).
lessons.tip: Before writing any argument, draw a quick sketch of the point. Ten seconds of drawing tells you the quadrant and stops the most common mistake in this chapter.
lessons.task: On a calculator or phone, compute (cos 20° + i sin 20°) by hand for n = 1, then predict where the point lands after multiplying by itself 18 times. Check with De Moivre that it should be -1.

quiz.explain: Reference angle π/4 in the third quadrant gives -(π - π/4) = -3π/4.

When you multiply two complex numbers in polar form, what happens?
quiz.explain: r₁e^(iθ₁) × r₂e^(iθ₂) = r₁r₂ e^(i(θ₁ + θ₂)).

quiz.explain: cos π + i sin π = -1 + 0i.

lessons.title: Roots of Complex Numbers and Regions of the Plane
lessons.content:
Imagine cutting a round birthday cake into 6 equal slices. If you place the cake on a plate with its centre at 0, the cuts land at perfectly evenly spaced angles: every 60 degrees. Roots of complex numbers behave exactly like those cake slices. Ask for the 6th roots of 1 and you get six points sitting evenly around a circle. Today we learn to find these roots, and then we learn to describe whole regions of the plane, like a slice, a disk or a ring, using simple formulas. Both skills are needed for everything that comes later in complex integration.

How many roots? In real numbers, x² = 4 has two answers, 2 and -2, but x² = -4 has none. In complex numbers, the story becomes clean and fair: every non-zero complex number has exactly n different nth roots. So there are 2 square roots, 3 cube roots, 4 fourth roots, and so on, always. This is closely tied to the fundamental theorem of algebra, which says every polynomial of degree n has exactly n roots in the complex numbers when you count repeated ones. We will even prove that theorem in lesson 10.

Running De Moivre backwards: We want w with wⁿ = z. Write z = r e^(iθ). We know that powering multiplies the angle by n and raises the length to the power n. So to undo it, take the nth root of the length and divide the angle by n. But here is the clever part: the angle θ is the same direction as θ + 2π, θ + 4π, and so on. Dividing those different angles by n gives genuinely different directions. That is where the n different roots come from.

The formula: The nth roots of z = r e^(iθ) are w_k = r^(1/n) e^(i(θ + 2πk)/n), for k = 0, 1, 2, ..., n - 1. Here r^(1/n) is the ordinary positive real root of the length. After k = n - 1 the answers start repeating, because k = n just adds a full 2π. All n roots have the same length r^(1/n), so they all sit on one circle. And consecutive roots are separated by an angle of 2π/n. That is the cake: equal slices.

Worked example, cube roots of 8i: Write 8i in polar form: length 8, angle π/2. Cube root of the length: 2. Angles: (π/2 + 2πk)/3 for k = 0, 1, 2, giving π/6, 5π/6 and 3π/2 (which is the same direction as -π/2). So the three roots are 2e^(iπ/6) = √3 + i, 2e^(i5π/6) = -√3 + i, and 2e^(-iπ/2) = -2i. Quick check on the last one: (-2i)³ = -8 i³ = -8(-i) = 8i. Correct! The three points form an equilateral triangle on the circle of radius 2.

Square roots in Cartesian form: For square roots there is also an algebra method. Find √(3 + 4i). Let (a + ib)² = 3 + 4i. Then a² - b² = 3 and 2ab = 4. Also taking moduli, a² + b² = |3 + 4i| = 5. Adding a² - b² = 3 and a² + b² = 5 gives 2a² = 8, a = ±2, then b = 2/a = ±1 with the same sign. So the square roots are 2 + i and -2 - i. Check: (2 + i)² = 4 + 4i + i² = 3 + 4i. This method is quick when the numbers are nice.

Roots of unity: The nth roots of 1 are called the nth roots of unity. Since 1 = e^(i0), they are e^(2πik/n) for k = 0 to n - 1. Usually we write ω = e^(2πi/n), and then the roots are 1, ω, ω², ..., ω^(n-1). For n = 4 they are 1, i, -1, -i. For n = 3, ω = e^(2πi/3) = -1/2 + i√3/2, and the roots are 1, ω, ω². They form a regular triangle, square, pentagon, and so on, inscribed in the unit circle.

The key facts about roots of unity: First, the sum of all nth roots of unity is 0 when n is at least 2. For cube roots: 1 + ω + ω² = 0. You can see it physically: the arrows are perfectly balanced around the centre, like three people pulling a rope in three equal directions. Second, their product is (-1)^(n+1). Third, ω^n = 1, so powers of ω repeat every n steps, just like powers of i repeat every 4 (i is a 4th root of unity!). Exam questions often ask you to prove 1 + ω + ω² = 0, or to simplify (1 + ω - ω²)³ using it.

Why roots of unity matter in CSE: The Fast Fourier Transform, one of the most important algorithms ever, uses exactly these points. To compute a Fourier transform of N samples, the FFT evaluates things at the N roots of unity, and the clever symmetry ω^(k + N/2) = -ω^k (for even N) lets it split the work in half again and again. That reduces the work from about N² operations to about N log N. Fast polynomial multiplication and big number multiplication use the same trick. So the cake slices you just learned are inside every music app and image compressor.

Solving equations: Roots help with polynomial equations. Solve z⁴ + 16 = 0. Then z⁴ = -16 = 16 e^(iπ). Fourth root of 16 is 2. Angles (π + 2πk)/4 = π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4, 7π/4. So the roots are 2e^(iπ/4) = √2 + √2 i, and similarly -√2 + √2 i, -√2 - √2 i, √2 - √2 i. Four points on the circle of radius 2, like the corners of a tilted square. Another useful fact: when a polynomial has real coefficients, its non-real roots come in conjugate pairs. You can see that here: √2 + √2 i and √2 - √2 i both appear.

Now, regions of the plane: Much of complex analysis talks about "for all z in some region". So we need a language for regions. The basic tool is distance: |z - a| is the distance from z to a. With it we can draw many shapes using a single line of math.

Circles and disks: |z - a| = r is the circle of radius r centred at a. |z - a| < r is the open disk: all points strictly inside the circle. |z - a| ≤ r is the closed disk, inside plus the boundary. For example |z - (1 + i)| < 2 is the inside of a circle of radius 2 centred at the point (1, 1). The open disk |z - a| < ε for a small ε is called a neighbourhood of a, and you will meet it again when we define limits.

Rings, called annuli: r₁ < |z - a| < r₂ is the ring between two circles with the same centre. For example 1 < |z| < 3 is a washer-shaped region, like a round bangle or a vada with a hole. Annuli become very important in lesson 11, where Laurent series live exactly in such rings.

Half-planes and lines: Re(z) > 0 is the right half-plane: every point to the right of the imaginary axis. Im(z) < 1 is everything below the horizontal line y = 1. |z - 1| = |z + 1| means points equally far from 1 and -1, which is the perpendicular bisector, here the imaginary axis. Arg z = π/4 is a ray from the origin. And 0 < Arg z < π/2 is the open first quadrant, a wedge. You can turn any of these into x and y form by putting z = x + iy. For example |z - 1| = |z + 1| gives (x - 1)² + y² = (x + 1)² + y², which simplifies to x = 0.

Open, closed, connected, domain: A set is open if every point has a little disk around it that stays inside the set; strict inequalities like |z| < 1 usually give open sets. A set is closed if it contains its boundary, like |z| ≤ 1. A set is connected if you can walk from any point to any other without leaving it. An open connected set is called a domain (some books say region). Most big theorems in this course, such as Cauchy's theorem, are stated for functions on domains. A domain with no holes is called simply connected: the disk |z| < 1 is simply connected, the ring 1 < |z| < 2 is not, because a loop around the hole cannot be shrunk to a point without leaving the ring. Remember that hole picture; it explains the whole residue story later.

Real life example 1, a Wi-Fi router's antenna pattern: Imagine a router at the origin with a signal strong enough within 20 metres. The covered area is |z| < 20 if we treat the floor plan as the complex plane. A second router at 30 + 0i covers |z - 30| < 20. The region where both overlap, where your phone might hop between them, is the intersection of two disks. Engineers planning Wi-Fi in a university like KUET or BUET sketch exactly these overlapping disks to avoid dead zones.

Real life example 2, signal constellations: When your phone sends data over 4G, it uses schemes such as QPSK, where each pair of bits is sent as one of four complex numbers, for example points at angles π/4, 3π/4, 5π/4 and 7π/4 on a circle, just like the roots of z⁴ = -16 we found (scaled). The receiver gets a noisy point and decides which of the four it was by finding which point is nearest: it simply compares distances |received - candidate|. That is a "region" decision: each candidate owns a quarter of the plane. Higher speed schemes like 16-QAM use 16 points on a grid instead.

Where students go wrong: Giving only one root when n roots exist; this is the most common error. Forgetting the 2πk and getting the same root n times. Taking the nth root of the angle instead of dividing the angle by n. Mixing up |z - a| < r (inside) with |z - a| > r (outside). Forgetting that |z + 2| = 3 is centred at -2, not +2, because z + 2 = z - (-2). And confusing open (strict inequality) with closed (≤) sets.

What exams ask: Find all cube roots or fourth roots of a number and plot them; solve equations like z⁵ = 1 or z³ + 8 = 0; prove 1 + ω + ω² = 0 and use it; find square roots by the a + ib method; sketch regions like |z - 2 + i| ≤ 3, 1 < |z| < 2, Re(z) ≥ 1, or |z - 1| = |z - i| and say whether they are open, closed, bounded, or domains.

Quick recap: Every non-zero complex number has exactly n nth roots, given by w_k = r^(1/n) e^(i(θ + 2πk)/n) for k = 0 to n - 1. They sit evenly on a circle, separated by 2π/n, like slices of cake. The nth roots of unity, 1, ω, ..., ω^(n-1), sum to zero and power the Fast Fourier Transform. Regions are described with distance: |z - a| < r is a disk, r₁ < |z - a| < r₂ is a ring, Re z > 0 is a half-plane. Open connected sets are domains, and domains with no holes are simply connected. Next lesson we build the famous complex functions: exponential, sine, cosine and logarithm.
key_points: Every non-zero complex number has exactly n distinct nth roots.
nth roots: w_k = r^(1/n) e^(i(θ + 2πk)/n), k = 0, 1, ..., n - 1, evenly spaced by 2π/n on one circle.
Roots of unity: 1, ω, ..., ω^(n-1) with ω = e^(2πi/n); their sum is 0 (n ≥ 2), e.g. 1 + ω + ω² = 0.
Roots of unity power the Fast Fourier Transform, cutting work from about N² to N log N.
|z - a| < r is an open disk, r₁ < |z - a| < r₂ is an annulus, Re z > 0 is a half-plane.
A domain is an open connected set; a simply connected domain has no holes.
lessons.tip: Always draw your roots. If they are not evenly spaced on one circle, you made a mistake somewhere, and the picture tells you instantly.
lessons.task: Take a paper plate or draw a circle. Mark the 5th roots of unity by stepping 72 degrees each time. Draw arrows from the centre to each and convince yourself they balance to zero.

quiz.q: How many distinct cube roots does 8i have?
quiz.explain: Every non-zero complex number has exactly n nth roots, so 3 cube roots.

quiz.q: If ω is a non-real cube root of unity, what is 1 + ω + ω²?
quiz.explain: The roots of unity are balanced around the centre, so their sum is 0.

quiz.q: Which region does |z + 2| < 3 describe?
options: Outside of a circle centred at -2
Open disk of radius 3 centred at -2
quiz.explain: z + 2 = z - (-2), so it is the distance from -2, and < means strictly inside.

quiz.q: What is the angle between two neighbouring 6th roots of a number?
quiz.explain: Neighbouring nth roots are separated by 2π/n = 2π/6 = π/3.

quiz.q: Why is the annulus 1 < |z| < 2 not simply connected?
options: A loop around the hole cannot shrink to a point inside it
quiz.explain: The ring has a hole in the middle, so loops around it cannot be shrunk inside the region.

lessons.title: Elementary Complex Functions: exp, sin, cos and log
lessons.content:
Think about a photocopy machine that can stretch, shrink and twist a picture. You put in a drawing, and out comes a changed drawing. A complex function is like that machine for points on the plane: you feed in a point z, and it gives back another point w = f(z). In ordinary school maths, a function like y = x² takes a number on a line to a number on a line, so you can draw its graph. A complex function takes a point on a plane to a point on another plane, which needs four dimensions to graph, so we think of it as a machine that moves points around instead. Today we meet the most important machines: polynomials, the exponential, sine and cosine, the hyperbolic functions, and the logarithm.

Writing a function as u + iv: Any complex function can be split into a real part and an imaginary part, each depending on x and y: f(z) = u(x, y) + i v(x, y). Take f(z) = z². With z = x + iy, z² = x² - y² + 2ixy. So u = x² - y² and v = 2xy. For f(z) = 1/z, we get 1/(x + iy) = (x - iy)/(x² + y²), so u = x/(x² + y²) and v = -y/(x² + y²). Splitting into u and v is the first step in almost every problem of the next few lessons, so practise it until it is automatic.

Polynomials and rational functions: Polynomials like f(z) = 3z³ - 2z + 5 are defined for every z, and rational functions like (z + 1)/(z² + 4) are defined everywhere except where the bottom is zero, here at z = 2i and z = -2i. Those bad points will later be called poles. Notice that z² + 4 has no real roots, but it has complex ones. That is a hint of something we will see often: a function can look perfectly fine on the real line but have trouble spots hiding off the axis, and those hidden spots control its behaviour.

The complex exponential: We define e^z for z = x + iy as e^z = e^x (cos y + i sin y). This is forced on us by Euler's formula: e^(x + iy) should equal e^x × e^(iy). So the real part x controls the size, |e^z| = e^x, and the imaginary part y controls the angle, arg e^z = y. Example: e^(1 + iπ/2) = e × (cos π/2 + i sin π/2) = ei. And e^(iπ) = -1, as before.

Properties of e^z: The usual rule e^(z₁ + z₂) = e^(z₁) e^(z₂) still holds. e^z is never zero, because its size e^x is always positive. But here is a big surprise: e^z is periodic! Since cos and sin repeat every 2π, e^(z + 2πi) = e^z. So the exponential repeats every time you move 2π up the imaginary direction. On the real line e^x never repeats, so this behaviour is completely new. It means e^z = 1 does not only have the solution z = 0; it has the solutions z = 2πik for every integer k.

Complex sine and cosine: From lesson 2 we know cos θ = (e^(iθ) + e^(-iθ))/2 for real θ. We simply use this as the definition for complex z: cos z = (e^(iz) + e^(-iz))/2 and sin z = (e^(iz) - e^(-iz))/(2i). For real z these give the usual sin and cos. The familiar identities still hold: sin²z + cos²z = 1, sin(z₁ + z₂) = sin z₁ cos z₂ + cos z₁ sin z₂, and both are periodic with period 2π. The derivatives also stay the same: (sin z)' = cos z and (cos z)' = -sin z.

The big surprise, sine can be huge: For real x, sin x always stays between -1 and 1. For complex z, that is no longer true! Try cos(i) = (e^(i·i) + e^(-i·i))/2 = (e^(-1) + e^(1))/2, which is about 1.543. And cos(3i) = (e^(-3) + e^3)/2, about 10.07. As you go up the imaginary axis, cos grows like an exponential. So in complex land, sin z = 5 has solutions, even though for real numbers it is impossible. Exam questions love "solve cos z = 2" for exactly this reason.

Hyperbolic functions: The hyperbolic cosine and sine are cosh z = (e^z + e^(-z))/2 and sinh z = (e^z - e^(-z))/2. You may have met them in Math I. Compare with cos and sin and you will see they are rotations of each other: cos(iz) = cosh z and sin(iz) = i sinh z. Also cosh²z - sinh²z = 1, with a minus where cos and sin had a plus. These relations let us split cos and sin into real and imaginary parts: sin(x + iy) = sin x cosh y + i cos x sinh y, and cos(x + iy) = cos x cosh y - i sin x sinh y. The cosh y factor is why sine and cosine blow up as y grows.

Worked example, solve cos z = 2: Let w = e^(iz). Then (w + 1/w)/2 = 2, so w² - 4w + 1 = 0, which gives w = 2 ± √3. Now e^(iz) = 2 ± √3. Both numbers are positive real, so taking logs: iz = ln(2 ± √3) + 2πik. Since 2 - √3 = 1/(2 + √3), ln(2 - √3) = -ln(2 + √3). So z = 2πk ± i ln(2 + √3), about 2πk ± 1.317i. Check: cos(1.317i) = cosh(1.317), which is about 2. The solutions sit above and below the real axis, never on it, which makes sense since real cosine never reaches 2.

The logarithm, the tricky one: We want log z to undo the exponential: if e^w = z, then w = log z. Write z = r e^(iθ) and w = u + iv. Then e^u e^(iv) = r e^(iθ), so e^u = r, meaning u = ln r, and v = θ + 2πk. So log z = ln|z| + i arg z. Because arg z has infinitely many values, log z also has infinitely many values, each differing by 2πi. Example: log(-1) = ln 1 + i(π + 2πk) = iπ(2k + 1). So log(-1) can be iπ, 3iπ, -iπ, and so on. This is what we call a multi-valued function.

Principal value and branches: To get one answer, we use the principal argument: Log z = ln|z| + i Arg z, with -π < Arg z ≤ π. This is the principal value, written with a capital L. So Log(-1) = iπ, Log(i) = iπ/2 and Log(1 + i) = ln √2 + iπ/4 = (1/2) ln 2 + iπ/4. The principal logarithm jumps when you cross the negative real axis: just above it the angle is near π, just below it near -π. That line is called a branch cut, and z = 0 is called a branch point, because circling around it changes the value of log. Picking one consistent set of values is choosing a branch. Log z is perfectly smooth everywhere except on the branch cut and at 0.

Careful with log rules: In real numbers ln(ab) = ln a + ln b always. With principal values, Log(z₁z₂) = Log z₁ + Log z₂ can fail! Example: z₁ = z₂ = -1. Log(1) = 0, but Log(-1) + Log(-1) = 2iπ. The rule holds for multi-valued log (as a set of values), but with principal values it only works if the sum of the arguments stays in -π to π. Watch for this in true/false questions.

Complex powers: How do we define something like i^i? We use z^c = e^(c log z). Since log i = i(π/2 + 2πk), i^i = e^(i × i(π/2 + 2πk)) = e^(-(π/2 + 2πk)). Astonishing: every value of i^i is a real number! The principal value is e^(-π/2), about 0.2079. Complex powers are usually multi-valued, and the principal value uses Log. For integer powers like z³ the multi-valuedness disappears, and for c = 1/n you get the n roots from lesson 3 again.

Real life example 1, decaying oscillations: When you pluck a guitar string or hit a cup in a tea stall, the sound vibrates and slowly dies. Engineers model it as e^(st) with a complex s = -a + iω. Then e^(st) = e^(-at)(cos ωt + i sin ωt). The real part -a makes it shrink (the fading), and the imaginary part ω makes it wiggle (the pitch). One complex exponential describes both behaviours. This is exactly how the Laplace transform, at the end of this course, thinks about every signal.

Real life example 2, the decibel and phase meter: Audio engineers working on a podcast in a Dhaka studio measure how a filter changes a sound. The filter multiplies each frequency by a complex number H. Taking the logarithm, Log H = ln|H| + i Arg H, splits it neatly into two useful parts: ln|H| tells how much louder or quieter (gain, usually turned into decibels), and Arg H tells how much the wave is delayed (phase). Bode plots, which you will see in Signals & Systems and Control, are exactly graphs of these two parts.

Where students go wrong: Assuming |sin z| ≤ 1 for complex z. Forgetting that e^z is periodic with period 2πi, and so writing only z = 0 for e^z = 1. Writing log(-1) is "undefined" as you would in school; in complex numbers it is iπ (principal). Using Log(z₁z₂) = Log z₁ + Log z₂ without checking. Forgetting that the principal argument decides the principal log, so Log(-1 - i) uses -3π/4, not 5π/4. And splitting e^(x + iy) as e^x + e^(iy), which is wrong; it is a product.

What exams ask: Express sin z, cos z, e^z or z² in the form u + iv; prove that |sin z|² = sin²x + sinh²y; solve cos z = 2, sin z = 2 or e^z = 1 + i; find all values and the principal value of log(-1 - i) or (1 + i)^i; show e^z is periodic; and show that Log(z₁z₂) is not always Log z₁ + Log z₂.

Quick recap: A complex function moves points of the plane, and splits as f = u + iv. The exponential e^z = e^x(cos y + i sin y) is never zero and has period 2πi. Sine and cosine are defined through exponentials, keep their identities and derivatives, but are not bounded. Hyperbolic functions are their rotated cousins. The logarithm log z = ln|z| + i arg z is multi-valued; the principal value Log z uses Arg z and has a branch cut along the negative real axis. Complex powers are defined by z^c = e^(c log z), which is why i^i is real. Next lesson we ask a deeper question: what does it mean for a complex function to have a derivative?
key_points: Any complex function splits as f(z) = u(x, y) + i v(x, y); for z², u = x² - y² and v = 2xy.
e^z = e^x(cos y + i sin y): |e^z| = e^x, never zero, and periodic with period 2πi.
cos z = (e^(iz) + e^(-iz))/2 and sin z = (e^(iz) - e^(-iz))/(2i); they are not bounded for complex z.
cos(iz) = cosh z and sin(iz) = i sinh z; sin(x + iy) = sin x cosh y + i cos x sinh y.
log z = ln|z| + i arg z is multi-valued; principal Log z uses Arg z in (-π, π] with a branch cut on the negative real axis.
Complex powers: z^c = e^(c log z); for example the principal value of i^i is e^(-π/2), a real number.
lessons.tip: Whenever you see sin, cos or a power of a complex number, rewrite it in exponentials first. Almost every proof in this chapter becomes algebra once you do.
lessons.task: With a calculator that handles complex numbers (or Python: import cmath), compute cmath.cos(3j), cmath.log(-1) and (1j)**(1j). Compare with the values in this lesson.

quiz.q: What is the period of e^z?
quiz.explain: e^(z + 2πi) = e^z (cos and sin of y repeat every 2π).

quiz.q: What is the principal value Log(-1)?
quiz.explain: Log(-1) = ln 1 + i Arg(-1) = iπ.

quiz.q: Which statement about sin z for complex z is true?
options: sin z can take any size, e.g. sin z = 5 has solutions
quiz.explain: sin(x + iy) contains cosh y and sinh y, which grow without bound.

quiz.q: What is the principal value of i^i?
quiz.explain: i^i = e^(i Log i) = e^(i × iπ/2) = e^(-π/2).

quiz.q: What is |e^(3 + 4i)|?
quiz.explain: |e^z| = e^x, where x = Re z = 3.

lessons.title: Limits, Continuity and the Complex Derivative
lessons.content:
Imagine you are walking towards the Shaheed Minar. On a straight road you can only come from two directions: from the front or from behind. But in an open field you could walk in from the north, from the east, in a spiral, in a zigzag, from any direction at all. A limit in ordinary calculus is the straight road: x can only approach a point from the left or the right. A limit in complex analysis is the open field: z can approach a point from infinitely many directions. That one difference makes the complex derivative much stricter, and, as a reward, functions that pass the test become unbelievably well behaved. This lesson builds the idea of limit, continuity and the complex derivative carefully, because the rest of the course leans on it.

Limits, the idea: We say the limit of f(z) as z approaches z₀ is L, written lim f(z) = L, if f(z) gets as close as we like to L whenever z is close enough to z₀ (but not equal to it). Closeness is measured by distance |f(z) - L| and |z - z₀|. In the formal version: for every ε > 0 there is a δ > 0 such that 0 < |z - z₀| < δ implies |f(z) - L| < ε. In words: whatever small target circle you draw around L, I can find a small circle around z₀ whose points all land inside your target. This is the same definition as in real calculus, but now the circles are real circles in a plane.

The key point, every direction must agree: Because z can come from any direction, the limit exists only if f(z) approaches the same L along every possible path. If two different paths give two different answers, the limit does not exist. This gives us a quick way to prove a limit does not exist: find two paths with different answers.

Example, a limit that fails: Consider f(z) = z̄/z as z approaches 0. Along the real axis, z = x, so z̄ = x and f = x/x = 1. Along the imaginary axis, z = iy, so z̄ = -iy and f = -iy/(iy) = -1. Two paths, two different answers, so the limit does not exist. A good habit: try the real axis, the imaginary axis, and the line y = x (or y = mx). If they disagree, you are done.

Example, a limit that works: The limit of z² as z approaches 1 + i. Polynomials are continuous, so we can just substitute: (1 + i)² = 1 + 2i + i² = 2i. And the limit of (z² + 1)/(z - i) as z approaches i? Substituting gives 0/0, so first factor: z² + 1 = (z - i)(z + i). Cancel the (z - i) and you get z + i, whose limit at i is 2i. This is exactly like the factoring trick from school limits.

Limit rules: The usual rules still work: the limit of a sum is the sum of the limits, the limit of a product is the product, and the limit of a quotient is the quotient as long as the bottom limit is not zero. Also, f(z) = u + iv tends to L = a + ib exactly when u tends to a and v tends to b. So a complex limit is really two real limits of functions of two variables, which you met in Math II.

Continuity: A function f is continuous at z₀ if f(z₀) is defined, the limit exists, and the limit equals f(z₀). In short: no jumps, no holes. Polynomials are continuous everywhere. Rational functions are continuous everywhere except where the denominator is zero. e^z, sin z and cos z are continuous everywhere. Log z is continuous everywhere except at 0 and along the branch cut on the negative real axis, where its imaginary part jumps from π to near -π. Sums, products and compositions of continuous functions are continuous.

Limits at infinity: In complex analysis there is only one infinity, not plus and minus infinity. As |z| grows without bound in any direction, we say z tends to infinity. For example 1/z tends to 0 as z tends to infinity. Some books picture this using the Riemann sphere, where the whole plane is wrapped onto a ball and infinity is the single north pole. You only need the idea: "large |z|" is one place.

The complex derivative: The derivative of f at z₀ is defined exactly like in school: f'(z₀) = lim (f(z₀ + Δz) - f(z₀))/Δz as Δz tends to 0. The formula looks identical, but Δz is now a tiny complex number that can come from any direction. The derivative exists only if this limit is the same for every direction. That is a far stronger demand than in real calculus.

Example, z² is differentiable everywhere: ((z + Δz)² - z²)/Δz = (2zΔz + Δz²)/Δz = 2z + Δz. As Δz goes to 0 from any direction, this goes to 2z. So (z²)' = 2z, just like real calculus. The same algebra shows (zⁿ)' = n z^(n-1) for any whole number n.

Example, z̄ is differentiable nowhere: Take f(z) = z̄. Then (f(z + Δz) - f(z))/Δz = Δz̄/Δz, where Δz̄ is the conjugate of Δz. From the limit example above, this is 1 along the real direction and -1 along the imaginary direction. The limit never exists, at any point. So f(z) = z̄, a perfectly smooth and continuous function (it is just a mirror reflection), has no complex derivative anywhere. This is the most famous example in the chapter, and it shows that being smooth as a map of the plane is not enough.

Another example, |z|²: Let f(z) = |z|² = z z̄. One can check that the difference quotient is z̄ + Δz̄ + z(Δz̄/Δz). As Δz goes to 0, the first two terms go to z̄, but the last term still depends on the direction unless z = 0. So |z|² is differentiable only at the single point z = 0, with derivative 0. Functions can be differentiable at isolated points without being nice anywhere around them. That is why the next lesson introduces a stronger idea, analyticity, which asks for differentiability in a whole neighbourhood.

Differentiation rules: The good news: all your familiar rules carry over. (f + g)' = f' + g'. (fg)' = f'g + fg'. (f/g)' = (f'g - fg')/g² where g is not zero. The chain rule (f(g(z)))' = f'(g(z)) g'(z). And the standard derivatives: (zⁿ)' = n z^(n-1), (e^z)' = e^z, (sin z)' = cos z, (cos z)' = -sin z, and (Log z)' = 1/z wherever Log is continuous (away from 0 and the branch cut). Example: d/dz of e^(z²) is 2z e^(z²). Example: d/dz of (z + 1)/(z - 1) is ((z - 1) - (z + 1))/(z - 1)² = -2/(z - 1)², valid for z ≠ 1.

Worked example, the derivative of 1/z from the definition: Let f(z) = 1/z with z not equal to 0. Then f(z + Δz) - f(z) = 1/(z + Δz) - 1/z = (z - (z + Δz))/(z(z + Δz)) = -Δz/(z(z + Δz)). Divide by Δz and the Δz on top cancels, leaving -1/(z(z + Δz)). Now let Δz go to 0 from any direction you like: the answer is always -1/z². Notice that Δz vanished from the ratio before we took the limit, so the direction could not matter. That is the sign of a well-behaved function. So 1/z is differentiable at every point except z = 0, where it is not even defined. Points like this, where a nice function suddenly breaks down, are called singularities, and they will become the stars of the show later in the course when we study residues. A second quick one: for f(z) = z³, the ratio becomes 3z² + 3zΔz + Δz², which tends to 3z² from every direction.

Differentiable means continuous: Just like in real calculus, if f has a derivative at a point, then f is continuous there. The reverse is false: z̄ is continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere. Keep that pair of facts as a mental check.

Real life example 1, a GPS tracker on a CNG: Imagine a CNG auto-rickshaw with a GPS tracker. Its position on the map at time t is a complex number z(t) = x(t) + i y(t). Here the input t is real but the output is complex. The derivative z'(t) = x'(t) + i y'(t) is the velocity: its modulus is the speed and its argument is the direction of travel. A ride-sharing app such as Pathao computes exactly this kind of quantity from the stream of GPS points to show your driver's heading. This kind of derivative (real input, complex output) is easy; it is the derivative with a complex input that has the strict "every direction" rule.

Real life example 2, smooth maps in image warping: Photo apps that bend images, like the "bulge" or "swirl" effect, are maps from the plane to the plane. If the warping map is given by a complex-differentiable function, then near each point it acts like multiplication by the complex number f'(z): a pure rotation plus a uniform zoom. That means tiny shapes keep their angles and do not get squashed into ellipses. We will study this property, called conformality, in lesson 8. A map like z̄ flips orientation, and many other smooth maps squash circles into ellipses; they are not complex-differentiable.

Where students go wrong: Checking only one path and declaring a limit exists; two equal paths prove nothing, but two different paths prove non-existence. Believing a function is differentiable just because its real and imaginary parts are smooth in x and y; z̄ has u = x and v = -y, both as smooth as can be, yet no derivative. Forgetting that the derivative of Log z fails on the branch cut. And mixing up "continuous" and "differentiable" in true/false questions.

What exams ask: Show that a limit like lim z̄/z or lim (x y)/(x² + y²) as z tends to 0 does not exist; evaluate limits by substitution or factoring; discuss continuity of a piecewise-defined function at 0; prove from the definition that zⁿ or 1/z is differentiable and find its derivative; show from the definition that z̄ or |z|² is not differentiable (except |z|² at 0); and differentiate using rules, like (z² + 1)³ or e^(sin z).

Quick recap: Complex limits require the same answer from every direction of approach; two paths with different answers prove the limit does not exist. Continuity means no jumps or holes, and polynomials, e^z, sin z and cos z are continuous everywhere. The complex derivative f'(z₀) = lim (f(z₀ + Δz) - f(z₀))/Δz uses the same formula as in school, but must agree for every direction of Δz. z² and every polynomial pass, while z̄ fails everywhere and |z|² passes only at 0. All the usual differentiation rules work. Next lesson we turn this strict direction test into simple equations, the Cauchy-Riemann equations, and meet analytic functions.
key_points: A complex limit must give the same value along every path of approach.
Two paths with different limits prove the limit does not exist; e.g. z̄/z at 0 gives 1 and -1.
Continuous means the limit exists and equals the function value: no jumps, no holes.
f'(z₀) = lim (f(z₀ + Δz) - f(z₀))/Δz, and Δz may approach 0 from any direction.
z² and all polynomials are differentiable everywhere; z̄ is differentiable nowhere; |z|² only at 0.
Sum, product, quotient and chain rules, and derivatives of e^z, sin z, cos z, Log z, work as in real calculus.
lessons.tip: To kill a limit, test three paths: real axis, imaginary axis, and y = mx. Keep m as a letter; if the answer depends on m, the limit does not exist.
lessons.task: Write the difference quotient Δz̄/Δz for Δz = 0.01, 0.01i and 0.01(1 + i). Compute each by hand and see that you get three different numbers.

quiz.q: Why does lim z̄/z as z → 0 not exist?
options: Because it gives 1 along the real axis and -1 along the imaginary axis
quiz.explain: Different paths give different values, so no single limit exists.

quiz.q: Where is f(z) = z̄ complex-differentiable?
quiz.explain: Δz̄/Δz depends on the direction of Δz at every point.

quiz.q: What is the derivative of (z + 1)/(z - 1)?
quiz.explain: Quotient rule: ((z - 1) - (z + 1))/(z - 1)² = -2/(z - 1)².

quiz.q: Where is |z|² complex-differentiable?
quiz.explain: The direction-dependent term vanishes only when z = 0.

quiz.q: Which statement is true?
options: Differentiable at a point implies continuous there
Real and imaginary parts being smooth guarantees a complex derivative
quiz.explain: Differentiability implies continuity, but not the other way; z̄ is the counterexample.

lessons.title: Analytic Functions and the Cauchy-Riemann Equations
lessons.content:
Last lesson we learned a tough rule: a complex derivative only exists if the ratio (f(z + Δz) - f(z))/Δz gives the same answer from every direction. Checking every direction by hand would take forever. Imagine a teacher who checks a whole class's homework by asking every student one by one. Slow! A smart teacher uses a quick test instead. The Cauchy-Riemann equations are exactly that quick test. Two short equations, and you instantly know whether a complex function can be differentiated. Functions that pass the test everywhere in a region are called analytic, and they are the heroes of this whole course.

Splitting f into two real functions: Any complex function can be written as f(z) = u(x, y) + i v(x, y), where z = x + iy. Here u is the real part and v is the imaginary part, and both are ordinary real functions of two variables. For example, f(z) = z² = (x + iy)² = x² - y² + i(2xy), so u = x² - y² and v = 2xy. For f(z) = z̄ = x - iy we get u = x and v = -y. Once a function is split like this, we can use partial derivatives from multivariable calculus: u_x means the derivative of u with respect to x while y is held fixed, and so on.

Where the equations come from: Suppose f is differentiable at a point. Then the limit is the same from every direction, so in particular it is the same from two easy directions. First let Δz = Δx be purely real (move horizontally). The ratio becomes (Δu + iΔv)/Δx, which tends to u_x + i v_x. Next let Δz = iΔy be purely imaginary (move vertically). The ratio becomes (Δu + iΔv)/(iΔy), which tends to (1/i)(u_y + i v_y) = v_y - i u_y. These two answers must be equal. Matching real parts gives u_x = v_y. Matching imaginary parts gives v_x = -u_y.

The Cauchy-Riemann equations: So we get the famous pair: u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x. A handy way to remember them: 'u x equals v y, and u y equals minus v x'. Some students remember the minus sign by saying 'the minus goes with the v x'. If f is differentiable at a point, these equations must hold there. And as a bonus, the derivative is easy to compute: f'(z) = u_x + i v_x. You can also write it as f'(z) = v_y - i u_y; both give the same number when the equations hold.

Necessary, and when sufficient: The Cauchy-Riemann (CR) equations are necessary: if they fail at a point, f is definitely not differentiable there. But passing them alone is not quite enough. The textbook warning example is f(z) = sqrt(|xy|): at the origin all four partial derivatives are 0, so the CR equations hold, yet along the line y = x the ratio does not go to 0, so f is not differentiable at 0. The fix is a sufficiency theorem: if u and v have continuous first partial derivatives near a point and satisfy the CR equations at that point, then f is differentiable there. In practice, for functions built from polynomials, exponentials, sines and cosines, the partials are continuous, so checking the CR equations is all you need.

Example 1, z² passes: u = x² - y², v = 2xy. Then u_x = 2x and v_y = 2x, equal. u_y = -2y and v_x = 2y, so u_y = -v_x. Both equations hold for every x and y, and the partials are continuous, so z² is differentiable everywhere. The derivative is f' = u_x + i v_x = 2x + i2y = 2z, just like in school.

Example 2, z̄ fails: u = x, v = -y. Then u_x = 1 but v_y = -1. The first equation fails at every point, so z̄ is differentiable nowhere. This matches what we found last lesson the slow way, by trying two directions. The CR test reached the same answer in one line.

Example 3, e^z passes: e^z = e^x e^(iy) = e^x cos y + i e^x sin y. So u = e^x cos y and v = e^x sin y. u_x = e^x cos y and v_y = e^x cos y, equal. u_y = -e^x sin y and v_x = e^x sin y, so u_y = -v_x. Passed everywhere. The derivative is u_x + i v_x = e^x cos y + i e^x sin y = e^z. The exponential is still its own derivative, even in the complex world.

Example 4, passing only on a line: Take f = x² + i y², so u = x² and v = y². u_x = 2x and v_y = 2y, so the first equation needs x = y. u_y = 0 and v_x = 0, so the second always holds. So f is differentiable only at points on the line y = x, and nowhere else. Keep this example in mind, because it shows the difference between differentiable and analytic.

Analytic functions: A function is analytic at a point z₀ if it is differentiable not just at z₀ but at every point of some small disk around z₀. A function is analytic in a domain (an open connected region) if it is analytic at every point of it. Other books say holomorphic or regular, which mean the same thing. The 'small disk' part matters. In Example 4, the function is differentiable on the line y = x, but any disk around a point of that line also contains points off the line, where it is not differentiable. So that function is analytic nowhere. Similarly, |z|² is differentiable only at 0 and analytic nowhere.

Entire functions and singular points: A function analytic in the whole complex plane is called entire. Polynomials, e^z, sin z, cos z, sinh z and cosh z are all entire. A rational function like 1/(z - 2) is analytic everywhere except z = 2. Such a point, where f stops being analytic but every disk around it still contains points where f is analytic, is called a singular point or singularity. Log z is analytic in the plane with the branch cut (zero and the negative real axis) removed. Sums, products and compositions of analytic functions are analytic, and so is a quotient wherever the bottom is not zero.

The polar form of the equations: Sometimes a function is easier in polar coordinates, z = r e^(iθ). Then u and v are functions of r and θ, and the CR equations become u_r = (1/r) v_θ and v_r = -(1/r) u_θ, valid for r > 0. The derivative can then be written as f'(z) = e^(-iθ)(u_r + i v_r). These are useful for powers and logarithms, where the polar form is natural.

Polar example, Log z: In polar form Log z = ln r + iθ (with θ the principal argument). So u = ln r and v = θ. u_r = 1/r and (1/r)v_θ = (1/r)(1) = 1/r, equal. v_r = 0 and -(1/r)u_θ = 0, equal. So Log z is analytic wherever it is continuous, which is away from the branch cut. Its derivative is e^(-iθ)(1/r + 0) = 1/(r e^(iθ)) = 1/z, matching the real rule d/dx ln x = 1/x.

Polar example, z^n: z^n = r^n (cos nθ + i sin nθ), so u = r^n cos nθ and v = r^n sin nθ. Then u_r = n r^(n-1) cos nθ, and (1/r) v_θ = (1/r) n r^n cos nθ = n r^(n-1) cos nθ. Equal. You can check the second equation the same way. This confirms that powers of z are analytic, and the derivative works out to n z^(n-1).

Nice consequences: Because the CR equations tie u and v so tightly together, analytic functions cannot do whatever they like. If f is analytic in a domain and f'(z) = 0 everywhere there, then f is constant, just as in real calculus. More surprising: if an analytic f is purely real everywhere in a domain (so v = 0), then the CR equations force u_x = 0 and u_y = 0, so f is constant. In the same way, if |f| is constant in a domain, then f itself is constant. A non-constant analytic function must change both its real and imaginary parts together.

A shortcut, the z and z̄ test: Here is a neat way to think about it. Write x = (z + z̄)/2 and y = (z - z̄)/(2i), and rewrite f in terms of z and z̄. The CR equations turn out to be the same as saying that f does not depend on z̄. So z², e^z and 1/z (written with z only) are analytic where defined, while anything with a z̄ in it, like z̄, |z|² = z z̄ or Re z = (z + z̄)/2, is suspicious. This is a good sanity check, but in exams you should still show the CR calculation.

Real life example 1, water around a Padma Bridge pillar: Engineers model smooth two-dimensional water flow using a 'complex potential', an analytic function w(z) = φ + iψ. The real part φ is the velocity potential, and the imaginary part ψ is the stream function: the curves ψ = constant are the paths the water follows. The CR equations guarantee that these flow lines and the equal-potential lines cross at right angles, and that the flow has no sources or swirls in the region. For a smooth flow past a round pillar, the textbook potential is w = U(z + a²/z), where U is the speed of the river and a is the pillar radius. One analytic function describes the whole flow pattern.

Real life example 2, electric fields in a circuit board: The same mathematics works for electrostatics. In a flat region with no charges, the electric potential is the real part of an analytic function, and the imaginary part gives the field lines. Engineers designing a printed circuit board or the gap between two metal plates use this to understand where the field is strongest. When you charge your phone in a Dhaka hostel room, the charger's design relied on field calculations that grew out of exactly these ideas.

Where students go wrong: The most common slip is the sign. It is u_y = -v_x, not u_y = v_x. Another mistake is to forget that the CR equations hold at a point does not automatically mean analytic: you need them to hold in a whole disk. Students also mix up 'differentiable on a line' with 'analytic on a line'; the second is impossible. Finally, when splitting f into u and v, be careful with i² = -1, especially for things like z³ or z e^z.

What exams ask: Typical questions are: state and derive the Cauchy-Riemann equations; show that a given function such as e^z, sin z or z³ is analytic and find its derivative; show that z̄ or |z|² is not analytic; find where a function like x² + i y² is differentiable; derive the polar form of the CR equations; and prove that an analytic function with constant modulus or with zero derivative is constant. Practise splitting functions into u and v quickly, because every one of these starts there.

Quick recap: Write f = u + iv. If f is differentiable at a point, then u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x there, and f' = u_x + i v_x. With continuous partial derivatives, these Cauchy-Riemann equations are also enough for differentiability. Analytic means differentiable in a whole disk around each point; entire means analytic everywhere. The polar form is u_r = (1/r)v_θ, v_r = -(1/r)u_θ. Next lesson we look at u and v on their own and discover they are harmonic functions, which leads to a recipe for building an analytic function from just its real part.
key_points: Write f = u + iv and split every function into real and imaginary parts first.
Cauchy-Riemann equations: u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x; then f' = u_x + i v_x.
CR equations are necessary; with continuous partial derivatives they are also sufficient.
Analytic at a point means differentiable in a whole disk around it; entire means analytic everywhere.
Polar form: u_r = (1/r)v_θ and v_r = -(1/r)u_θ; Log z and z^n pass it.
An analytic function with zero derivative, constant modulus or only real values on a domain is constant.
lessons.tip: Make a small table for each function: u, v, u_x, u_y, v_x, v_y. Filling the six boxes first makes the CR check almost automatic and stops sign mistakes.
lessons.task: On paper, split f(z) = z³ into u and v (hint: u = x³ - 3xy², v = 3x²y - y³), check both Cauchy-Riemann equations, and confirm that u_x + i v_x equals 3z².

quiz.q: Which pair is the Cauchy-Riemann equations?
quiz.explain: Matching the horizontal and vertical limits gives u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x.

quiz.q: For f = z², what is f' using f' = u_x + i v_x?
quiz.explain: u_x = 2x and v_x = 2y, so f' = 2x + 2iy = 2z.

quiz.q: Why is z̄ not analytic anywhere?
options: u_x = 1 but v_y = -1, so a CR equation fails everywhere
It has a singular point at 0
quiz.explain: With u = x and v = -y, the first CR equation fails at every point.

quiz.q: f = x² + i y² is differentiable only on y = x. Where is it analytic?
quiz.explain: Analytic needs differentiability in a whole disk, and no disk fits inside a line.

quiz.q: What does 'entire function' mean?
options: Analytic in the whole complex plane
Defined only on the real line
quiz.explain: Entire functions, like polynomials and e^z, are analytic at every point of the plane.

lessons.title: Harmonic Functions and Harmonic Conjugates
lessons.content:
Imagine a thin metal sheet lying on a tin roof in Dhaka on a sunny afternoon. One edge touches a hot iron frame, another edge touches a cool wet wall, and after a while the temperature at every point stops changing. Here is the magical part: in that calm, settled state, the temperature at any point is exactly the average of the temperatures around it. No point is a lonely hot spot and no point is a secret cold pocket. Functions that behave like this are called harmonic functions, and they turn out to be best friends with the analytic functions we met in the last lesson.

Laplace's equation: A real function u(x, y) is called harmonic in a domain D if it has continuous second partial derivatives there and satisfies u_xx + u_yy = 0 at every point of D. This equation is called Laplace's equation, and the expression u_xx + u_yy is often written as ∇²u (read 'del squared u') or Δu. In words: the way u curves in the x-direction is exactly cancelled by the way it curves in the y-direction. If the surface bends up one way, it must bend down the other way, like a horse saddle or a Pringles chip.

Quick examples: Take u = x² - y². Then u_xx = 2 and u_yy = -2, so u_xx + u_yy = 0. Harmonic! Now take u = x² + y². Then u_xx = 2 and u_yy = 2, and the sum is 4, not 0, so it is not harmonic; it is a bowl, bending up in both directions. Next, u = e^x cos y: u_xx = e^x cos y and u_yy = -e^x cos y, sum 0, harmonic again. Simple linear functions like u = 3x + 5y + 7 are harmonic too, because all their second derivatives are zero.

Why analytic gives harmonic: Suppose f(z) = u + iv is analytic in a domain. The Cauchy-Riemann equations say u_x = v_y and u_y = -v_x. Differentiate the first with respect to x: u_xx = v_yx. Differentiate the second with respect to y: u_yy = -v_xy. Add them: u_xx + u_yy = v_yx - v_xy. A big fact we will prove later with Cauchy's integral formula is that an analytic function has derivatives of every order, so all these partial derivatives are continuous and the mixed partials are equal: v_yx = v_xy. So the sum is 0 and u is harmonic. The same trick shows v_xx + v_yy = 0, so v is harmonic too.

Harmonic conjugate: If u and v are both harmonic and f = u + iv is analytic, we call v a harmonic conjugate of u. For f(z) = z² = (x² - y²) + i(2xy), the function 2xy is a harmonic conjugate of x² - y². Careful: the order matters. Is x² - y² a harmonic conjugate of 2xy? That would need 2xy + i(x² - y²) to be analytic. Check CR with U = 2xy and V = x² - y²: U_x = 2y but V_y = -2y. They are not equal, so no. The correct partner is -(x² - y²), because 2xy - i(x² - y²) = -i z², which is analytic. Rule: if v is a conjugate of u, then -u is a conjugate of v.

How many conjugates? A harmonic conjugate is unique only up to adding a real constant. If v works, then v + 5 works too, because adding 5i to an analytic function keeps it analytic. In a simply connected domain (a region with no holes, like a disk or the whole plane), every harmonic function has a harmonic conjugate. In a domain with a hole, this can fail, and we will see a famous example soon. So exam answers always end with '+ C', and forgetting it costs marks.

Finding a conjugate, worked example 1: Let u = x² - y² + x. First check that it is harmonic: u_xx = 2, u_yy = -2, sum 0. Good. Now use CR. From v_y = u_x = 2x + 1, integrate with respect to y while treating x as a constant: v = 2xy + y + g(x). The g(x) is the 'constant' of integration, which may still depend on x. Next use the second equation v_x = -u_y. We have v_x = 2y + g'(x) and -u_y = -(-2y) = 2y. So g'(x) = 0, which means g is a constant C. Answer: v = 2xy + y + C, and f = u + iv = z² + z + iC.

Worked example 2: Let u = e^x cos y. We already know it is harmonic. From v_y = u_x = e^x cos y, integrate in y: v = e^x sin y + g(x). Then v_x = e^x sin y + g'(x), and -u_y = -(-e^x sin y) = e^x sin y. So g'(x) = 0 and v = e^x sin y + C. Putting it together, f = e^x cos y + i e^x sin y = e^x (cos y + i sin y) = e^(x + iy) = e^z, plus the constant iC. So the conjugate of e^x cos y is e^x sin y, exactly the imaginary part of e^z from lesson 04.

Worked example 3: Let u = y³ - 3x²y. Check: u_xx = -6y and u_yy = 6y, sum 0, harmonic. From v_y = u_x = -6xy, integrate in y: v = -3xy² + g(x). Then v_x = -3y² + g'(x). Now -u_y = -(3y² - 3x²) = -3y² + 3x². Matching gives g'(x) = 3x², so g(x) = x³ + C. Therefore v = x³ - 3xy² + C. Which f is this? Recall z³ = (x³ - 3xy²) + i(3x²y - y³). Our u is minus the imaginary part of z³ and our v is the real part, so u + iv = i z³. You can check: i z³ = i(x³ - 3xy²) - (3x²y - y³), which matches.

The Milne-Thomson idea: The method above works, but it is long. Milne-Thomson found a shortcut that builds f straight from u without ever writing v. Start from f'(z) = u_x + i v_x. By CR, v_x = -u_y, so f'(z) = u_x - i u_y. Call φ1(x, y) = u_x and φ2(x, y) = u_y. The trick: replace x by z and y by 0. Then f'(z) = φ1(z, 0) - i φ2(z, 0). Integrate once with respect to z and you get f(z) plus a constant. The reason this works is deep (an analytic function is completely fixed by its values on a small piece of a line), but using it is very easy.

Milne-Thomson, worked: Take u = x² - y² + x again. φ1 = u_x = 2x + 1 and φ2 = u_y = -2y. Put x = z, y = 0: φ1(z, 0) = 2z + 1 and φ2(z, 0) = 0. So f'(z) = 2z + 1, and integrating gives f(z) = z² + z + C. Same answer as before, in three lines! Now u = e^x cos y: φ1 = e^x cos y becomes e^z, and φ2 = -e^x sin y becomes -e^z sin 0 = 0. So f'(z) = e^z and f(z) = e^z + C. If only v is given, use f'(z) = v_y + i v_x instead, again with x = z, y = 0. Example: v = 2xy gives v_y = 2x and v_x = 2y, so f'(z) = 2z and f = z² + C.

Harmonic in polar form: Sometimes a function is easier in polar coordinates z = r e^(iθ). Laplace's equation then becomes u_rr + (1/r) u_r + (1/r²) u_θθ = 0. Example: u = r^n cos(nθ). Here u_rr = n(n - 1) r^(n-2) cos nθ, (1/r)u_r = n r^(n-2) cos nθ and (1/r²)u_θθ = -n² r^(n-2) cos nθ. Adding: (n² - n + n - n²) r^(n-2) cos nθ = 0. Harmonic! That makes sense, because r^n cos nθ is just the real part of z^n.

The function ln r: Take u = ln r = ln|z| on the plane without the origin. Then u_r = 1/r and u_rr = -1/r², while u_θθ = 0. So u_rr + (1/r)u_r = -1/r² + 1/r² = 0. Harmonic. Its conjugate is θ, because ln r + iθ = Log z near any point. But θ jumps by 2π every time you walk once around the origin, so there is no single conjugate on the whole punctured plane. This is the famous example of a harmonic function without a global harmonic conjugate, and it happens exactly because the domain has a hole at 0.

Mean value property: Harmonic functions have a lovely averaging property. If u is harmonic in a domain and a closed disk of radius r around a point z0 sits inside it, then u(z0) equals the average of u over the circle of radius r around z0. In formula form: u(z0) = (1/2π) times the integral of u(z0 + r e^(iθ)) dθ from 0 to 2π. This is the precise version of our roof story: the temperature at the centre is the average of the temperatures on any ring around it.

Maximum principle: From the averaging property comes a strong rule. A harmonic function that is not constant cannot have a maximum or minimum inside its domain. Why? If the centre were the hottest point, the average around it would be lower, but the average must equal the centre. So on a bounded region, the largest and smallest values of u always appear on the boundary. On our tin roof, the hottest and coldest points are on the edges, never in the middle, as long as nothing inside is heating or cooling the sheet.

Right-angle families: Draw the curves where u = constant and the curves where v = constant. Wherever f'(z) ≠ 0, these two families cross at right angles. The reason is short: the gradient of u is (u_x, u_y), the gradient of v is (v_x, v_y) = (-u_y, u_x) by CR, and their dot product is -u_x u_y + u_y u_x = 0. Gradients are perpendicular to level curves, so the curves are perpendicular too. For f = z², the hyperbolas x² - y² = c cross the hyperbolas xy = k at right angles, making a neat grid of curved squares.

Where physics uses this: In steady heat flow, u is the temperature and the curves v = constant show the paths heat travels along. In electrostatics, u can be the electric potential, its level curves are equipotential lines, and the conjugate's level curves are electric field lines. In an ideal fluid, u is the velocity potential, v is the stream function, and the curves v = constant are the streamlines that tiny floating leaves would follow. The pair u + iv is then called the complex potential.

Real life example 1, a tin roof on a computer: Engineers in Bangladesh cannot solve every heat problem with a formula, so they let the computer use the averaging property. Draw a 3 by 3 grid of points over the sheet. Suppose the centre point has neighbours with temperatures 40, 30, 20 and 30 degrees. The harmonic rule says the centre should be (40 + 30 + 20 + 30)/4 = 30 degrees. For a big grid, the computer repeats 'replace each inside point by the average of its four neighbours' again and again until nothing changes. This is called Jacobi relaxation, and the same idea is used in image editing to smoothly fill a scratched part of a photo.

Real life example 2, water around a bridge pillar: Think of the river flowing past the pillars of the Padma Bridge. Far from the pillar the water moves almost straight. Near the pillar it bends around it. In the simplest ideal model, mathematicians describe this with a complex potential such as F(z) = U(z + a²/z) for a round pillar of radius a in a stream of speed U. The real part is the velocity potential and the imaginary part is the stream function. Setting the imaginary part to different constants draws the streamlines, and the circle |z| = a itself is one streamline, so water flows around the pillar and never through it.

Common mistakes: The most common slip is forgetting to check that u is harmonic before searching for a conjugate; if it is not harmonic, no conjugate exists and the integration will lead to a contradiction. Another is the sign in v_x = -u_y. Students also forget g(x) when integrating with respect to y, or forget the final constant. Remember that a sum of harmonic functions is harmonic, but a product usually is not: x is harmonic, yet x · x = x² is not. And remember the order: v conjugate of u does not mean u conjugate of v.

What exams ask: Typical questions are 'Show that u = ... is harmonic and find its harmonic conjugate', 'Find the analytic function f(z) whose real part is ...', usually expected by the Milne-Thomson method, 'Show that the families u = c1 and v = c2 are orthogonal', and 'Prove that the real and imaginary parts of an analytic function are harmonic'. Polar questions such as 'show that u = r² cos 2θ is harmonic and find v' also appear. Write the six partial derivatives in a small table first, and these questions become routine.

Recap: A harmonic function satisfies Laplace's equation u_xx + u_yy = 0. The real and imaginary parts of any analytic function are harmonic, and v is called a harmonic conjugate of u when u + iv is analytic. You find v by integrating the Cauchy-Riemann equations, or skip v and build f directly with Milne-Thomson: f'(z) = u_x(z, 0) - i u_y(z, 0). Harmonic functions obey the mean value property and the maximum principle, and their level curves cross the conjugate's level curves at right angles. Next lesson we use analytic functions as maps that bend the plane while keeping angles: conformal mapping.
key_points: u is harmonic if it has continuous second partials and u_xx + u_yy = 0 (Laplace's equation).
Real and imaginary parts of an analytic function are both harmonic.
v is a harmonic conjugate of u when u + iv is analytic; it is unique up to a real constant, and order matters.
Find v by integrating v_y = u_x, then fix g(x) using v_x = -u_y.
Milne-Thomson: f'(z) = u_x(z, 0) - i u_y(z, 0); integrate to get f(z) directly.
Polar Laplace: u_rr + (1/r)u_r + (1/r²)u_θθ = 0; ln r and r^n cos nθ are harmonic.
Mean value property and maximum principle: max and min of a nonconstant harmonic function sit on the boundary.
Level curves u = c and v = k cross at right angles where f'(z) ≠ 0.
lessons.tip: Before hunting for a conjugate, always spend ten seconds checking u_xx + u_yy = 0. If it fails, stop: no conjugate exists, and you have saved yourself a page of wrong integration.
