lessons.task: On paper, take u = x³ - 3xy². Check that it is harmonic, find its harmonic conjugate with the CR method, then find f(z) again with Milne-Thomson. Both answers should give f(z) = z³ + C.

quiz.q: Which function is harmonic?
quiz.explain: For x² - y², u_xx = 2 and u_yy = -2, so u_xx + u_yy = 0.

quiz.q: A harmonic conjugate of u = e^x cos y is:
quiz.explain: e^x cos y + i e^x sin y = e^z, which is analytic.

quiz.q: In the Milne-Thomson method, f'(z) is found from:
quiz.explain: f' = u_x + i v_x = u_x - i u_y by CR; then put x = z and y = 0.

quiz.q: If v is a harmonic conjugate of u, then a harmonic conjugate of v is:
quiz.explain: If u + iv is analytic, then -i(u + iv) = v - iu is analytic, so -u is the conjugate of v.

quiz.q: A nonconstant harmonic function on a bounded region takes its maximum value:
options: at the centre of the region
quiz.explain: By the maximum principle, the max and min appear on the boundary, not inside.

lessons.title: Conformal Mapping and Bilinear Transformations
lessons.content:
Open Google Maps and zoom out until you see the whole world. Greenland looks almost as big as Africa, but Africa is really about fourteen times larger. Is the map wrong? Not exactly. The world map you usually see uses the Mercator projection, which stretches sizes near the poles but keeps every small angle correct. A ship's captain sailing from Chattogram can draw a straight line on it and read the right compass direction. A map that keeps angles but is allowed to change sizes is called conformal, and analytic functions are the perfect machines for making such maps.

Functions as maps: A complex function w = f(z) takes a point z = x + iy in one plane and sends it to a point w = u + iv in another plane. We cannot draw a graph of it, because that would need four dimensions. So instead we draw two pictures side by side: the z-plane and the w-plane. Then we ask simple questions. Where does this line go? What does this circle become? Which region gets filled? Thinking of functions as maps turns algebra into pictures, and pictures are much easier to remember.

What conformal means: Take two smooth curves crossing at a point z0 at some angle, say 60 degrees, measured from the first curve to the second. Apply the map. The images are two new curves crossing at f(z0). If the angle between the new curves is again 60 degrees, with the same direction of turning, the map is conformal at z0. The key theorem is short: if f is analytic at z0 and f'(z0) ≠ 0, then f is conformal at z0. That single condition, f' not zero, is what you check in exams.

Why it works: Near z0, f(z) ≈ f(z0) + f'(z0)(z - z0). Multiplying by the complex number f'(z0) means two things: rotate by arg f'(z0) and scale by |f'(z0)|. Every tiny arrow leaving z0 is rotated by the same angle and stretched by the same factor, so the angle between any two arrows does not change. The number |f'(z0)| is called the magnification at z0, and tiny areas get multiplied by |f'(z0)|². For f(z) = z² at z0 = 1 + i, f'(z0) = 2 + 2i, so small shapes are rotated by 45 degrees and stretched by |2 + 2i| = 2√2 ≈ 2.83.

Critical points: Where f'(z0) = 0 the rule breaks. Such points are called critical points. For f(z) = z², f'(0) = 0, so 0 is critical. Watch what happens there: z = r e^(iθ) goes to r² e^(2iθ), so every angle at the origin is doubled. The positive real axis (angle 0) and the positive imaginary axis (angle 90 degrees) meet at a right angle, but their images, the positive real axis and the negative real axis, meet at 180 degrees. In general, if the first k - 1 derivatives vanish at z0 and the k-th does not, angles at z0 are multiplied by k.

The simplest maps: A translation w = z + b slides every point by b. A rotation w = e^(iα) z turns the plane by angle α around 0. A scaling w = kz with real k > 0 stretches everything from 0. Put them together and you get the linear map w = az + b: rotate by arg a, scale by |a|, then shift by b. Example: w = (1 + i)z + 2. Since 1 + i = √2 e^(iπ/4), it rotates by 45 degrees, stretches by √2, then moves right by 2. The point z = 1 goes to 1 + i + 2 = 3 + i. These maps send lines to lines and circles to circles and never bend anything.

The map w = z²: In polar form, r e^(iθ) goes to r² e^(2iθ): squares the distance and doubles the angle. So the first quadrant (angles 0 to 90 degrees) opens up into the whole upper half-plane (angles 0 to 180 degrees). In Cartesian form, u = x² - y² and v = 2xy. The hyperbolas x² - y² = c go to vertical lines u = c, and hyperbolas 2xy = k go to horizontal lines v = k. A vertical line x = c (with c ≠ 0) becomes u = c² - y², v = 2cy; removing y gives v² = 4c²(c² - u), a parabola opening to the left.

The map w = 1/z: In polar form, r e^(iθ) becomes (1/r) e^(-iθ). The distance flips (2 becomes 1/2) and the angle changes sign, so the inside of the unit circle and the outside swap places. The best fact about 1/z: it sends circles and lines to circles and lines, if we agree that a line is a 'circle through infinity'. Example: the line x = 1, with z = 1 + iy, goes to w = 1/(1 + iy) = (1 - iy)/(1 + y²). So u = 1/(1 + y²) and v = -y/(1 + y²), and u² + v² = 1/(1 + y²) = u. That is (u - 1/2)² + v² = 1/4: a circle with centre 1/2 and radius 1/2.

The point at infinity: For maps like 1/z it helps to add one extra point, ∞, to the plane. The result is called the extended complex plane, and you can picture it as a ball (the Riemann sphere) where the north pole is ∞. With this, 1/z sends 0 to ∞ and ∞ to 0, and every line becomes just a circle that passes through the north pole. This small trick makes the rules for the next family of maps very clean.

The map w = e^z: Write e^z = e^x e^(iy). The real part x controls the distance e^x and the imaginary part y controls the angle. So a vertical line x = c becomes a circle of radius e^c, and a horizontal line y = c becomes a ray from 0 at angle c. The horizontal strip 0 < y < π is mapped onto the whole upper half-plane, and the strip 0 < y < 2π covers the whole plane except the ray of non-negative real numbers. Because e^z repeats every 2πi, it is not one-to-one on the whole plane, which is exactly why Log z needed branches in lesson 04.

Bilinear (Möbius) transformations: The star of this lesson is w = (az + b)/(cz + d), where a, b, c, d are complex numbers with ad - bc ≠ 0. Why that condition? If ad - bc = 0, the top is a multiple of the bottom and w is just a constant, which is useless. The derivative is w' = (ad - bc)/(cz + d)², which is never zero, so a Möbius map is conformal everywhere except at z = -d/c, the point it sends to ∞. Its inverse is z = (dw - b)/(-cw + a), which is again a Möbius map.

Why circles stay circles: When c ≠ 0 we can rewrite w = a/c + ((bc - ad)/c) · 1/(cz + d). Read this as a recipe: first z → cz + d (rotate, scale, shift), then take 1/z, then multiply by (bc - ad)/c, then add a/c. Each step sends circles and lines to circles and lines, so the whole Möbius map does too. A line may become a circle and a circle may become a line, but you never get an ellipse or a parabola. This is the most quoted fact about bilinear maps.

Fixed points: A fixed point is a z with f(z) = z. For a Möbius map, z = (az + b)/(cz + d) gives cz² + (d - a)z - b = 0, a quadratic, so there are at most two fixed points unless the map is the identity w = z. Example: w = 1/z gives z² = 1, so z = 1 and z = -1 stay put. Example: w = (z - 1)/(z + 1) gives z² + z = z - 1, so z² = -1 and the fixed points are i and -i. When c = 0 the map is linear and ∞ is also a fixed point.

Cross-ratio: There is exactly one Möbius map sending three different points z1, z2, z3 to three different points w1, w2, w3. To find it, use the cross-ratio, which Möbius maps keep unchanged. One common textbook form is: (w - w1)(w2 - w3) / ((w - w3)(w2 - w1)) = (z - z1)(z2 - z3) / ((z - z3)(z2 - z1)). Put in the six points and solve for w. If one point is ∞, simply drop the two factors that contain it. Different books order the cross-ratio differently; any consistent order gives the same final map.

Worked cross-ratio problem: Find the map sending z = -1, 0, 1 to w = -1, -i, 1. The right side is (z + 1)(0 - 1)/((z - 1)(0 + 1)) = -(z + 1)/(z - 1). The left side is (w + 1)(-i - 1)/((w - 1)(-i + 1)), and (-1 - i)/(1 - i) simplifies to -i. So i(w + 1)/(w - 1) = (z + 1)/(z - 1). Solving and tidying up gives w = (iz + 1)/(z + i). Check: z = 0 gives 1/i = -i, z = 1 gives (i + 1)/(1 + i) = 1, z = -1 gives (1 - i)/(-1 + i) = -1. Since three real points went onto the unit circle, the whole real line goes onto the unit circle, and z = i goes to 0, so the upper half-plane becomes the unit disk.

A famous ready-made map: Another map you will meet everywhere is w = (z - i)/(z + i). For a point in the upper half-plane, z is closer to i than to -i, so |z - i| < |z + i| and |w| < 1. Real points are equally far from i and -i, so they land on |w| = 1. So this map also squeezes the whole upper half-plane into the unit disk. Engineers love it, because a hard problem on an infinite half-plane becomes an easier problem on a small round disk.

Real life example 1, maps for ships and phones: The Mercator projection is conformal. That is why sailors and pilots used it for centuries: a route with a fixed compass bearing, called a rhumb line, shows up as a straight line. When a ship leaves Chattogram port heading south-west, the navigator can read the angle with a protractor. The price is size: areas near the poles are blown up, so Greenland, about 2.2 million square kilometres, looks as large as Africa, about 30 million. The web map on your phone uses a version of the same idea, Web Mercator, so street corners in Dhaka look like real right angles.

Real life example 2, wings from circles: In lesson 07 we saw that ideal flow around a round pillar is easy to describe. Flow around an aeroplane wing is not. The Joukowski map w = z + 1/z fixes this. A circle passing through z = 1 and slightly shifted from the origin is mapped to a wing-shaped curve, the Joukowski airfoil. Because the map is conformal away from its critical points z = ±1, the streamlines around the circle become streamlines around the wing. Early aircraft engineers used exactly this trick, and today computer graphics uses conformal maps to wrap flat textures onto 3D faces with little angle distortion.

Common mistakes: Students often say 'analytic means conformal' and forget the condition f'(z0) ≠ 0; z² is analytic at 0 but not conformal there. Another slip is assuming a Möbius map sends lines to lines; it may send a line to a circle. People also forget to check ad - bc ≠ 0, mix up the order of points in the cross-ratio, or keep factors with ∞ instead of dropping them. Finally, remember that conformal maps keep angles, not lengths or areas.

What exams ask: Expect 'Show that w = f(z) is conformal except at ...', 'Find the image of the line x = 1 (or the circle |z - 1| = 1) under w = 1/z', 'Find the image of the strip 0 < y < π under w = e^z', 'Find the fixed points of w = (az + b)/(cz + d)', and 'Find the bilinear transformation that maps z1, z2, z3 to w1, w2, w3'. Draw both planes for every answer; a small sketch often earns marks even if the algebra slips.

Recap: A function w = f(z) can be seen as a map from the z-plane to the w-plane. If f is analytic and f'(z0) ≠ 0, the map is conformal at z0: it locally rotates by arg f'(z0) and scales by |f'(z0)|, so angles stay the same. z² doubles angles at 0, 1/z swaps inside and outside the unit circle, and e^z turns strips into sectors. Möbius maps (az + b)/(cz + d) with ad - bc ≠ 0 send circles and lines to circles and lines, have at most two fixed points, and are fixed by three points through the cross-ratio. Next we start integrating along curves in the complex plane.
key_points: Think of w = f(z) as a map from the z-plane to the w-plane and ask where lines, circles and regions go.
If f is analytic and f'(z0) ≠ 0, f is conformal at z0: it rotates by arg f'(z0) and scales by |f'(z0)|.
At a critical point (f'(z0) = 0) angles are multiplied; z² doubles angles at 0.
w = z² opens the first quadrant into the upper half-plane; w = e^z sends the strip 0 < y < π to the upper half-plane.
w = 1/z swaps inside and outside the unit circle and sends circles and lines to circles and lines.
Möbius map w = (az + b)/(cz + d) needs ad - bc ≠ 0, is conformal except at -d/c, and has at most two fixed points.
Three points fix a Möbius map; find it with the cross-ratio, dropping factors that contain ∞.
lessons.tip: For every mapping question, draw the z-plane and the w-plane side by side and test two or three easy points (like 0, 1, i) first. The picture tells you what the final answer should look like before any algebra.
lessons.task: On graph paper, take the points 1, 1 + i, i, -1 + i and -1 on the z-plane, compute their images under w = z² and w = 1/z, and plot them on a second grid. Notice how the right angle at 1 + i between the horizontal and vertical directions survives under z².

quiz.q: An analytic function f is guaranteed to be conformal at z0 when:
quiz.explain: Nonzero derivative means a local rotate-and-scale, which keeps angles.

quiz.q: Under w = z², the first quadrant is mapped onto:
quiz.explain: Angles 0 to 90 degrees are doubled to 0 to 180 degrees, giving the upper half-plane.

quiz.q: The fixed points of w = 1/z are:
quiz.explain: z = 1/z gives z² = 1, so z = 1 and z = -1.

quiz.q: Which condition must a bilinear map w = (az + b)/(cz + d) satisfy?
quiz.explain: If ad - bc = 0 the map is constant.

quiz.q: Under w = 1/z, the line x = 1 becomes:
options: the circle with centre 1/2 and radius 1/2

lessons.title: Complex Line Integrals
lessons.content:
Suppose you travel from Mohakhali to Motijheel in Dhaka. You can take the main road or slip through the small lanes. The distance is different, the time is different, maybe the rickshaw fare is different too. In maths we often add up something along a path, like the work done by a force or the water flowing across a line, and the big question is: does the answer depend on the path? In the complex plane this question has a beautiful answer, and it all starts with the complex line integral, the topic of this lesson.

Curves in the plane: A curve C in the complex plane is described by a function z(t) = x(t) + i y(t), where the parameter t runs from a to b. Think of t as time and z(t) as the position of an ant walking. The curve is smooth if z'(t) = x'(t) + i y'(t) exists, is continuous, and is never zero, so the ant never stops or makes a sharp turn. A contour is several smooth curves joined end to end, like a path made of straight roads meeting at corners.

Closed and simple: A curve is closed if it ends where it starts, z(b) = z(a). It is simple if it never crosses itself. A simple closed curve, like a circle, a square or a triangle, splits the plane into an inside and an outside. We say it is positively oriented when we walk around it counterclockwise, so the inside is always on our left. Unless a question says otherwise, every closed contour in this course is taken counterclockwise.

Standard parametrisations: Two recipes cover most exam questions. The straight segment from z1 to z2 is z(t) = z1 + t(z2 - z1), with 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, and z'(t) = z2 - z1. The circle with centre a and radius r is z(t) = a + r e^(it), with 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π, and z'(t) = i r e^(it). For example, the segment from 1 to 2 + i is z(t) = 1 + t(1 + i), and the unit circle is z(t) = e^(it). Learn these two by heart.

Definition of the integral: The complex line integral of f along C is ∫_C f(z) dz = ∫ from a to b of f(z(t)) z'(t) dt. The idea comes from a Riemann sum: chop the curve into tiny steps Δz_k, multiply each step by the value of f there, and add: Σ f(z_k) Δz_k. As the steps shrink, the sum approaches the integral. The substitution dz = z'(t) dt turns this into an ordinary integral in t, which you already know how to do. Separating real and imaginary parts, it equals ∫(u dx - v dy) + i ∫(v dx + u dy).

Worked example 1: Find ∫_C z dz where C is the straight line from 0 to 1 + i. Parametrise: z(t) = (1 + i)t, 0 ≤ t ≤ 1, so z'(t) = 1 + i. Then f(z(t)) z'(t) = (1 + i)t · (1 + i) = (1 + i)² t = 2i t. Integrating from 0 to 1 gives 2i · (1/2) = i. So ∫_C z dz = i. Notice we never had to split into u and v; just multiply complex numbers carefully.

Worked example 2, same path, different function: Now find ∫_C z̄ dz along the same line. Here z̄(t) = (1 - i)t, so the integrand is (1 - i)t · (1 + i) = 2t, and the integral from 0 to 1 is 1. Next take a different path from 0 to 1 + i: first along the real axis from 0 to 1, then straight up to 1 + i. On the first piece z = t, z̄ = t, dz = dt, giving ∫ t dt = 1/2. On the second piece z = 1 + it, z̄ = 1 - it, dz = i dt, giving ∫ (1 - it) i dt from 0 to 1 = i(1 - i/2) = i + 1/2. Total: 1 + i.

Path dependence: So for z̄, the straight path gives 1 but the corner path gives 1 + i. The answer depends on the road! Do the same corner path for f = z: the first piece gives 1/2, the second gives ∫ (1 + it) i dt = i(1 + i/2) = i - 1/2, and the total is i, the same as the straight path. This is no accident. In lesson 05 we saw that z is analytic and z̄ is analytic nowhere. Analytic functions tend to give path-independent answers, and the rest of this lesson and the next explain why.

Worked example 3, the most important integral: Let C be the circle |z - a| = r, counterclockwise. Find ∮_C dz/(z - a). Parametrise z = a + r e^(it), dz = i r e^(it) dt. Then 1/(z - a) = 1/(r e^(it)), so the integrand becomes i r e^(it)/(r e^(it)) = i. Integrating i from 0 to 2π gives 2πi. Notice two surprises: the answer is not zero even though the curve is closed, and it does not depend on r at all. Remember this number, 2πi; it is the seed of the residue theorem later in the course.

Powers of (z - a): More generally, for any integer n, ∮ (z - a)^n dz around that circle equals i r^(n+1) times the integral of e^(i(n+1)t) dt from 0 to 2π. When n + 1 ≠ 0, the integral of e^(i(n+1)t) over a full turn is 0, because it goes around the unit circle a whole number of times and cancels itself. When n = -1, the exponent is zero and we get 2πi. So the rule is: ∮ (z - a)^n dz = 0 for every integer n except n = -1, where it is 2πi. For example, ∮ dz/(z - a)² = 0 and ∮ (z - a)³ dz = 0.

Basic properties: Complex line integrals behave just like real ones. They are linear: ∫(αf + βg) dz = α∫f dz + β∫g dz. Reversing the direction of the curve changes the sign: ∫ over -C equals -∫ over C. And if a contour is made of pieces C1 and C2, the integral over the whole is the sum of the integrals over the pieces. These three rules let you break hard paths into easy segments, exactly as we did with the corner path.

Antiderivatives: If F is analytic on a domain containing C and F'(z) = f(z), then ∫_C f(z) dz = F(end) - F(start), just like the fundamental theorem of calculus. Check example 1: F(z) = z²/2, so the answer is (1 + i)²/2 - 0 = 2i/2 = i. Correct, and no parametrisation needed! Another one: ∫ e^z dz from 0 to iπ along any path equals e^(iπ) - e^0 = -1 - 1 = -2. Consequence: if f has an antiderivative, the integral around any closed curve is 0, because start and end are the same point.

Why 1/z gives 2πi: On the plane without 0, 1/z looks like it has the antiderivative Log z. But Log z is not continuous on any full circle around 0; its imaginary part, the angle, jumps by 2π when you go once around. So 1/z has no single antiderivative on a region that surrounds 0, and the closed integral can be nonzero. The jump in the angle, 2π, multiplied by i, is exactly the 2πi we computed. For powers (z - a)^n with n ≠ -1, the antiderivative (z - a)^(n+1)/(n + 1) has no jump, so the closed integral is 0.

Three equivalent facts: For a continuous f on a domain D, these three statements are either all true or all false. One: f has an antiderivative in D. Two: the integral of f between any two points does not depend on the path in D. Three: the integral of f around every closed contour in D is 0. z, z², e^z and sin z pass all three on the whole plane. z̄ fails, as we saw. And 1/z passes in a region not surrounding 0, but fails in a region that goes around 0.

Length of a curve: The length of C is L = ∫ from a to b of |z'(t)| dt. For a circle of radius r, |z'(t)| = |i r e^(it)| = r, so L = 2πr, as expected. For the segment from z1 to z2, |z'(t)| = |z2 - z1|, so L = |z2 - z1|, the ordinary distance. You need L for the next tool, which is the most useful inequality in the course.

The ML-inequality: If |f(z)| ≤ M at every point of C and C has length L, then |∫_C f(z) dz| ≤ M L. It simply says the size of a sum is at most the biggest piece times the number of pieces. Example: on the circle |z| = 2, bound ∫ dz/(z² + 1). On this circle, |z² + 1| ≥ |z|² - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3, so |f| ≤ 1/3 = M, and L = 4π. So the integral has size at most 4π/3. We do not know the exact value yet, but we know it cannot be bigger than about 4.19.

ML for big semicircles: Here is the way ML-inequality is used most often. Take the upper half of the circle |z| = R, with R > 1, and f(z) = 1/(z² + 1). On it, |z² + 1| ≥ R² - 1, so M = 1/(R² - 1), and L = πR. So the integral is at most πR/(R² - 1). As R grows, this goes to 0, roughly like π/R. In lesson 14 this exact trick lets us throw away the big arc and compute real integrals like the integral of dx/(x² + 1) over the whole real line.

Real life example 1, a river and its flow: Imagine the Buriganga flowing past Sadarghat, and let the water velocity at each point be V = p + iq. Engineers want two numbers for a closed loop drawn on the water: the circulation, which tells how much the water swirls around the loop, and the flux, which tells how much water leaves through it. A neat fact is that the complex integral ∮ conj(V) dz equals (circulation) + i (flux), where circulation = ∮(p dx + q dy) and flux = ∮(p dy - q dx). One complex integral delivers both numbers at once.

Real life example 2, is the point inside? In computer graphics, drawing a filled shape such as a letter in a font or an SVG icon means deciding, for each pixel, whether it lies inside a closed outline. One rule, called the nonzero winding rule, uses the winding number n(C, a) = (1/2πi) ∮_C dz/(z - a), which counts how many times C goes around the point a. If it is 0, the pixel is outside; otherwise it is inside. Real software counts crossings instead of integrating, but the idea is exactly this integral. A computer can also approximate any line integral as a Riemann sum: total = 0; for each small step from z_k to z_(k+1): total += f(z_k) * (z_(k+1) - z_k).

Common mistakes: The number one mistake is forgetting the factor z'(t) and integrating f(z(t)) dt alone. Another is confusing dz with |dz|; the second one gives arc length, not the complex integral. Students also walk the wrong way around a circle, which flips the sign, or use the antiderivative of 1/z on a closed curve around 0 and wrongly get 0. Finally, when using ML, remember that |z² + 1| ≥ |z|² - 1 comes from the reverse triangle inequality; do not write |z² + 1| ≤ ... when you need a lower bound for the denominator.

What exams ask: Expect 'Evaluate ∫ z̄ dz (or Re z dz, or z² dz) along the line from A to B and along a given broken path; is it path independent?', 'Evaluate ∮ dz/(z - a) and ∮ (z - a)^n dz over the circle |z - a| = r', 'Use an antiderivative to evaluate ∫ from 0 to 1 + i of z² dz', and 'Use the ML-inequality to find an upper bound for ...'. Always write the parametrisation, z'(t), and the limits of t on separate lines; it keeps the work clean and earns method marks.

Recap: A curve is written as z(t) for a ≤ t ≤ b, and ∫_C f dz = ∫ f(z(t)) z'(t) dt. Segments use z1 + t(z2 - z1) and circles use a + r e^(it). The integral of z̄ depends on the path, while for analytic functions with an antiderivative F the answer is F(end) - F(start) and closed integrals vanish. The key result ∮ dz/(z - a) = 2πi, and ∮ (z - a)^n dz = 0 for other integers n. The ML-inequality |∫ f dz| ≤ ML bounds integrals we cannot compute exactly. Next lesson, Cauchy explains exactly when closed integrals are zero, and what happens when they are not.
key_points: A curve is z(t) = x(t) + i y(t), a ≤ t ≤ b; closed contours are taken counterclockwise unless told otherwise.
Segment: z1 + t(z2 - z1), 0 ≤ t ≤ 1. Circle: a + r e^(it), 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π.
∫_C f(z) dz = ∫ f(z(t)) z'(t) dt; never forget the z'(t).
∮ dz/(z - a) = 2πi around a circle centred at a; ∮ (z - a)^n dz = 0 for every other integer n.
If F' = f on a domain, ∫_C f dz = F(end) - F(start) and closed integrals are 0.
z̄ gives path-dependent integrals; analytic functions with antiderivatives do not.
ML-inequality: |∫_C f dz| ≤ M L, with M a bound for |f| on C and L the length of C.
lessons.tip: Use a fixed three-line layout for every line integral: z(t) = ..., z'(t) = ..., limits of t. Then substitute. Most lost marks in this topic come from a missing z'(t) or wrong limits, not from hard calculus.

lessons.title: Cauchy's Theorem and Cauchy's Integral Formula
lessons.content:
Last lesson left us with a puzzle. Around a closed circle, ∮ z dz came out as 0, but ∮ dz/z came out as 2πi. Why does one function vanish and the other not? Imagine a pond in Ramna Park. If the pond is perfectly calm everywhere inside a loop of rope, nothing swirls around the rope. But if there is a tiny whirlpool hidden somewhere inside the loop, the water swirls, and the rope feels it. Augustin-Louis Cauchy turned this picture into two of the most powerful theorems in mathematics, and this lesson is all about them.

Cauchy's integral theorem: Let f be analytic in a simply connected domain D, which means D has no holes, and let C be any simple closed contour in D. Then ∮_C f(z) dz = 0. That is the whole theorem. No parametrisation, no calculation: if the function is analytic everywhere on and inside the curve, the integral is zero. The version proved by Goursat even works without assuming that f' is continuous, so it is often called the Cauchy-Goursat theorem.

A quick reason why: Write f = u + iv and dz = dx + i dy. Then ∮ f dz = ∮(u dx - v dy) + i ∮(v dx + u dy). Green's theorem from multivariable calculus changes each loop integral into a double integral over the inside: the first becomes the double integral of (-v_x - u_y) and the second becomes the double integral of (u_x - v_y). By the Cauchy-Riemann equations, u_y = -v_x and u_x = v_y, so both integrands are zero. So the whole integral is zero. This proof assumes continuous partial derivatives, which Goursat later showed is not needed.

Using the theorem: ∮ e^z dz, ∮ sin z dz, ∮ (z³ + 2z) dz around any simple closed contour are all 0, because these functions are entire. What about ∮ dz/(z - 3) around |z| = 1? The only trouble point is z = 3, which is outside the unit circle, so the function is analytic on and inside C and the answer is 0. Now ∮ dz/z around |z| = 1: the trouble point 0 is inside, so the theorem says nothing, and indeed we found 2πi. Careful: the converse is false. ∮ dz/z² around |z| = 1 is also 0, even though 1/z² is not analytic at 0.

Why simply connected matters: In a ring-shaped region, like 1 < |z| < 3, the function 1/z is analytic everywhere in the region, yet its integral around |z| = 2 is 2πi, not 0. The loop surrounds a hole that is not part of the domain, and the hole contains the bad point. So always check two things: is f analytic on the curve, and is it analytic at every point inside the curve, not only in the ring where the curve lives?

Deforming the contour: A very handy consequence is the deformation principle. Suppose C1 is a big closed curve, C2 is a smaller closed curve inside it, both counterclockwise, and f is analytic in the region between them, including both curves. Then ∮_C1 f dz = ∮_C2 f dz. You can shrink or reshape the curve freely, as long as you do not drag it across a bad point. So ∮ dz/(z - a) = 2πi around a square, a triangle or a potato shape, as long as a is inside, because you can shrink it to a small circle around a.

Several holes: If inside a big curve C there are several bad points, put a tiny circle C1, C2, ..., Ck around each one. Then ∮_C f dz = ∮_C1 f dz + ∮_C2 f dz + ... + ∮_Ck f dz. The big integral is the sum of the small ones. This is the idea behind the residue theorem in lesson 13, where each small circle contributes a single number.

Cauchy's integral formula: Now the second, even more surprising theorem. Let f be analytic on and inside a simple closed contour C, and let z0 be a point inside C. Then f(z0) = (1/2πi) ∮_C f(z)/(z - z0) dz. Read it slowly: if you know the values of f only on the boundary curve, you can compute f at every point inside. The edge decides the middle. Real functions are nothing like this; knowing a real function at the ends of an interval tells you nothing about the middle.

Why it is true: The function f(z)/(z - z0) is analytic everywhere inside C except at z0. By the deformation principle we can shrink C to a tiny circle of radius r around z0. On that tiny circle, f(z) is almost exactly f(z0), because f is continuous. So the integral is almost f(z0) ∮ dz/(z - z0) = f(z0) · 2πi. Making r smaller makes 'almost' as close as we like, and since the integral does not change with r, it must equal exactly 2πi f(z0).

Worked examples: Find ∮ e^z/(z - 1) dz around |z| = 2. The point 1 is inside, and f(z) = e^z is entire, so the answer is 2πi f(1) = 2πi e. Next, ∮ cos z / z dz around |z| = 1: here z0 = 0 and f = cos z, so the answer is 2πi cos 0 = 2πi. Next, ∮ e^z/(z - 3) dz around |z| = 1: the point 3 is outside, so the integrand is analytic inside and Cauchy's theorem gives 0. Always first ask: is z0 inside the curve?

Moving factors into f: Often the denominator has two factors. Find ∮ dz/(z² + 1) around the circle |z - i| = 1. Factor: z² + 1 = (z - i)(z + i). Only z = i is inside this circle; -i is at distance 2 from i, so it is outside. Write the integrand as [1/(z + i)]/(z - i), so f(z) = 1/(z + i), which is analytic inside. The answer is 2πi f(i) = 2πi · 1/(2i) = π. The trick is to keep only the factor whose zero is inside in the denominator, and push everything else into f.

Two points inside: Find ∮ e^z/(z(z - 1)) dz around |z| = 3. Both 0 and 1 are inside. Use partial fractions: 1/(z(z - 1)) = 1/(z - 1) - 1/z. So the integral becomes ∮ e^z/(z - 1) dz - ∮ e^z/z dz = 2πi e - 2πi · 1 = 2πi(e - 1). Another quick one: ∮ dz/(z² - 1) around |z| = 2. Since 1/(z² - 1) = (1/2)[1/(z - 1) - 1/(z + 1)], the answer is (1/2)(2πi - 2πi) = 0.

The formula for derivatives: Differentiate Cauchy's formula with respect to z0 again and again, and you get f^(n)(z0) = (n!/2πi) ∮_C f(z)/(z - z0)^(n+1) dz. The big consequence: if f is analytic, then f', f'', f''' and every higher derivative exist and are analytic too. This is the fact we borrowed in lesson 07 to prove that the real and imaginary parts of an analytic function are harmonic. Real functions can be differentiable once and not twice; analytic functions never stop.

Derivative examples: Find ∮ e^(2z)/z³ dz around |z| = 1. Here z0 = 0 and the power is 3 = n + 1, so n = 2 and f(z) = e^(2z). Since f''(z) = 4e^(2z), f''(0) = 4, and the integral is (2πi/2!) · 4 = 4πi. Next, ∮ e^z/z⁴ dz around |z| = 1: n = 3, f'''(0) = 1, so the answer is (2πi/3!) · 1 = πi/3. A common slip is using n! with n equal to the power in the denominator; remember the power is n + 1.

Cauchy's inequality: Suppose f is analytic on and inside the circle |z - z0| = R and |f| ≤ M on that circle. Using the derivative formula and the ML-inequality, |f^(n)(z0)| ≤ (n!/2π) · (M/R^(n+1)) · 2πR = n! M / R^n. For n = 1: |f'(z0)| ≤ M/R. This little inequality, called Cauchy's estimate, is what powers the next two famous theorems.

Liouville's theorem: If f is entire, meaning analytic on the whole plane, and bounded, meaning |f(z)| ≤ M for every z, then f is a constant. Proof: for any point z0 and any radius R, Cauchy's estimate gives |f'(z0)| ≤ M/R. Let R grow to infinity; the bound goes to 0, so f'(z0) = 0 everywhere, and f is constant. A shocking consequence: sin z is entire but not constant, so it must be unbounded. Indeed sin(iy) = i sinh y, and sinh 10 is already more than 11,000. On the real line sin x stays between -1 and 1, but in the complex plane it shoots off.

The fundamental theorem of algebra: Every polynomial p(z) of degree at least 1 has at least one complex root. Proof using Liouville: suppose p has no root. Then 1/p(z) is entire. Also |p(z)| grows to infinity as |z| does, so 1/p(z) is bounded. By Liouville, 1/p is constant, so p is constant, a contradiction. Dividing out one root at a time, a polynomial of degree n has exactly n roots counted with multiplicity. For example, z² + 1 = 0 has roots i and -i, and z³ - 1 = 0 has the three cube roots of unity from lesson 03.

Real life example 1, derivatives from a circle: Computers often need derivatives of functions they can only evaluate. Cauchy's formula gives a clever method: sample f at N equally spaced points on a small circle around z0 and take a weighted average. With ω = e^(2πi/N), f'(z0) ≈ (1/(N r)) Σ f(z0 + r ω^k) ω^(-k), summing k from 0 to N - 1. Try f = e^z, z0 = 0, r = 1, N = 4: the points are 1, i, -1, -i, and the sum works out to 2 sinh 1 + 2 sin 1 ≈ 4.033, so the estimate is about 1.008, very close to the true value e^0 = 1 with only four samples. With more points the error shrinks extremely fast, which is why scientific software uses this trick.

Real life example 2, roots everywhere in CSE: The fundamental theorem of algebra quietly supports a lot of computer science. Every square matrix has a characteristic polynomial, so every n by n matrix has exactly n eigenvalues in the complex numbers. A 2 by 2 rotation matrix that turns a game sprite by angle θ has no real eigenvalues, but it has the complex ones e^(iθ) and e^(-iθ). Google's PageRank, face recognition with principal component analysis and the stability tests for control systems in lesson 25 all rely on eigenvalues that are guaranteed to exist.

Common mistakes: The biggest mistake is not checking which points are inside the contour; draw the circle and mark the bad points every time. Another is leaving a factor like 1/(z + i) in the denominator instead of moving it into f. In the derivative formula, students mix up n and n + 1, or forget the n!. Some apply Cauchy's theorem in a ring-shaped domain where it does not hold. And Liouville needs both entire and bounded; 1/z is bounded far away from 0 but is not entire, so it is not constant for any contradiction.

What exams ask: Typical questions: 'State and prove Cauchy's integral theorem (using Green's theorem)', 'State Cauchy's integral formula and evaluate ∮ ... around |z| = 2', 'Evaluate ∮ e^(2z)/(z + 1)⁴ dz around |z| = 3 using the derivative formula', 'State and prove Liouville's theorem', and 'Deduce the fundamental theorem of algebra'. For the last one, the order is: assume no root, 1/p is entire and bounded, Liouville makes it constant, contradiction.

Recap: Cauchy's integral theorem says the integral of an analytic function around a closed contour in a simply connected domain is 0, and contours can be deformed as long as they do not cross bad points. Cauchy's integral formula, f(z0) = (1/2πi) ∮ f(z)/(z - z0) dz, says boundary values decide interior values, and its derivative version f^(n)(z0) = (n!/2πi) ∮ f(z)/(z - z0)^(n+1) dz shows analytic functions are infinitely differentiable. Cauchy's estimate leads to Liouville's theorem, and Liouville gives the fundamental theorem of algebra. Next lesson: power series, Taylor and Laurent.
key_points: Cauchy's integral theorem: f analytic on and inside a simple closed contour C (simply connected domain) gives ∮_C f dz = 0.
The converse is false, and holes matter: 1/z on a ring around 0 gives 2πi.
Contours can be deformed without crossing bad points; a big contour equals the sum of small circles around each bad point.
Cauchy's integral formula: f(z0) = (1/2πi) ∮ f(z)/(z - z0) dz for z0 inside C.
Derivatives: f^(n)(z0) = (n!/2πi) ∮ f(z)/(z - z0)^(n+1) dz, so analytic functions are infinitely differentiable.
Move factors whose zeros are outside C into f; use partial fractions when several points are inside.
Cauchy's estimate |f^(n)(z0)| ≤ n! M / R^n gives Liouville: bounded entire functions are constant.
Fundamental theorem of algebra: every nonconstant polynomial has a complex root, so degree n means n roots.
lessons.tip: Before using any formula, sketch the contour and put a dot at every point where the denominator is zero. Then decide: no dots inside means Cauchy's theorem (answer 0); one dot means the integral formula; several dots means partial fractions or one small circle per dot.
lessons.task: On paper, evaluate ∮ (z² + 1)/(z - 2) dz around |z| = 3 and around |z| = 1. Then evaluate ∮ e^z/(z - 1)² dz around |z| = 2 using the derivative formula. Expected answers: 10πi, 0 and 2πi e.

lessons.title: Power Series, Taylor Series and Laurent Series
lessons.content:
Imagine you are at a shop in Dhaka and you have to pay exactly 1,786 taka. Nobody prints a special note for every price. You simply build the amount from 1000s, 100s, 10s and 1s. Power series do the same thing for functions. They build complicated functions like e^z, sin z or 1/(1 - z) out of the simplest building blocks there are: 1, z, z², z³ and so on, each multiplied by a number. Add enough blocks and you get as close to the real function as you like. This lesson shows how that works, where it works, and what to do when it breaks down near a singular point.

What a power series is: A power series centred at z0 is an infinite sum a0 + a1(z - z0) + a2(z - z0)² + a3(z - z0)³ + ..., written in short as the sum of a_n (z - z0)^n for n = 0, 1, 2, .... The numbers a_n are the coefficients and z0 is the centre. The most famous one is the geometric series 1 + z + z² + z³ + ..., centred at 0 with every coefficient equal to 1. When |z| < 1 its sum is exactly 1/(1 - z). Try z = 1/2: 1 + 0.5 + 0.25 + 0.125 + ... creeps up to 2, and 1/(1 - 0.5) is also 2. When |z| ≥ 1 the terms never shrink, so the sum cannot settle and the series diverges.

The circle of convergence: Here is a beautiful fact. For every power series there is a number R, somewhere between 0 and infinity, called the radius of convergence. The series converges (in fact absolutely) at every z with |z - z0| < R and diverges at every z with |z - z0| > R. In the complex plane the set |z - z0| < R is a disk, so the region where a power series works is always a round disk around its centre, never a square or a strange blob. That is exactly why we call R a radius. R = 0 means the series only works at the centre itself, and R = infinity means it works everywhere.

Finding R with the ratio test: The quickest tool is the ratio formula R = lim |a_n / a_(n+1)| as n goes to infinity, whenever that limit exists. A version that always works is the Cauchy-Hadamard formula 1/R = limsup |a_n|^(1/n). Let us try four examples. For the sum of z^n / n!, a_n / a_(n+1) = (n + 1)!/n! = n + 1, which goes to infinity, so R = infinity. For the sum of n z^n the ratio is n/(n + 1), which goes to 1, so R = 1. For the sum of z^n / 2^n the ratio is exactly 2, so R = 2. For the sum of n! z^n the ratio is 1/(n + 1), which goes to 0, so R = 0 and the series is useless except at z = 0.

On the edge of the disk: The theorem says nothing about points exactly on the circle |z - z0| = R, and that is on purpose, because anything can happen there. The geometric series diverges at every point of |z| = 1, because its terms z^n have size 1 and never shrink to 0. The sum of z^n / n² converges at every point of |z| = 1, because the sizes 1/n² add up to a finite number. The sum of z^n / n is the mixed case: at z = 1 it becomes 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ..., which diverges, but at z = -1 it becomes 1 - 1/2 + 1/3 - ..., which converges. So on the boundary you must check point by point.

Power series are analytic: Inside its disk of convergence a power series is not just some function, it is an analytic function. Even better, you may differentiate it term by term, and the new series has the same radius R. For example, differentiate both sides of 1/(1 - z) = 1 + z + z² + z³ + ... and you get 1/(1 - z)² = 1 + 2z + 3z² + 4z³ + ..., still valid for |z| < 1. You can integrate term by term too. This makes power series very friendly: inside the disk you can treat them almost like very long polynomials.

Taylor's theorem in the complex world: Now flip the question. Given an analytic function, can we write it as a power series? Yes, always. If f is analytic in the disk |z - z0| < R, then for every z in that disk f(z) = sum of a_n (z - z0)^n with a_n = f^(n)(z0)/n!. Using Cauchy's integral formula from the last lesson, the same coefficient is a_n = (1/2πi) ∮ f(w)/(w - z0)^(n+1) dw around any small circle about z0. When z0 = 0 the series is called a Maclaurin series. This is stronger than real calculus. A real function can have derivatives of every order and still not equal its Taylor series (the classic example is e^(-1/x²) with value 0 at x = 0). In complex analysis, analytic means the Taylor series really equals the function in the whole disk.

The standard series to know by heart: e^z = 1 + z + z²/2! + z³/3! + ..., valid for all z. sin z = z - z³/3! + z⁵/5! - ..., valid for all z. cos z = 1 - z²/2! + z⁴/4! - ..., valid for all z. 1/(1 - z) = 1 + z + z² + ..., valid for |z| < 1. 1/(1 + z) = 1 - z + z² - z³ + ..., valid for |z| < 1. Log(1 + z) = z - z²/2 + z³/3 - ..., valid for |z| < 1 using the principal branch. Notice the pattern: the entire functions e^z, sin z and cos z have R = infinity, while the ones with a problem point at z = 1 or z = -1 stop at radius 1.

The radius is the distance to the nearest trouble: Here is the most useful shortcut of all. The Taylor series of f about z0 converges in the biggest open disk around z0 that contains no singular point of f. So R is simply the distance from z0 to the nearest singularity. Take f(z) = 1/(1 + z²). On the real line, 1/(1 + x²) is perfectly smooth for every x, yet its Maclaurin series 1 - x² + x⁴ - x⁶ + ... only works for |x| < 1. Real calculus cannot explain why. Complex numbers can: 1 + z² = 0 at z = i and z = -i, both at distance 1 from 0. Hidden poles off the real line limit the radius. Mystery solved.

Worked example, a centre other than 0: Expand f(z) = 1/z about z0 = 1. Do not grind out derivatives, use the geometric series. Write z = 1 + (z - 1), so 1/z = 1/(1 + (z - 1)) = 1 - (z - 1) + (z - 1)² - (z - 1)³ + .... This works when |z - 1| < 1, and indeed the only singularity of 1/z is at 0, which is at distance 1 from the centre. Quick check at z = 1.5: 1 - 0.5 + 0.25 - 0.125 + 0.0625 - ... adds up to 2/3, and 1/1.5 is also 2/3. The general coefficient is (-1)^n, which matches f^(n)(1)/n! = (-1)^n n!/n! if you do want to check by derivatives.

Tricks that save time: Most exam series come from the standard ones by substitution, multiplication or differentiation. Replace z by z² in e^z to get e^(z²) = 1 + z² + z⁴/2! + z⁶/3! + .... Replace z by -z² in 1/(1 - z) to get 1/(1 + z²) = 1 - z² + z⁴ - ..., valid for |z| < 1. Multiply sin z by z to get z sin z = z² - z⁴/3! + .... Divide sin z by z to get sin z / z = 1 - z²/3! + z⁴/5! - ..., which also shows that sin z / z behaves nicely at 0 once we give it the value 1 there. Because a Taylor series is unique, any honest method that produces a power series for f in the disk gives the right answer.

Why we need Laurent series: Taylor series need f to be analytic at the centre. But some of the most interesting functions blow up exactly at the point we care about, like 1/z, e^(1/z) or 1/(z(z - 1)) near 0. For these we allow negative powers too: f(z) = sum over all integers n of a_n (z - z0)^n = ... + a_(-2)/(z - z0)² + a_(-1)/(z - z0) + a0 + a1(z - z0) + .... This is a Laurent series, named after the French engineer Pierre Alphonse Laurent. The part with negative powers is called the principal part, and the part with non-negative powers is called the analytic (or regular) part.

Where a Laurent series lives: The non-negative powers form an ordinary power series, so they converge inside some circle, |z - z0| < R. The negative powers form a power series in 1/(z - z0), so they converge outside some circle, |z - z0| > r. Both halves must work at once, so a Laurent series lives in an annulus (a ring) r < |z - z0| < R. Laurent's theorem says: if f is analytic in such an annulus, it has exactly one Laurent series there, with a_n = (1/2πi) ∮ f(w)/(w - z0)^(n+1) dw for every integer n, taken counterclockwise around any circle inside the ring. The inner radius r can be 0 (a punctured disk) and the outer radius R can be infinity.

One coefficient to watch: In that formula, look at n = -1. It says a_(-1) = (1/2πi) ∮ f(w) dw. So the single number a_(-1) tells you the value of a whole contour integral! This number is called the residue of f at z0, and the next three lessons are built around it. Keep an eye on the 1/(z - z0) term every time you write a Laurent series.

Worked example, a punctured disk: Expand e^(1/z) about 0. Put w = 1/z into e^w = 1 + w + w²/2! + ... to get e^(1/z) = 1 + 1/z + 1/(2! z²) + 1/(3! z³) + ..., valid for all z ≠ 0, so the ring is 0 < |z| < infinity. There are infinitely many negative powers, and the coefficient of 1/z is 1. Another quick one: sin z / z³ = (z - z³/6 + z⁵/120 - ...)/z³ = 1/z² - 1/6 + z²/120 - ..., valid for |z| > 0. Here the principal part is just 1/z², and the coefficient of 1/z is 0.

Worked example, one function with three answers: Take f(z) = 1/((z - 1)(z - 2)) and expand about 0. Partial fractions first: f(z) = 1/(z - 2) - 1/(z - 1). Check: combining gives ((z - 1) - (z - 2))/((z - 1)(z - 2)) = 1/((z - 1)(z - 2)). The singular points 1 and 2 cut the plane into three regions around 0: the disk |z| < 1, the ring 1 < |z| < 2, and the outside |z| > 2. Each region gets its own series. The trick is always the same: rewrite each fraction as something times 1/(1 - w) where |w| < 1 in that region.

Region |z| < 1: Here both |z| < 1 and |z/2| < 1. So 1/(z - 1) = -1/(1 - z) = -(1 + z + z² + ...), and 1/(z - 2) = -(1/2)·1/(1 - z/2) = -(1/2 + z/4 + z²/8 + ...). Subtracting, f(z) = sum over n ≥ 0 of (1 - 1/2^(n+1)) z^n = 1/2 + (3/4)z + (7/8)z² + .... No negative powers appear, so this is just the Taylor series. Check: f(0) = 1/((-1)(-2)) = 1/2, which matches the first term.

Region 1 < |z| < 2: Now |z| > 1, so the old expansion of 1/(z - 1) fails. Instead pull out z: 1/(z - 1) = (1/z)·1/(1 - 1/z) = 1/z + 1/z² + 1/z³ + ..., which is fine because |1/z| < 1. The fraction 1/(z - 2) still uses |z/2| < 1 as before. So f(z) = -(1/2 + z/4 + z²/8 + ...) - (1/z + 1/z² + 1/z³ + ...). Powers in both directions appear: a true Laurent series, with a_(-1) = -1.

Region |z| > 2: Now pull z out of both fractions: 1/(z - 2) = (1/z)·1/(1 - 2/z) = 1/z + 2/z² + 4/z³ + .... So f(z) = sum over n ≥ 0 of (2^n - 1)/z^(n+1) = 0/z + 1/z² + 3/z³ + 7/z⁴ + .... Only negative powers this time. Sanity check: for huge z, (z - 1)(z - 2) is about z², so f should look like 1/z², and it does. Same function, three different series. The region decides the series, so always read which ring the question asks for.

Real life example 1, your calculator: When you press sin(0.1) on a calculator or phone, the device has no magic table of every sine. Math libraries first shrink the input into a small range and then use polynomial approximations, close cousins of the Taylor series. Try it by hand: sin(0.1) ≈ 0.1 - 0.1³/6 = 0.1 - 0.000167 = 0.099833. The true value is 0.0998334... Two terms already give five correct decimal places, because near 0 the higher powers shrink super fast. Engineers in Bangladesh writing firmware for cheap microcontrollers in irrigation pumps or IPS units use exactly this idea when they need sin or e^x without a big library.

Real life example 2, digital signals: In digital signal processing, a list of samples x[0], x[1], x[2], ... (say, a voice note recorded on your phone) is turned into a function X(z) = sum of x[n] z^(-n). This is the Z-transform, and it is nothing but a Laurent series in z. The set of z where it converges is called the region of convergence, and it is always a ring of the form r < |z| < R, exactly the annulus you just met. Telecom engineers designing filters for mobile networks look at this ring to decide whether a filter is stable. You will meet this again in the last lesson of the course.

Common mistakes and exam questions: The number one mistake is using 1/(1 - w) = 1 + w + w² + ... when |w| > 1 in the region asked, so always check which quantity is small. Second, using a_n = f^(n)(z0)/n! for a Laurent series; that formula only works when f is analytic at z0. Third, forgetting to test boundary points separately when asked about convergence on |z - z0| = R. Typical exam questions: find the radius of convergence of a given series; find the Taylor series of f about a point and state where it is valid; expand f(z) = 1/((z - 1)(z - 2)) or similar in a given ring; write down the principal part of a Laurent series.

Recap: A power series converges in a disk of radius R and is analytic there, and you can differentiate it term by term. Every analytic function equals its Taylor series in the largest disk that avoids its singular points, so R is the distance to the nearest singularity. When the centre itself is a problem, Laurent series add negative powers and live in rings. The same function can have different Laurent series in different rings, and the coefficient a_(-1), the residue, is about to turn hard integrals into simple arithmetic.
key_points: A power series sum a_n (z - z0)^n converges inside a disk |z - z0| < R and diverges outside it.
R can be found with R = lim |a_n/a_(n+1)| or 1/R = limsup |a_n|^(1/n); points on the circle must be checked separately.
Inside its disk a power series is analytic and can be differentiated or integrated term by term.
An analytic function equals its Taylor series, with a_n = f^(n)(z0)/n!, in the largest disk free of singularities.
The radius of a Taylor series is the distance from the centre to the nearest singular point (that is why 1/(1 + x²) has R = 1).
A Laurent series allows negative powers and lives in an annulus r < |z - z0| < R; it is unique in that annulus.
The negative-power part is the principal part; the coefficient a_(-1) is the residue.
The same function can have different Laurent series in different rings, e.g. 1/((z - 1)(z - 2)) has three around 0.
lessons.tip: Memorise the geometric series 1/(1 - w) = 1 + w + w² + ... for |w| < 1 like your phone number. Almost every Laurent expansion in an exam is just this one series with a clever choice of w, so the real skill is deciding which w is small in the given region.
lessons.task: On paper, expand f(z) = 1/((z - 1)(z + 2)) about 0 in the three regions |z| < 1, 1 < |z| < 2 and |z| > 2. Then pick z = 0.5, 1.5 and 3, add the first five terms of the matching series on your phone calculator, and compare with the exact value of f.

quiz.q: What is the radius of convergence of the series sum z^n / n! ?
quiz.explain: a_n/a_(n+1) = n + 1 goes to infinity, so R = infinity. This series is e^z, which works for every z.

quiz.q: The Maclaurin series of 1/(1 + z²) has radius of convergence:
quiz.explain: The singularities are at z = i and z = -i, both at distance 1 from 0, so R = 1.

quiz.q: For f(z) = 1/((z - 1)(z - 2)), the Laurent series in the ring 1 < |z| < 2 contains:
options: Both positive and negative powers of z
No powers of z at all
quiz.explain: In this ring 1/(z - 1) gives negative powers and 1/(z - 2) gives non-negative powers, so both appear.

quiz.q: The part of a Laurent series with negative powers of (z - z0) is called:
quiz.explain: The negative powers form the principal part; the non-negative powers form the analytic (regular) part.

quiz.q: Where does the series sum n! z^n converge?
quiz.explain: The ratio a_n/a_(n+1) = 1/(n + 1) goes to 0, so R = 0: the series converges only at its centre z = 0.

lessons.title: Zeros, Singularities and Residues
lessons.content:
Picture three kinds of trouble on a Dhaka road. The first is a tiny dent that a worker can fill with one bucket of tar, and then the road is perfect again. The second is a pothole of a known depth: your rickshaw drops into it hard, but you know exactly how deep it goes. The third is pure chaos, a spot where the road twists in every direction at once. Complex functions have the same three kinds of trouble points, called removable singularities, poles and essential singularities. In this lesson we learn to spot each one, measure it, and pull out one magic number from it: the residue.

Zeros first: A zero of f is a point z0 where f(z0) = 0. If f is analytic there, we can measure how strongly it vanishes. We say z0 is a zero of order m if f(z0) = f'(z0) = ... = f^(m-1)(z0) = 0 but f^(m)(z0) ≠ 0. An equivalent and often easier test: f(z) = (z - z0)^m g(z) where g is analytic and g(z0) ≠ 0. Examples: z³ has a zero of order 3 at 0. sin z has a simple zero (order 1) at 0, because sin 0 = 0 but cos 0 = 1. And 1 - cos z = z²/2! - z⁴/4! + ... = z²(1/2 - z²/24 + ...), so it has a zero of order 2 at 0.

Zeros stay apart: Here is a fact with no real-calculus twin as strong as it. The zeros of an analytic function that is not identically zero are isolated: around each zero there is a small disk with no other zero. For example, the zeros of sin z, even in the whole complex plane, are exactly z = nπ for integers n, nicely spaced out. This is why it makes sense to talk about the order of each zero, and it will help us find the order of poles too.

What a singular point is: A point z0 is a singular point of f if f is not analytic at z0, but every disk around z0 contains points where f is analytic. It is isolated if f is analytic in a punctured disk 0 < |z - z0| < r, so the trouble sits alone. 1/z has an isolated singularity at 0. Not every singularity is isolated: the principal Log z is not analytic anywhere on its branch cut, the non-positive real axis, and the function 1/sin(1/z) has poles at z = 1/(nπ) that crowd closer and closer to 0, so 0 is not isolated. In this course the residue tools work only for isolated singularities.

The Laurent test for classification: Around an isolated singularity, f has a Laurent series valid in 0 < |z - z0| < r (lesson 11). Look only at the principal part, the negative powers. If it has no terms at all, z0 is a removable singularity. If it has finitely many terms, with the most negative one being a_(-m)/(z - z0)^m and a_(-m) ≠ 0, z0 is a pole of order m. A pole of order 1 is called a simple pole. If it has infinitely many terms, z0 is an essential singularity. That is the whole classification, and it matches our three road troubles perfectly.

Removable singularities: Take f(z) = sin z / z at 0. Its Laurent series is 1 - z²/3! + z⁴/5! - ..., with no negative powers at all. So the trouble is fake: if we define f(0) = 1, the function becomes analytic at 0. A practical test: z0 is removable exactly when the limit of f(z) as z goes to z0 exists and is finite (equivalently, f stays bounded near z0, by Riemann's theorem). Another example: (e^z - 1)/z = 1 + z/2! + z²/3! + ..., removable at 0 with value 1.

Poles: At a pole, |f(z)| goes to infinity as z approaches z0, from every direction. The order tells you how fast. Quick test: z0 is a pole of order m if the limit of (z - z0)^m f(z) exists, is finite and is not zero. For example, 1/(z - 2)³ has a pole of order 3 at 2. For a fraction f = g/h, if g(z0) ≠ 0 and h has a zero of order m at z0, then f has a pole of order m. So 1/(z²(z + 1)) has a pole of order 2 at 0 and a simple pole at -1.

Watch for cancellation: When the top also vanishes, subtract the orders. sin z / z³: the top has a zero of order 1 at 0 and the bottom has order 3, so the pole has order 3 - 1 = 2. The Laurent series agrees: sin z / z³ = 1/z² - 1/6 + .... Likewise (1 - cos z)/z⁴: top order 2, bottom order 4, so a pole of order 2. And sin z / z: top order 1, bottom order 1, difference 0, so removable. If the top's order is bigger than or equal to the bottom's, the singularity is removable.

Essential singularities: The star example is e^(1/z) at 0, whose Laurent series 1 + 1/z + 1/(2! z²) + ... never stops. Its behaviour is wild. Come to 0 along the positive real axis: e^(1/x) shoots to infinity. Come along the negative real axis: e^(1/x) shrinks to 0. Come along the imaginary axis: z = iy gives e^(-i/y), whose modulus is always exactly 1. No single limit, not even infinity. The Casorati-Weierstrass theorem says that near an essential singularity, f gets as close as you like to every complex number. Picard's great theorem goes further: f actually takes every complex value, with at most one exception, infinitely often in any tiny disk around the point. For e^(1/z) the only value it misses is 0.

The residue: For an isolated singularity z0, the residue Res(f, z0) is the coefficient a_(-1) of 1/(z - z0) in the Laurent series valid in 0 < |z - z0| < r. Why that one coefficient? Integrate the Laurent series term by term around a small circle z = z0 + ρe^(iθ). Then ∮ (z - z0)^n dz = ∫ ρ^(n+1) i e^(i(n+1)θ) dθ from 0 to 2π, which is 0 for every n except n = -1, where it equals 2πi. So every term dies except one, and ∮ f dz = 2πi a_(-1). The residue is literally what is left over after integrating, which is where the name comes from.

Residues straight from Laurent series: At a removable singularity the residue is 0, since there are no negative powers. For e^(1/z) at 0 the coefficient of 1/z is 1, so the residue is 1. For sin z / z³ the series 1/z² - 1/6 + ... has no 1/z term, so the residue is 0 even though it is a pole. For z² e^(1/z) = z²(1 + 1/z + 1/(2z²) + 1/(6z³) + 1/(24z⁴) + ...) = z² + z + 1/2 + 1/(6z) + ..., the residue is 1/6. At an essential singularity this Laurent method is usually the only way, because the formulas below need a pole.

Simple poles, formula one: If z0 is a simple pole, Res(f, z0) = lim (z - z0) f(z) as z goes to z0. The idea: multiplying by (z - z0) kills the pole and leaves exactly a_(-1) at z0. Example: f(z) = 1/((z - 1)(z - 2)). At z = 1, (z - 1)f(z) = 1/(z - 2), which equals -1 at z = 1, so the residue is -1. At z = 2, (z - 2)f(z) = 1/(z - 1), which equals 1, so the residue is 1. Compare with lesson 11: in the ring 1 < |z| < 2 the series about 0 had a 1/z coefficient of -1, but that is the coefficient about 0, not a residue at 0, so do not mix them up.

Simple poles, formula two: If f = p/q where p(z0) ≠ 0, q(z0) = 0 and q'(z0) ≠ 0, then Res(f, z0) = p(z0)/q'(z0). This is super handy when the bottom does not factor easily. Example: 1/(z² + 1) at z = i: p = 1, q' = 2z, so the residue is 1/(2i) = -i/2. At z = -i it is 1/(-2i) = i/2. Another one: cot z = cos z / sin z at z = nπ: the residue is cos(nπ)/cos(nπ) = 1 for every integer n. And e^z/(z⁴ - 1) at z = 1: e/(4·1³) = e/4.

Poles of order m: If z0 is a pole of order m, then Res(f, z0) = (1/(m - 1)!) times the limit as z goes to z0 of the (m - 1)th derivative of (z - z0)^m f(z). For m = 1 this is just formula one. Example: f(z) = e^z / z³ at 0, order 3. Here z³ f(z) = e^z, its second derivative is e^z, which is 1 at 0, and dividing by 2! gives 1/2. Check with Laurent: e^z / z³ = 1/z³ + 1/z² + 1/(2z) + 1/6 + ..., so the coefficient of 1/z is indeed 1/2.

Another order-two example: f(z) = 1/(z²(z + 1)). At 0 (order 2): z² f(z) = 1/(z + 1), its derivative is -1/(z + 1)², which is -1 at 0, and dividing by 1! gives -1. At -1 (simple): (z + 1) f(z) = 1/z², which is 1 at z = -1. The two residues add to 0. That is not luck: for a rational function whose bottom degree is at least two more than its top degree, the residues at all its poles always add up to 0. It is a free check on your arithmetic.

When formulas get messy, use series: Find the residue of 1/(z sin z) at 0. The bottom z sin z = z² - z⁴/6 + ... has a zero of order 2, so this is a pole of order 2. Instead of differentiating a fraction, write 1/(z sin z) = (1/z²)·1/(1 - z²/6 + ...) = (1/z²)(1 + z²/6 + ...) = 1/z² + 1/6 + .... There is no 1/z term, so the residue is 0. A neat shortcut: this function is even (f(-z) = f(z)), and an even function's Laurent series about 0 has only even powers, so its residue at 0 is always 0.

Choosing a method: Removable point: residue 0, done. Simple pole with an easy factor: use lim (z - z0) f(z). Simple pole of p/q with an awkward q: use p(z0)/q'(z0). Pole of order 2 or 3: use the derivative formula. High-order pole or essential singularity: expand known series and read off the 1/(z - z0) coefficient. Always find the order first, because using the simple-pole formula on a double pole gives nonsense (usually infinity).

Real life example 1, the swing at a village mela: Push a jhula at just the right rhythm and it swings higher and higher. Engineers describe systems like this with a transfer function H(s), a fraction of polynomials. The poles of H(s) are the system's natural frequencies and decay rates, the rhythms where its response blows up or rings. Knowing where the poles are, and how strong they are, tells an engineer whether a bridge, a car's suspension or a power supply circuit will settle down or shake itself apart.

Real life example 2, the cover-up trick: In circuit analysis with Laplace transforms (lesson 23) you often split F(s) = 1/((s + 1)(s + 2)) into A/(s + 1) + B/(s + 2). The Heaviside cover-up method says: to get A, cover the (s + 1) factor and put s = -1 into what is left, giving 1/(-1 + 2) = 1. That is exactly the residue of F at -1 by formula one! Similarly B = 1/(-2 + 1) = -1, the residue at -2. Students in EEE labs at BUET and other universities use this trick every week, often without knowing they are computing residues.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Calling sin z / z a pole because the bottom is zero, without checking the top. Getting the pole order wrong by forgetting to subtract the order of a zero on top. Using lim (z - z0) f(z) on a pole of order 2 or more. Trying a derivative formula at an essential singularity, where only the Laurent series works. Mixing up the Laurent coefficient about one point with the residue at another point. Typical exam questions: find and classify all singularities of a given f; find the order of each pole; find the residues at all poles; find the residue of something like z² e^(1/z) or e^z/z³.

Recap: Zeros have orders, and zeros of an analytic function are isolated. An isolated singularity is removable, a pole of order m, or essential, depending on whether its principal part has zero, finitely many or infinitely many terms. The residue is the 1/(z - z0) coefficient, and it equals (1/2πi) times the integral around a small circle. You can get it from a limit, from p/q', from the order-m derivative formula, or straight from a Laurent series. Next lesson we add residues up and turn whole contour integrals into a few lines of arithmetic.
key_points: z0 is a zero of order m if f(z) = (z - z0)^m g(z) with g analytic and g(z0) ≠ 0; zeros of a non-zero analytic function are isolated.
An isolated singularity is classified by its Laurent principal part: none means removable, finitely many terms means a pole, infinitely many means essential.
Removable: the limit of f exists (e.g. sin z / z at 0). Pole of order m: (z - z0)^m f(z) has a finite non-zero limit.
For g/h, the pole order is (order of zero of h) minus (order of zero of g); zero or negative means removable.
Near an essential singularity f comes arbitrarily close to every value (Casorati-Weierstrass), e.g. e^(1/z) at 0.
The residue is the coefficient a_(-1), and ∮ f dz around a small circle equals 2πi times it.
Simple pole: Res = lim (z - z0) f(z) = p(z0)/q'(z0). Order m: Res = (1/(m-1)!) lim d^(m-1)/dz^(m-1) [(z - z0)^m f(z)].
At essential singularities (and for messy poles) read the residue straight from the Laurent series.
lessons.tip: Before computing any residue, write the order of the singularity next to it in your copy. Most lost marks in this topic come from using the wrong formula for the wrong order, not from hard algebra.
lessons.task: Take f(z) = z/((z - 1)²(z + 2)). On paper, list its singularities, give the order of each, and find both residues (one simple-pole formula, one order-2 formula). Then check that the residues add up to 0, as they must for this rational function.

quiz.q: What kind of singularity does sin z / z have at z = 0?
quiz.explain: Its Laurent series 1 - z²/6 + ... has no negative powers, so defining f(0) = 1 removes the trouble.

quiz.q: What kind of singularity does e^(1/z) have at z = 0?
quiz.explain: e^(1/z) = 1 + 1/z + 1/(2! z²) + ... has infinitely many negative powers, so it is essential.

quiz.q: What is the residue of 1/(z² + 1) at z = i?
quiz.explain: Using p/q': 1/(2z) at z = i gives 1/(2i) = -i/2.

quiz.q: What is the residue of e^z / z³ at z = 0?
quiz.explain: e^z/z³ = 1/z³ + 1/z² + 1/(2z) + ..., so the 1/z coefficient is 1/2.

quiz.q: What is the order of the pole of 1/(z²(z + 1)) at z = 0?
quiz.explain: The bottom has a zero of order 2 at 0 and the top is 1, so the pole has order 2.

lessons.title: The Residue Theorem
lessons.content:
Think about a cricket match at Mirpur. If you want the team total, you do not need to replay every ball. You just add up what each batter scored. The residue theorem works the same way. A contour integral around a closed curve sounds like a long journey, point by point around the whole loop. But the theorem says you only need to visit the few special points inside the loop, read off one number at each (the residue), add them up and multiply by 2πi. The whole journey collapses into a tiny sum. This is one of the most powerful results in all of mathematics, and you already have every piece you need.

The two facts we already know: From lesson 10, Cauchy's integral theorem says that if f is analytic everywhere inside and on a simple closed contour C, then ∮_C f dz = 0. From lesson 12, around a small circle centred at an isolated singularity z0, ∮ f dz = 2πi Res(f, z0), because every term of the Laurent series integrates to 0 except the 1/(z - z0) term. The residue theorem simply glues these two facts together.

The statement: Let C be a simple closed contour traversed once counterclockwise (the positive direction). Suppose f is analytic inside and on C, except at finitely many isolated singular points z1, z2, ..., zk that lie strictly inside C, with none on C itself. Then ∮_C f dz = 2πi [Res(f, z1) + Res(f, z2) + ... + Res(f, zk)]. Singular points outside C do not matter at all, no matter how many there are or how nasty they are.

Why it is true: Draw a tiny circle around each singular point inside C, small enough that the circles do not overlap or touch C. In the region between C and the little circles, f is analytic. By the deformation principle (Cauchy's theorem for a region with holes), the integral around C equals the sum of the integrals around the little circles, all taken counterclockwise. Each little circle gives 2πi times the residue at its centre. Add them, and you have the theorem. In short: you can shrink the big loop down onto the trouble points, and each trouble point pays its residue.

Why this is such a big deal: Before this theorem, evaluating a contour integral meant choosing a parametrisation z(t), computing dz = z'(t) dt, and grinding through a real integral that was often ugly or impossible in closed form. With the theorem, the shape of the curve hardly matters. A circle, a square or a wobbly potato-shaped loop all give the same answer, as long as they enclose the same singular points. What matters is only which special points are inside and their residues. That shift, from the whole path to a few points, is the key idea of the rest of this course.

The four-step recipe: Step 1, find all singular points of f, usually by setting the bottom equal to 0. Step 2, decide which ones are inside C; draw a picture and compute distances, because |z - a| < r means inside the circle |z - a| = r. Step 3, compute the residue at each inside point using the tools from lesson 12. Step 4, add the residues and multiply by 2πi. If C is traversed clockwise instead, multiply the final answer by -1.

Example 1, one pole inside: Evaluate ∮ 1/((z - 1)(z - 3)) dz around |z| = 2. The singular points are z = 1 and z = 3. Since |1| = 1 < 2, the point 1 is inside; since |3| = 3 > 2, the point 3 is outside and is ignored. The residue at 1 is the value of 1/(z - 3) at z = 1, which is -1/2. So the integral is 2πi × (-1/2) = -πi. Three lines of work for an integral that would be painful to do with a parametrisation.

Example 2, two poles that cancel: Evaluate ∮ 1/((z - 1)(z - 2)) dz around |z| = 3. Both 1 and 2 are inside. From lesson 12 the residues are -1 and 1, which add to 0, so the integral is 0. Careful: the integral is 0 not because f is analytic (it is not), but because the residues cancel. This also matches lesson 11: in |z| > 2 the Laurent series of this function about 0 started at 1/z², with no 1/z term, and the coefficient of 1/z there is exactly (1/2πi) times the integral around a big circle.

Example 3, a nice surprise: Evaluate ∮ e^z/(z² + 1) dz around |z| = 2. The poles are i and -i, both inside since their modulus is 1. Using p/q', the residue at i is e^i/(2i) and the residue at -i is e^(-i)/(-2i). Their sum is (e^i - e^(-i))/(2i), which is exactly sin 1 by Euler's formula. So the integral is 2πi sin 1, roughly 2πi × 0.8415. Notice how lesson 4's formula for sin z appears all by itself.

Example 4, a pole of high order: Evaluate ∮ e^(2z)/z⁴ dz around |z| = 1. The only singular point is 0, a pole of order 4. Rather than differentiating three times, use the series: e^(2z) = 1 + 2z + (2z)²/2! + (2z)³/3! + ..., so dividing by z⁴, the 1/z term comes from the z³ term of e^(2z), whose coefficient is 2³/3! = 8/6 = 4/3. The residue is 4/3 and the integral is 2πi × 4/3 = 8πi/3. The order-m derivative formula gives the same: (1/3!) × 8e^0 = 4/3.

Example 5, one pole in and one pole out: Evaluate ∮ z/((z - 1)²(z + 3)) dz around |z| = 2. The singular points are 1 (order 2) and -3 (simple). Since |-3| = 3 > 2, only z = 1 counts. Using the order-2 formula, Res = d/dz [z/(z + 3)] at z = 1 = 3/(z + 3)² at z = 1 = 3/16. So the integral is 2πi × 3/16 = 3πi/8. If the contour had been |z| = 4, both poles would be inside, and the residues would add to 0 (bottom degree 3, top degree 1), giving 0.

Example 6, essential singularities are fine too: The theorem only asks for isolated singular points, so essential ones are allowed. ∮ e^(1/z) dz around |z| = 1 equals 2πi × 1 = 2πi, because the residue of e^(1/z) at 0 is 1. And ∮ z² e^(1/z) dz around the same circle equals 2πi × 1/6 = πi/3, using the residue found in lesson 12. No other method makes these integrals this easy.

Example 7, trigonometric functions: Evaluate ∮ tan z dz around |z| = 2. tan z = sin z / cos z has poles where cos z = 0, namely z = π/2 + nπ. Inside |z| = 2 we have π/2 ≈ 1.571 and -π/2; the next ones, ±3π/2 ≈ ±4.712, are outside. At each pole, p/q' gives sin z/(-sin z) = -1. So the integral is 2πi × (-1 - 1) = -4πi.

Old friends as special cases: If there are no singular points inside, the sum is empty and we get Cauchy's theorem: the integral is 0. If f is analytic and we integrate f(z)/(z - z0), the only singular point is the simple pole z0 with residue f(z0), so ∮ f(z)/(z - z0) dz = 2πi f(z0): Cauchy's integral formula. With f(z)/(z - z0)^(n+1) we get the derivative version too. The residue theorem is the big umbrella over everything in lesson 10.

Checking with the residue at infinity: When a contour encloses every finite singular point, there is a shortcut. One defines the residue at infinity by Res(f, ∞) = -Res((1/z²) f(1/z), 0), and then the integral over a large enough counterclockwise circle equals -2πi Res(f, ∞). For a rational function whose bottom degree is at least two more than its top degree, that residue is 0, so the sum of all finite residues is 0. This is a great check: if your residues for such a function do not add up to zero, something is wrong.

Counting zeros, the argument principle: Apply the residue theorem to f'/f. At a zero of order m, f'/f has a simple pole with residue m; at a pole of order p, it has a simple pole with residue -p. So (1/2πi) ∮ f'(z)/f(z) dz = Z - P, the number of zeros minus the number of poles inside C, counted with their orders (assuming none lie on C). This lets you count roots of an equation without solving it, and it is the mathematics behind the Nyquist stability test used in control engineering.

Real life example 1, keeping a drone steady: A small delivery drone, or the controller that keeps a voltage regulator steady during load-shedding switchovers, is a feedback system. Engineers need every pole of the closed-loop system to sit in the left half of the s-plane, otherwise the system wobbles and blows up. The Nyquist test draws one curve, counts how many times it circles the point -1, and uses the argument principle to count unstable poles without solving any equation. That is the residue theorem running inside real hardware design.

Real life example 2, going back from Laplace to time: In lesson 23 you will invert Laplace transforms. One exact formula for the inverse is a contour integral (the Bromwich integral), and under the usual conditions it equals the sum of the residues of F(s)e^(st) at the poles of F. Take F(s) = 1/((s + 1)(s + 2)). The residue at -1 is e^(-t)/(−1 + 2) = e^(-t), and at -2 it is e^(-2t)/(−2 + 1) = -e^(-2t). So f(t) = e^(-t) - e^(-2t). This is how a circuit's current is found from its transformed equation.

Inside or outside, done carefully: For the circle |z - 1| = 2, the point -0.5 has |(-0.5) - 1| = 1.5 < 2, so it is inside. The point 2i has |2i - 1| = sqrt(1 + 4) = sqrt(5) ≈ 2.24 > 2, so it is outside, even though it looks close on a rough sketch. The point 3 has |3 - 1| = 2, so it lies exactly on the circle, and then the theorem in this form does not apply at all. Always compute the distance; never guess from a sketch.

Common mistakes and exam questions: Including poles that lie outside the contour. Forgetting the factor 2πi, or writing 2π instead. Ignoring direction: a clockwise contour flips the sign. Applying the theorem when a singular point lies on C. Using the wrong residue formula for the pole order. Typical exam questions: state and prove the residue theorem; evaluate ∮ around |z| = 2 (or |z - 1| = 1, and so on) of a rational function, an e^z fraction, tan z or e^(1/z); show that an integral is 0; count the zeros of a polynomial inside a circle using the argument principle.

Recap: For a positively oriented simple closed contour with finitely many isolated singular points inside and none on it, ∮ f dz = 2πi times the sum of the residues inside. The proof shrinks the contour onto small circles around each singular point. The recipe is find, locate, compute, add. Cauchy's theorem and integral formula are special cases, and the argument principle counts zeros and poles. Next lesson we aim this tool at ordinary real integrals that calculus finds hard.
key_points: Residue theorem: for a positively oriented simple closed C, ∮_C f dz = 2πi × (sum of residues of f at singular points inside C).
Singular points must be isolated, finitely many inside, and none on C; points outside C are ignored.
Proof idea: deform C into small circles around each singular point; each contributes 2πi × its residue.
Recipe: find singular points, decide which are inside by computing distances, compute residues, add and multiply by 2πi.
A clockwise contour gives the negative of the counterclockwise answer.
Cauchy's theorem and Cauchy's integral formula are special cases of the residue theorem.
Argument principle: (1/2πi) ∮ f'/f dz = (zeros - poles inside C), counted with order; it underlies the Nyquist stability test.
lessons.tip: Always start by drawing the contour and marking every singular point with a dot, then write 'in' or 'out' next to each after computing its distance. This one small picture prevents the most common mistake in the whole topic.
lessons.task: Evaluate ∮ (z + 2)/(z(z - 1)) dz around three different circles: |z| = 1/2, |z - 1| = 1/2 and |z| = 3. Work out which poles are inside each time, find the residues (you should get -2 at 0 and 3 at 1), and write the three answers. Then explain in one line why the big circle gives 2πi.

quiz.q: What is ∮ 1/((z - 1)(z - 3)) dz around |z| = 2 (counterclockwise)?
quiz.explain: Only z = 1 is inside; its residue is 1/(1 - 3) = -1/2, so the integral is 2πi × (-1/2) = -πi.

quiz.q: Which situation means the residue theorem, as stated, cannot be used directly?
options: A pole lies exactly on the contour C
An essential singularity lies inside C
quiz.explain: The theorem needs every singular point to be off the contour. Poles outside are ignored, and isolated essential singularities inside are fine.

quiz.q: What is ∮ e^(1/z) dz around |z| = 1?
quiz.explain: The residue of e^(1/z) at 0 is the coefficient of 1/z, which is 1, so the integral is 2πi.

quiz.q: What is ∮ 1/((z - 1)(z - 2)) dz around |z| = 3?
quiz.explain: Both poles are inside, with residues -1 and 1, which add to 0.

quiz.q: If the contour is traversed clockwise instead of counterclockwise, the answer:
quiz.explain: Reversing the direction of a contour integral flips its sign.

lessons.title: Real Integrals by Residues
lessons.content:
Imagine you need to cross the Buriganga, but the bridge right in front of you is closed. A smart boatman says: take a small detour by boat, it is quicker than walking around. Real integrals are sometimes like that closed bridge. Integrals such as the integral of 1/(1 + x⁴) over the whole real line, or of dθ/(2 + cos θ) from 0 to 2π, are horrible with ordinary calculus tricks. But if you take a detour through the complex plane, close up a contour, and use the residue theorem from lesson 13, the answer often falls out in a few lines. This lesson shows the three classic detours that every exam loves.

The big idea: The residue theorem is about closed contours, while a real integral runs along a line or over an angle. So we have to build a closed contour whose integral we can compute by residues, and from which the real integral can be read off. Two tricks do almost all the work. For integrals over 0 to 2π we turn the angle into a trip around the unit circle. For integrals over the whole real line we add a big semicircle on top and show that its contribution vanishes as it grows.

Type 1, integrals over a full turn: Consider an integral of the form ∫ from 0 to 2π of R(cos θ, sin θ) dθ, where R is a rational function that stays finite for all θ. Put z = e^(iθ). As θ goes from 0 to 2π, z goes once counterclockwise around the unit circle |z| = 1. Then dz = i e^(iθ) dθ = iz dθ, so dθ = dz/(iz). Euler's formula gives cos θ = (z + 1/z)/2 and sin θ = (z - 1/z)/(2i). After substituting, the integral becomes the contour integral of a rational function of z around |z| = 1, and we only need residues at poles strictly inside the unit circle.

Worked example, ∫ from 0 to 2π of dθ/(2 + cos θ): Substitute: 2 + cos θ = 2 + (z + 1/z)/2 = (z² + 4z + 1)/(2z). So the integrand becomes [2z/(z² + 4z + 1)] × [dz/(iz)] = (2/i) × dz/(z² + 4z + 1). The roots of z² + 4z + 1 = 0 are z = -2 ± sqrt(3). Numerically, -2 + sqrt(3) ≈ -0.268 is inside the unit circle and -2 - sqrt(3) ≈ -3.732 is outside. Call the inside one α. The residue of 1/(z² + 4z + 1) at α is 1/(2α + 4) = 1/(2 sqrt(3)). So the integral is 2πi × (2/i) × 1/(2 sqrt(3)) = 2π/sqrt(3) ≈ 3.628.

A general formula and a check: The same steps prove that for a > |b|, ∫ from 0 to 2π of dθ/(a + b cos θ) = 2π/sqrt(a² - b²), and the same value holds with sin θ in place of cos θ.
