Check our example: a = 2, b = 1 gives 2π/sqrt(3). Another: ∫ from 0 to 2π of dθ/(5 - 4 sin θ) = 2π/sqrt(25 - 16) = 2π/3. A quick sanity test: if b = 0, the formula gives 2π/a, which is obviously right because the integrand is the constant 1/a. In exams you are usually asked to derive it, not just quote it.

Tips for Type 1: Always multiply through so that no 1/z is left in the denominator, then factor the resulting polynomial. Remember the extra dz/(iz), it is easy to forget. Only poles with |z| < 1 count; for denominators like z² + 4z + 1, the two roots multiply to 1 (the constant term), so one root is inside and the other outside, which is a nice check. If the integrand contains cos(nθ), use cos(nθ) = (z^n + z^(-n))/2, or better, take the real part of z^n.

Type 2, rational functions over the real line: Now consider ∫ from -∞ to ∞ of p(x)/q(x) dx, where p and q are polynomials, q has no real zeros, and the degree of q is at least two more than the degree of p. Then ∫ from -∞ to ∞ of p(x)/q(x) dx = 2πi × (sum of the residues of p(z)/q(z) at its poles in the upper half-plane, Im z > 0). Poles in the lower half-plane are ignored completely.

Why the semicircle trick works: Take the contour made of the segment from -R to R on the real axis plus the upper semicircle C_R of radius R, traversed counterclockwise. For R big enough it encloses every upper half-plane pole, so by the residue theorem the total integral is 2πi times their residues, no matter how big R gets. On the semicircle, the degree condition means |p(z)/q(z)| ≤ K/R² for some constant K. The length of C_R is πR. By the ML-inequality from lesson 9, the semicircle integral is at most πR × K/R² = πK/R, which goes to 0. So as R goes to infinity, only the real-line part survives.

Worked example, ∫ dx/(1 + x²): The poles of 1/(1 + z²) are i and -i; only i is in the upper half-plane. The residue at i is 1/(2i). So the integral is 2πi × 1/(2i) = π. Check with calculus: the antiderivative is arctan x, which goes from -π/2 to π/2, giving π. The two methods agree, and now we trust the machine for harder ones. Since the integrand is even, we also get ∫ from 0 to ∞ of dx/(1 + x²) = π/2.

Worked example, a double pole: Find ∫ dx/(1 + x²)². The only upper pole is i, now of order 2. Using the order-2 formula, the residue is the derivative of 1/(z + i)² at z = i, which is -2/(z + i)³ = -2/(2i)³ = -2/(-8i) = 1/(4i). So the integral is 2πi × 1/(4i) = π/2. A real-calculus route would need a trig substitution and a double-angle formula; here it is three lines.

Worked example, ∫ dx/(1 + x⁴): The poles are the four fourth roots of -1: e^(iπ/4), e^(3iπ/4), e^(5iπ/4), e^(7iπ/4). The first two are in the upper half-plane. At a simple pole z0 of 1/(z⁴ + 1), p/q' gives 1/(4z0³) = z0/(4z0⁴) = -z0/4, since z0⁴ = -1. So the sum of the two residues is -(e^(iπ/4) + e^(3iπ/4))/4. Now e^(iπ/4) + e^(3iπ/4) = (√2/2 + i√2/2) + (-√2/2 + i√2/2) = i√2. The sum of residues is -i√2/4, and the integral is 2πi × (-i√2/4) = 2π√2/4 = π/√2 ≈ 2.221.

Type 3, Fourier-type integrals: These look like ∫ from -∞ to ∞ of (p(x)/q(x)) cos(mx) dx or the same with sin(mx), where m > 0. They appear all over signal processing and in the Fourier transforms of lessons 19 and 20. The tempting move is to use cos(mz) directly, but that fails: cos(mz) = (e^(imz) + e^(-imz))/2, and on the upper semicircle e^(-imz) has size e^(my), which explodes. The fix is to use e^(imz) instead. In the upper half-plane z = x + iy with y ≥ 0, so |e^(imz)| = e^(-my) ≤ 1. Compute ∫ (p/q) e^(imx) dx by residues, then take the real part for cos and the imaginary part for sin.

Jordan's lemma: For Type 3 the degree condition can be relaxed. Jordan's lemma says: if m > 0 and |g(z)| ≤ M_R on the upper semicircle C_R with M_R going to 0 as R grows, then the integral of e^(imz) g(z) over C_R goes to 0. The key estimate behind it is ∫ from 0 to π of e^(-R sin θ) dθ < π/R. So for Fourier-type integrals it is enough that the degree of q is at least one more than the degree of p, not two.

Worked example, ∫ cos x/(x² + 1) dx: Use f(z) = e^(iz)/(z² + 1). The only upper pole is i, with residue e^(i·i)/(2i) = e^(-1)/(2i). So ∫ e^(ix)/(x² + 1) dx = 2πi × e^(-1)/(2i) = π/e. Taking real parts, ∫ cos x/(x² + 1) dx = π/e ≈ 1.156. The imaginary part gives ∫ sin x/(x² + 1) dx = 0, which makes sense because that integrand is odd. More generally, for m > 0 and a > 0, ∫ cos(mx)/(x² + a²) dx = (π/a) e^(-ma).

Worked example where Jordan is needed: Find ∫ x sin x/(x² + 1) dx. Here the degree difference is only 1, so the plain ML-inequality fails, but Jordan's lemma rescues us. Use z e^(iz)/(z² + 1). The residue at i is i e^(-1)/(2i) = 1/(2e). So ∫ x e^(ix)/(x² + 1) dx = 2πi/(2e) = πi/e, and taking the imaginary part, ∫ x sin x/(x² + 1) dx = π/e.

Poles on the real axis, a pointer: If q has a real zero, the integral is improper at that point, and the method needs a small semicircle (an indentation) around the pole, giving what is called a Cauchy principal value. The most famous result of this kind is the Dirichlet integral ∫ from 0 to ∞ of sin x/x dx = π/2. Most courses state this case briefly; know the result and that it uses an indented contour.

Real life example 1, a spectral line: In physics and engineering, the Lorentzian curve 1/(π(1 + x²)) describes the shape of spectral lines and resonance peaks, and in statistics it is the Cauchy distribution. Why the factor 1/π? Because the total area must be 1, and we just showed ∫ dx/(1 + x²) = π. Its Fourier transform, ∫ cos(ωx)/(1 + x²) dx = π e^(-|ω|), is our Type 3 example with m = |ω|. These are exactly the integrals a lab student at a university in Dhaka or Rajshahi needs when fitting a resonance peak.

Real life example 2, noise in a simple filter: An RC low-pass filter, the humble resistor-capacitor pair in every phone charger and audio circuit, has power response 1/(1 + (ωRC)²). To find how much noise gets through, engineers compute ∫ from 0 to ∞ of dω/(1 + (ωRC)²). Substituting x = ωRC turns it into (1/RC) × ∫ from 0 to ∞ of dx/(1 + x²) = π/(2RC) in radians per second. Dividing by 2π to convert to hertz gives the well-known noise bandwidth of 1/(4RC). A residue calculation hides inside that textbook formula.

Common mistakes and exam questions: In Type 1, forgetting dθ = dz/(iz), or counting a pole outside the unit circle. In Type 2, using lower half-plane poles, or skipping the check that the degree of q is at least two more than p. In Type 3, using cos(mz) instead of e^(imz), or forgetting to take the real or imaginary part at the end. Not checking for poles on the real axis. Typical exam questions: evaluate ∫ from 0 to 2π of dθ/(a + b cos θ); evaluate ∫ dx/(x² + 1)(x² + 4) or ∫ dx/(1 + x⁴); evaluate ∫ cos(mx)/(x² + a²) dx; state and use Jordan's lemma.

Recap: Residues can compute real integrals by detouring through the complex plane. For integrals over 0 to 2π of rational functions of cos θ and sin θ, put z = e^(iθ) and use poles inside the unit circle. For ∫ p/q over the whole real line with degree of q at least degree of p plus two, close with an upper semicircle and use upper half-plane poles. For Fourier-type integrals use e^(imz) with m > 0, Jordan's lemma, and real or imaginary parts. This closes the complex-analysis part of the course; next we move to Fourier series, where many of these integrals will come back.
key_points: Real integrals can be evaluated by building a closed contour and using the residue theorem.
For ∫ from 0 to 2π of R(cos θ, sin θ) dθ, put z = e^(iθ), dθ = dz/(iz), cos θ = (z + 1/z)/2, sin θ = (z - 1/z)/(2i), and use poles inside |z| = 1.
For a > |b|, ∫ from 0 to 2π of dθ/(a + b cos θ) = 2π/sqrt(a² - b²).
If deg q ≥ deg p + 2 and q has no real zeros, ∫ p/q dx over the real line = 2πi × (sum of residues in the upper half-plane).
The semicircle contributes nothing as R grows, by the ML-inequality (Type 2) or Jordan's lemma (Type 3).
For ∫ (p/q) cos(mx) dx with m > 0, use e^(imz), not cos(mz), then take the real part (imaginary part for sin).
Standard results: ∫ dx/(1 + x²) = π, ∫ dx/(1 + x²)² = π/2, ∫ dx/(1 + x⁴) = π/√2, ∫ cos x/(x² + 1) dx = π/e.
lessons.tip: For every real integral, first write down which type it is (full turn, rational on the real line, or Fourier type) and which poles will count. Most mistakes come from picking the wrong set of poles, not from the residue arithmetic.
lessons.task: Use residues to show that ∫ from -∞ to ∞ of dx/((x² + 1)(x² + 4)) = π/6. Hint: the upper poles are i and 2i. Then check your answer numerically: on your phone calculator, estimate the integral by adding f(x) × 0.5 for x = -10, -9.5, ..., 10 (or use any free online integrator) and compare with π/6 ≈ 0.5236.

quiz.q: For ∫ from 0 to 2π of R(cos θ, sin θ) dθ, the standard substitution is:
quiz.explain: z = e^(iθ) turns the angle into a trip around the unit circle, with dθ = dz/(iz).

quiz.q: What is ∫ from -∞ to ∞ of dx/(1 + x²)?
quiz.explain: The upper pole is i with residue 1/(2i), so the integral is 2πi × 1/(2i) = π.

quiz.q: When closing with an upper semicircle for ∫ p(x)/q(x) dx, which poles are used?
options: Only poles on the real axis
quiz.explain: Only the poles enclosed by the upper semicircle contour, those with Im z > 0, contribute.

quiz.q: What is ∫ from 0 to 2π of dθ/(2 + cos θ)?
quiz.explain: Only the pole -2 + √3 lies inside the unit circle; the result is 2π/sqrt(a² - b²) with a = 2, b = 1.

quiz.q: To evaluate ∫ cos x/(x² + 1) dx by residues, the right choice is:
options: cos z/(z² + 1) on an upper semicircle
e^(iz)/(z² + 1), then take the real part
quiz.explain: e^(iz) stays bounded in the upper half-plane, while cos z and e^(-iz) blow up there. The answer is π/e.

lessons.title: Periodic Functions and Fourier Series
lessons.content:
Think about the ceiling fan in your room. Every second it spins around and comes back to the same position, again and again. Or think about the azaan from the nearby mosque, five times every single day, or the sun rising each morning over Cox's Bazar. Things that repeat are everywhere. In the 1800s a French mathematician named Joseph Fourier had a wild idea: almost any repeating pattern, even a jagged one with sharp corners, can be built by adding together simple smooth waves, sines and cosines. That idea is called a Fourier series, and it is one of the most useful tools in all of science and engineering. In this lesson we learn what periodic functions are, why sines and cosines are the perfect building blocks, and the formulas that tell us exactly how much of each wave to use.

Periodic function: A function f(x) is called periodic if there is a positive number T such that f(x + T) = f(x) for every x. The number T is a period. The smallest such positive T is called the fundamental period, and most of the time when people say 'the period' they mean this smallest one. For example, sin x and cos x both have period 2π, because going round a full circle brings you back to the same point. The function tan x has period π. A constant function like f(x) = 5 is periodic with every positive T, so it has no smallest period at all, which is a funny special case.

Periods of sin nx and cos nx: If you squeeze a wave, its period shrinks. The function sin 2x repeats after π, sin 3x repeats after 2π/3, and in general sin nx and cos nx have fundamental period 2π/n. Here is the key observation: every one of these functions also repeats after 2π, because 2π is just n copies of 2π/n. So sin x, sin 2x, sin 3x, cos x, cos 2x and so on all fit neatly into the same window of length 2π. That is why we can add them together and still get a function with period 2π. A sum of periodic functions with period 2π is again periodic with period 2π.

The big idea of a Fourier series: Suppose f(x) has period 2π. Fourier said we can write it as f(x) = a0/2 + (a1 cos x + b1 sin x) + (a2 cos 2x + b2 sin 2x) + (a3 cos 3x + b3 sin 3x) + ... going on forever. In short, f(x) = a0/2 + Σ (an cos nx + bn sin nx), with n running from 1 to infinity. The numbers a0, an and bn are called the Fourier coefficients. The term a0/2 is the average height of the function, sometimes called the DC part. The terms with n = 1 are called the fundamental, and the terms with n = 2, 3, 4 and so on are called the harmonics. It is like a recipe: the function is the dish, and the coefficients tell you how many spoons of each wave go in.

An analogy with colours: When you mix paint, you can make thousands of colours from a few basic ones. Light works the same way: a prism splits white sunlight into a rainbow of separate colours. A Fourier series is a prism for functions. It takes a complicated repeating shape and splits it into pure waves of different frequencies. Once you know the amount of each pure wave, you know the whole shape. Engineers love this because pure waves are easy to handle: when a sine wave goes through an electric circuit, it comes out as a sine wave of the same frequency, only bigger or smaller and shifted.

Why we need orthogonality: The obvious question is, how do we find the coefficients? If f is a big messy sum, how do we fish out just b3, for example? The trick is a property called orthogonality. In ordinary geometry, two vectors are orthogonal when their dot product is zero, like the x-axis and y-axis meeting at a right angle. For functions on the interval from -π to π, the 'dot product' of two functions g and h is the integral of g(x)h(x) dx from -π to π. Two functions are called orthogonal on that interval when this integral is zero. Sines and cosines turn out to be orthogonal to each other in exactly this sense.

The orthogonality relations: Here are the facts, with all integrals taken from -π to π and m, n positive whole numbers. First, the integral of sin mx cos nx is 0 for every m and n. Second, the integral of sin mx sin nx is 0 when m is not equal to n, and equals π when m = n. Third, the integral of cos mx cos nx is 0 when m is not equal to n, and equals π when m = n. Also the integral of cos nx alone, or of sin nx alone, over a full period is 0 for n ≥ 1, while the integral of 1 is 2π. These few lines are the engine of the whole subject, so it is worth knowing them by heart.

Checking one relation: Let us verify one, so it does not feel like magic. Take m = 2 and n = 3 and look at sin 2x sin 3x. A product-to-sum identity says sin A sin B = [cos(A - B) - cos(A + B)]/2. So sin 2x sin 3x = [cos x - cos 5x]/2. Over -π to π, the integral of cos x is 0 and the integral of cos 5x is 0, because each one covers whole periods and the positive and negative parts cancel. So the answer is 0. Now take m = n = 3: sin² 3x = [1 - cos 6x]/2. The integral of 1/2 over a length 2π is π, and the cos 6x part gives 0. So the answer is π, just as promised.

Finding a0: Now we use orthogonality like a fishing net. Start from f(x) = a0/2 + Σ (an cos nx + bn sin nx) and integrate both sides from -π to π. Every cos nx and sin nx term integrates to 0. Only the constant survives: the integral of a0/2 over length 2π is π a0. So the integral of f equals π a0, which gives a0 = (1/π) times the integral of f(x) dx from -π to π. This is why the constant term is written as a0/2: with that choice, the formula for a0 looks exactly like the formulas for the other an. Then a0/2 is simply the average value of f over one period.

Finding an and bn: To catch an, multiply both sides by cos mx and integrate from -π to π. Every sin term dies because sin times cos integrates to 0. Every cos nx cos mx term dies unless n = m. The constant times cos mx also integrates to 0. Only one term survives, am times π. So am = (1/π) ∫ f(x) cos mx dx. In the same way, multiplying by sin mx and integrating catches bm = (1/π) ∫ f(x) sin mx dx. These are the Euler formulas, also called the Euler-Fourier formulas. Written together: a0 = (1/π)∫ f dx, an = (1/π)∫ f(x) cos nx dx, bn = (1/π)∫ f(x) sin nx dx, all over -π to π.

A note on conventions: Different textbooks write the constant term differently. Some write a0/2 with a0 = (1/π)∫ f dx, like we did. Others write just a0 and then use a0 = (1/(2π))∫ f dx. Both give the same final series; only the label changes. In an exam, use whichever your teacher uses and stay consistent. Also, any interval of length 2π works: you can integrate from 0 to 2π instead of -π to π and get the same coefficients, because a periodic function has the same area over every full period.

Easy example by inspection: Suppose f(x) = 3 + 2 cos x - sin 3x. This is already a Fourier series! Matching it with the general form, a0/2 = 3 so a0 = 6, a1 = 2, b3 = -1, and every other coefficient is 0. If you plug f into the Euler formulas, orthogonality gives exactly these numbers back. Another one: f(x) = sin² x. Using sin² x = (1 - cos 2x)/2, we get a0/2 = 1/2 and a2 = -1/2, and everything else is zero. Lesson: if your function is already a combination of sines and cosines, use trig identities first and save yourself the integration.

A full worked example, setting up: Let f(x) = x² for -π < x < π, and extend it to repeat with period 2π. Picture a chain of bowl shapes, one after another. We need a0, an and bn. First, a0 = (1/π) ∫ x² dx from -π to π = (1/π)(2π³/3) = 2π²/3. So the average value a0/2 is π²/3. Next, bn = (1/π) ∫ x² sin nx dx. Here x² is symmetric and sin nx is antisymmetric, so their product is antisymmetric and the integral over -π to π is 0. So every bn = 0. (Lesson 17 will turn this shortcut into a proper rule about even and odd functions.)

The worked example, computing an: an = (1/π) ∫ x² cos nx dx from -π to π = (2/π) ∫ x² cos nx dx from 0 to π. Integrating by parts twice, an antiderivative of x² cos nx is x² sin nx / n + 2x cos nx / n² - 2 sin nx / n³. At x = π, the sine terms vanish because sin nπ = 0, and cos nπ = (-1)^n, leaving 2π(-1)^n / n². At x = 0 everything is 0. So an = (2/π)(2π(-1)^n / n²) = 4(-1)^n / n². Putting it together: x² = π²/3 + 4 Σ (-1)^n cos nx / n² = π²/3 - 4 cos x + cos 2x - (4/9) cos 3x + ... for -π ≤ x ≤ π.

A beautiful bonus: Put x = π into that series. The left side is π². On the right, cos nπ = (-1)^n, so (-1)^n cos nπ = 1 for every n. We get π² = π²/3 + 4(1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + ...). Rearranging, 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + ... = π²/6. This famous result, the Basel problem, was first solved by Euler. Fourier series hand it to us almost for free. Exam papers love this kind of question: 'find the Fourier series of x² and hence show that Σ 1/n² = π²/6'.

Two handy facts you will use constantly: sin nπ = 0 for every integer n, and cos nπ = (-1)^n, which is 1 for even n and -1 for odd n. Also sin(nπ/2) cycles 1, 0, -1, 0, and cos 2nπ = 1. Nearly every Fourier calculation ends with plugging limits like 0, π or π/2 into these, so it pays to have them ready. Integration by parts, often written as ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du, is the other tool you need. Many students use the 'tabular' or DI method to speed up repeated integration by parts with polynomials.

Real life example 1, electricity at home: The electricity coming into homes in Bangladesh is alternating current with a frequency of 50 hertz, meaning the voltage wave repeats 50 times every second. Ideally it is a pure sine wave. But many devices, like phone chargers, LED lights and the IPS backup systems common in Dhaka flats, draw current in sharp, chopped-up bursts. That current is still periodic with the same 50 Hz period, so Fourier series says it is a sum of a 50 Hz fundamental plus harmonics at 100 Hz, 150 Hz, 200 Hz and so on. Power engineers measure these harmonics because large harmonics can heat up transformers and wires.

Real life example 2, music: When a harmonium or a guitar string plays a note, the sound wave is periodic. A pure sine wave sounds dull, like a tuning fork. A real instrument plays the fundamental note plus a set of harmonics at 2, 3, 4 times that frequency, each with its own strength. Those strengths are basically the Fourier coefficients of the sound wave. They are why a flute and a violin playing the same note sound different: same fundamental, different recipe of harmonics. The equalizer bars in your phone's music app show a running picture of how strong different frequencies are, which is the same idea.

Common mistakes: Students often forget the 1/π in front of the integrals, or use 1/(2π) for an and bn by mistake. Another common slip is writing a0 instead of a0/2 in the series after using the a0 = (1/π)∫ f formula, which doubles the average. Some forget that the function must be treated as periodic: the series describes the repeating extension, not just the piece you were given. Others make sign errors with cos nπ. Finally, many students try to integrate when the function is already a trig polynomial; always look for identities first.

What exams ask: Typical questions are: define a periodic function and find the period of something like sin 3x + cos 2x (answer 2π, the least common multiple of 2π/3 and π); state and prove the orthogonality relations; derive the Euler formulas; find the Fourier series of a given function on -π to π or 0 to 2π, then use it to sum a numerical series such as Σ 1/n² or Σ (-1)^(n+1)/n². Showing the integration by parts steps neatly usually earns most of the marks.

Recap: A periodic function repeats with some period T. Sines and cosines of nx all share the period 2π and are orthogonal on any interval of length 2π, meaning integrals of their products vanish unless the two functions are the same. That orthogonality lets us pull out each Fourier coefficient with a single integral: a0 = (1/π)∫ f, an = (1/π)∫ f cos nx, bn = (1/π)∫ f sin nx. The series f(x) = a0/2 + Σ (an cos nx + bn sin nx) rebuilds the function wave by wave. Next lesson, we work through the classic examples, the square wave, the sawtooth and |x|, and see what happens at sharp jumps.
key_points: A function is periodic with period T if f(x + T) = f(x) for all x; sin nx and cos nx have fundamental period 2π/n but all repeat after 2π.
A Fourier series writes a 2π-periodic function as f(x) = a0/2 + Σ (an cos nx + bn sin nx).
Orthogonality on (-π, π): ∫ sin mx cos nx = 0 always; ∫ sin mx sin nx and ∫ cos mx cos nx are 0 for m ≠ n and π for m = n ≥ 1.
Euler formulas: a0 = (1/π)∫ f dx, an = (1/π)∫ f cos nx dx, bn = (1/π)∫ f sin nx dx over one period.
a0/2 is the average value of f; any interval of length 2π gives the same coefficients.
Use sin nπ = 0 and cos nπ = (-1)^n to simplify; check trig identities before integrating.
The series of x² on (-π, π) is π²/3 + 4 Σ (-1)^n cos nx / n², which gives Σ 1/n² = π²/6.
lessons.tip: Write the three orthogonality integrals and the three Euler formulas on a small card and redo the derivation from memory once a day for a week. When you can derive them, you never have to memorise them again.
lessons.task: On paper or in Desmos (free in any phone browser), plot y = x² for -π < x < π, then plot π²/3 - 4cos x + cos 2x - (4/9)cos 3x. Add one more term, + (1/4)cos 4x, and watch the wave hug the bowl shape more closely.

quiz.q: What is the fundamental period of cos 4x?
quiz.explain: cos nx has fundamental period 2π/n, so cos 4x has period 2π/4 = π/2.

quiz.q: Over -π to π, what is the integral of sin 3x sin 3x?
quiz.explain: For m = n ≥ 1, the integral of sin mx sin nx over a full period is π.

quiz.q: Which formula gives bn for a 2π-periodic f?
options: (1/π)∫ f(x) sin nx dx over -π to π
(1/2π)∫ f(x) cos nx dx over -π to π
(1/π)∫ f(x) cos nx dx over 0 to π
∫ f(x) sin nx dx over 0 to 2π
quiz.explain: By orthogonality, multiplying by sin nx and integrating over a full period gives bn = (1/π)∫ f sin nx dx.

quiz.q: For f(x) = 3 + 2cos x - sin 3x, what is b3?
quiz.explain: The function is already a Fourier series; the coefficient of sin 3x is -1.

quiz.q: In the series f(x) = a0/2 + Σ(...), what does a0/2 represent?
options: The average value of f over one period
quiz.explain: a0/2 = (1/2π)∫ f dx over a period, which is the mean value of f.

lessons.title: Fourier Series Worked Examples: Square Wave, Sawtooth, |x| and Gibbs
lessons.content:
Learning the Euler formulas is like learning the rules of cricket. You only really understand the game after you play a few overs. In this lesson we play. We take the three most famous shapes in all of signal processing, the square wave, the sawtooth and the triangle-like |x|, and find their Fourier series step by step. Along the way we meet the Dirichlet conditions, which tell us when a Fourier series actually works, and a strange little troublemaker called the Gibbs phenomenon, which shows up whenever a function jumps.

Quick reminder: For a 2π-periodic function, f(x) = a0/2 + Σ (an cos nx + bn sin nx), with a0 = (1/π)∫ f dx, an = (1/π)∫ f cos nx dx and bn = (1/π)∫ f sin nx dx, all over -π to π. We will keep using sin nπ = 0 and cos nπ = (-1)^n. One shortcut we borrow early from Lesson 17: if a function is odd (f(-x) = -f(x)), all an are 0 and bn = (2/π)∫ f sin nx dx from 0 to π. If it is even (f(-x) = f(x)), all bn are 0 and an = (2/π)∫ f cos nx dx from 0 to π. These simply come from the fact that the integral of an odd function over -π to π is zero.

The square wave: Define f(x) = -1 for -π < x < 0 and f(x) = 1 for 0 < x < π, then repeat with period 2π. Picture a light switch flicked off and on at a steady rhythm, or the clock signal inside a computer chip that flips between low and high. The graph is flat steps with sudden jumps at x = 0, ±π, ±2π and so on. Notice f(-x) = -f(x), so the square wave is odd. Therefore every an, including a0, is 0. That makes sense: the wave spends equal time at +1 and -1, so its average is 0.

Square wave, computing bn: bn = (2/π) ∫ sin nx dx from 0 to π = (2/π)[-cos nx / n] from 0 to π = (2/π)(1 - cos nπ)/n = (2/(nπ))(1 - (-1)^n). When n is even, (-1)^n = 1 and bn = 0. When n is odd, (-1)^n = -1 and bn = 4/(nπ). So only odd harmonics appear: f(x) = (4/π)(sin x + sin 3x / 3 + sin 5x / 5 + sin 7x / 7 + ...). The amplitudes shrink like 1/n, which is quite slow. That slow shrinking is the signature of a function with jumps.

A bonus from the square wave: Put x = π/2, where f = 1. Since sin(π/2) = 1, sin(3π/2) = -1, sin(5π/2) = 1 and so on, we get 1 = (4/π)(1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/7 + ...). So 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/7 + ... = π/4. This is the Leibniz series for π. It is lovely that a picture of a switch flicking on and off secretly contains the number π.

The sawtooth wave: Now let f(x) = x for -π < x < π, repeated with period 2π. The graph climbs in a straight line from -π up to π, then drops suddenly back to -π and climbs again, like the teeth of a saw. Old TV screens swept their electron beam across the screen with exactly this kind of ramp, and many music synthesizers produce a sawtooth sound. Since f(-x) = -x = -f(x), this is odd, so an = 0 for all n including n = 0.

Sawtooth, computing bn: bn = (2/π) ∫ x sin nx dx from 0 to π. By parts with u = x and dv = sin nx dx, we get ∫ x sin nx dx = -x cos nx / n + sin nx / n². At π this is -π(-1)^n / n; at 0 it is 0. So bn = (2/π)(-π(-1)^n / n) = 2(-1)^(n+1) / n. The series is x = 2(sin x - sin 2x / 2 + sin 3x / 3 - sin 4x / 4 + ...). This time every harmonic appears, odd and even, and once again the amplitudes fall like 1/n, because the sawtooth also has jumps.

What happens at the jump: At x = π the sawtooth jumps from π (coming from the left) down to -π (on the right). What does the series give there? Every term is sin nπ = 0, so the series gives 0. Interesting: 0 is exactly halfway between π and -π. That is not a coincidence, and it leads us to the convergence theorem. Also try x = π/2: the series gives 2(1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - ...) = 2(π/4) = π/2, which matches f(π/2) = π/2. Good, the series works away from the jump.

The |x| wave: Let f(x) = |x| for -π < x < π, repeated. The graph is a row of upside-down V shapes, a triangle wave, like the zigzag roof of a factory shed. This one has no jumps at all. It is continuous, but it has sharp corners at x = 0 and x = ±π. Since |-x| = |x|, it is even, so all bn = 0. For a0: a0 = (2/π) ∫ x dx from 0 to π = (2/π)(π²/2) = π. So the average a0/2 = π/2, which makes sense because the values range between 0 and π.

|x|, computing an: an = (2/π) ∫ x cos nx dx from 0 to π. By parts, ∫ x cos nx dx = x sin nx / n + cos nx / n². At π: 0 + (-1)^n / n². At 0: 0 + 1/n². So an = (2/π)((-1)^n - 1)/n². For even n this is 0. For odd n it is (2/π)(-2/n²) = -4/(πn²). So |x| = π/2 - (4/π)(cos x + cos 3x / 9 + cos 5x / 25 + ...). Here the amplitudes fall like 1/n², much faster than 1/n. With just three or four terms the graph already looks almost perfect.

A bonus from |x|: Put x = 0, where |x| = 0. Then 0 = π/2 - (4/π)(1 + 1/9 + 1/25 + ...), so 1 + 1/9 + 1/25 + 1/49 + ... = π²/8. That is the sum of 1 over the odd squares. Combined with Σ 1/n² = π²/6 from Lesson 15, you can check it: the even squares 1/4 + 1/16 + ... are (1/4)(π²/6) = π²/24, and π²/6 - π²/24 = π²/8. Everything fits together.

Smoothness and decay: Compare the three examples. Square wave and sawtooth have jumps, and their coefficients shrink like 1/n. The |x| wave is continuous with corners, and its coefficients shrink like 1/n². Rule of thumb: the smoother the function, the faster its Fourier coefficients go to zero. A function whose derivatives of every order are continuous has coefficients that shrink faster than any power of 1/n. This is why sharp edges in a picture or a sound need lots of high-frequency content, and why smooth signals can be compressed well.

The Dirichlet conditions: When does a Fourier series actually converge to the function? A common sufficient set of conditions, named after Dirichlet, says: f is periodic with period 2π; in one period f has only a finite number of discontinuities, each a finite jump; f has only a finite number of maxima and minima in one period; and the integral of |f| over one period is finite. Square waves, sawtooths, |x|, x² and almost every function you meet in engineering satisfy these. These conditions are sufficient, not necessary: some functions break them and still have nice series.

The convergence theorem: If f satisfies the Dirichlet conditions, then its Fourier series converges at every x. At a point where f is continuous, it converges to f(x). At a jump, it converges to the average of the left and right limits, [f(x-) + f(x+)]/2. For the square wave at x = 0, the left limit is -1 and the right limit is 1, so the series gives 0. Check: every sin(n·0) = 0, so yes, 0. For the sawtooth at x = π, the average of π and -π is 0, which matches what we found. Exams love asking 'what does the series converge to at the jump?'.

The Gibbs phenomenon: Now the troublemaker. Take the square wave and add up the first N terms. As N grows, the partial sums get closer to the flat steps almost everywhere. But right next to each jump, the partial sum overshoots, rising above 1 to about 1.18 before settling down. You might think adding more terms will kill this bump. It does not. The bump gets narrower and moves closer to the jump, but its height stays at roughly 9 percent of the jump size. For the square wave the jump is 2, and the overshoot is about 0.18. This stubborn overshoot is called the Gibbs phenomenon, named after the American scientist J. Willard Gibbs.

Why Gibbs does not break the theorem: The convergence theorem talks about one fixed point x at a time. At any fixed x away from the jump, the bump eventually moves past it, so the partial sums do converge to f(x) there. The overshoot never disappears, but it slides towards the jump and gets squeezed into a thinner and thinner region. So we have pointwise convergence, but not uniform convergence near the jump. In practice, engineers fight Gibbs ringing by gently tapering the high-frequency coefficients instead of cutting them off sharply, using smoothing techniques such as Fejér (Cesàro) averaging or window functions.

Real life example 1, a computer's clock and data: Inside your laptop, a clock signal switches between low and high millions or billions of times per second. It is close to a square wave. Its Fourier series says it contains the fundamental frequency plus the odd harmonics 3, 5, 7 times higher. Circuit board designers must care about those high harmonics, because they can leak out as radio interference. When a cable or circuit cuts off the high harmonics, the sharp edges become rounded, and the received signal can show ringing near the edges, which is the Gibbs effect in real hardware.

Real life example 2, pictures and video: When you send a photo on Messenger or watch a video on YouTube with a weak mobile connection in a village, the image is compressed. JPEG compression uses a close cousin of Fourier series, the discrete cosine transform, and throws away weak high-frequency parts. Around sharp edges, like black text on a white signboard, you can sometimes see faint ripples or 'mosquito noise'. These artefacts come from the same idea: sharp edges need many high frequencies, and when you remove some, the edges ring.

Common mistakes: Many students forget that an odd function has a0 = 0 too, or they compute (1 - (-1)^n) wrongly and keep even terms for the square wave. Another mistake is claiming the series equals f at a jump; it equals the average. Some think Gibbs overshoot shrinks to zero with more terms; it does not, it only gets narrower. Also be careful with |x|: its series contains cosines only, and the constant term is π/2, not π. Finally, always draw the periodic extension before computing; sometimes the 'continuous' piece you were given creates jumps when repeated.

What exams ask: Find the Fourier series of the square wave, the sawtooth f(x) = x, or f(x) = |x| on (-π, π), then deduce π/4 = 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - ... or π²/8 = 1 + 1/9 + 1/25 + .... State the Dirichlet conditions. State what the series converges to at a point of discontinuity. Explain the Gibbs phenomenon in a few lines, mentioning the roughly 9 percent overshoot that does not vanish. Sketching the function and the first two or three partial sums also gains marks.

Recap: The square wave has series (4/π)Σ sin nx / n over odd n; the sawtooth x has series 2Σ (-1)^(n+1) sin nx / n; and |x| has series π/2 - (4/π)Σ cos nx / n² over odd n. Jumps make coefficients decay like 1/n; corners make them decay like 1/n². Under the Dirichlet conditions, the series converges to f where f is continuous and to the midpoint at jumps. Near jumps, partial sums overshoot by about 9 percent of the jump, the Gibbs phenomenon. Next lesson: even and odd shortcuts in full, half-range series, and functions with any period 2L.
key_points: Square wave (-1 on (-π,0), 1 on (0,π)): f = (4/π)(sin x + sin 3x/3 + sin 5x/5 + ...), odd harmonics only.
Sawtooth f(x) = x on (-π,π): x = 2Σ (-1)^(n+1) sin nx / n.
Jumps give coefficients ~1/n, corners give ~1/n²; smoother functions have faster-decaying coefficients.
Dirichlet conditions: periodic, finitely many finite jumps, finitely many maxima/minima, absolutely integrable over a period.
At a jump the series converges to [f(x-) + f(x+)]/2, the midpoint.
Gibbs phenomenon: partial sums overshoot near a jump by about 9% of the jump, and more terms only make the bump narrower.
lessons.tip: Before you compute any coefficient, sketch at least two periods of the function. The sketch tells you whether it is odd or even, where the jumps are, and what the series should give at those jumps, which catches most mistakes.
lessons.task: In Desmos or on graph paper, plot the square wave partial sums (4/π)(sin x + sin 3x/3) and then add sin 5x/5, sin 7x/7 and sin 9x/9. Look near x = 0: measure roughly how high the first peak goes. You should see it stay near 1.18 even as you add terms.

quiz.q: Which harmonics appear in the Fourier series of the standard square wave?
quiz.explain: bn = (2/(nπ))(1 - (-1)^n) is 0 for even n and 4/(nπ) for odd n, and an = 0 because the wave is odd.

quiz.q: At a jump from -1 to 1, the Fourier series converges to:
quiz.explain: Under the Dirichlet conditions the series converges to the average of the left and right limits, (-1 + 1)/2 = 0.

quiz.q: What is the constant term a0/2 in the Fourier series of |x| on (-π, π)?
quiz.explain: a0 = (2/π)∫ x dx over 0 to π = π, so a0/2 = π/2, the average of |x|.

quiz.q: As more terms are added, what happens to the Gibbs overshoot near a jump?
options: Its height stays about 9% of the jump but it gets narrower
It moves away from the jump
quiz.explain: The overshoot height tends to about 9% of the jump size; only its width shrinks as N grows.

quiz.q: Why do the coefficients of |x| decay faster than those of the square wave?
options: |x| is continuous (only corners), while the square wave has jumps
quiz.explain: Smoother functions have faster-decaying coefficients: jumps give ~1/n, corners give ~1/n².

lessons.title: Even and Odd Functions, Half-Range Series and Period 2L
lessons.content:
Imagine folding a sheet of paper exactly down the middle and looking at an ink blot. If the blot on the left is a perfect mirror image of the blot on the right, you only need to study one half to know the whole thing. Mathematicians use the same trick with functions. When a function has mirror symmetry, half of its Fourier coefficients vanish before you even pick up your pen. In this lesson we make that idea precise with even and odd functions, then use it to build half-range series for functions defined only on a piece of an interval, and finally free ourselves from the period 2π and handle any period 2L.

Even functions: A function is even if f(-x) = f(x) for every x. Its graph is a mirror image across the y-axis. Examples: x², x⁴, cos x, cos nx, |x|, and any constant. If you know an even function for x ≥ 0, you know it everywhere, because the left half is the reflection of the right half. A key fact: if f is even, then the integral of f from -a to a equals 2 times the integral from 0 to a. The two halves contribute equal areas.

Odd functions: A function is odd if f(-x) = -f(x) for every x. Its graph has rotational symmetry about the origin: spin it 180 degrees and it lands on itself. Examples: x, x³, sin x, sin nx, tan x. An odd function must pass through 0 at x = 0 if it is defined there, because f(0) = -f(0) forces f(0) = 0. The key fact: if f is odd, the integral from -a to a is 0, because the area on the right is exactly cancelled by the negative area on the left.

Products of even and odd: Multiplying functions follows the same rules as multiplying signs. Even times even is even, like (+)(+). Odd times odd is even, like (-)(-). Even times odd is odd, like (+)(-). So x² cos x is even, x sin x is even (odd times odd), and x² sin x is odd. These rules are the whole reason for the shortcuts that follow. Sums behave simply too: the sum of two even functions is even and the sum of two odd functions is odd, but even plus odd is usually neither.

Neither even nor odd: Most functions, like e^x or x + x², are neither. But here is a neat fact: every function can be split into an even part plus an odd part. The even part is fe(x) = [f(x) + f(-x)]/2 and the odd part is fo(x) = [f(x) - f(-x)]/2. Add them and you get f(x) back. For e^x, the even part is cosh x and the odd part is sinh x. For x + x², the even part is x² and the odd part is x. In Fourier terms, the even part produces the cosine terms and the odd part produces the sine terms.

Fourier series of an even function: Let f be even on (-π, π). Then f(x) cos nx is even times even, which is even, so an = (1/π)∫ f cos nx dx over -π to π = (2/π)∫ f(x) cos nx dx over 0 to π. And f(x) sin nx is even times odd, which is odd, so bn = 0 for every n. The series is a pure cosine series: f(x) = a0/2 + Σ an cos nx, with a0 = (2/π)∫ f dx from 0 to π. We saw this with x² in Lesson 15 and |x| in Lesson 16: no sine terms at all.

Fourier series of an odd function: Now let f be odd. Then f(x) cos nx is odd times even, which is odd, so every an = 0, including a0. And f(x) sin nx is odd times odd, which is even, so bn = (2/π)∫ f(x) sin nx dx from 0 to π. The series is a pure sine series: f(x) = Σ bn sin nx. The square wave and the sawtooth from Lesson 16 were odd, which is why only sine terms appeared. Spotting symmetry first can cut your work in half and remove a whole class of errors.

Half-range series, the idea: Often a function is given only on half an interval, say 0 < x < π, for example the shape of a guitar string between its two fixed ends, or the temperature along a rod. We are free to decide what the function does on -π < x < 0, because nobody told us. If we extend it as an even function (reflect it in the y-axis), we get a cosine series. If we extend it as an odd function (reflect it through the origin), we get a sine series. Both series equal the original f on 0 < x < π, at points where f is continuous. They only differ outside the original piece. These are called half-range cosine and half-range sine series.

Half-range formulas on (0, π): Half-range cosine series: f(x) = a0/2 + Σ an cos nx with an = (2/π)∫ f(x) cos nx dx from 0 to π, for n = 0, 1, 2, .... Half-range sine series: f(x) = Σ bn sin nx with bn = (2/π)∫ f(x) sin nx dx from 0 to π. Notice that you only ever integrate over the given piece, 0 to π. The even or odd extension is a picture in your head that justifies the formula; you never need to write it as a formula.

Example: f(x) = 1 on (0, π): The half-range sine series uses bn = (2/π)∫ sin nx dx from 0 to π = (2/(nπ))(1 - (-1)^n), which is 4/(nπ) for odd n and 0 for even n. So 1 = (4/π)(sin x + sin 3x / 3 + sin 5x / 5 + ...) on (0, π). That is exactly the square wave from Lesson 16, because the odd extension of the constant 1 is the square wave. The half-range cosine series of the same function is just 1, since the even extension is the constant 1 itself. Same function, two very different series.

Example: f(x) = x on (0, π): The half-range cosine series comes from the even extension, which is |x|, so x = π/2 - (4/π)(cos x + cos 3x / 9 + cos 5x / 25 + ...) on 0 ≤ x ≤ π. The half-range sine series comes from the odd extension, which is the sawtooth, so x = 2(sin x - sin 2x / 2 + sin 3x / 3 - ...) on 0 ≤ x < π. Which is better? The cosine series has coefficients like 1/n², because the even extension has no jumps, so it converges faster. The sine series has coefficients like 1/n, because the odd extension jumps at x = π.

Functions with any period 2L: Real signals rarely have period exactly 2π. A heartbeat might repeat every 0.8 seconds; the mains supply repeats every 0.02 seconds. The fix is a change of variable. If f has period 2L, set t = πx/L. As x runs from -L to L, t runs from -π to π, and the function becomes 2π-periodic in t. Converting back gives f(x) = a0/2 + Σ [an cos(nπx/L) + bn sin(nπx/L)], with an = (1/L)∫ f(x) cos(nπx/L) dx and bn = (1/L)∫ f(x) sin(nπx/L) dx, both from -L to L, and a0 = (1/L)∫ f dx. Put L = π and you get the old formulas back.

Half-range series on (0, L): The same symmetry shortcuts carry over. For an even function of period 2L, or the half-range cosine series of f on (0, L), an = (2/L)∫ f(x) cos(nπx/L) dx from 0 to L. For an odd function, or the half-range sine series, bn = (2/L)∫ f(x) sin(nπx/L) dx from 0 to L. These are the formulas used most often in exams and in solving physics problems like the vibrating string.

Worked example with period 2L: Let f(x) = x² on (-1, 1), period 2, so L = 1. It is even, so bn = 0. a0 = (2/1)∫ x² dx from 0 to 1 = 2/3, so a0/2 = 1/3. an = 2∫ x² cos(nπx) dx from 0 to 1. Using the same antiderivative pattern as before with k = nπ, the boundary terms leave 2cos(nπ)/(nπ)² at x = 1, so an = 2 × 2(-1)^n/(n²π²) = 4(-1)^n/(n²π²). Hence x² = 1/3 + (4/π²) Σ (-1)^n cos(nπx)/n². Check at x = 1: 1 = 1/3 + (4/π²)(π²/6) = 1/3 + 2/3. It works.

Worked half-range sine example: Find the half-range sine series of f(x) = x on (0, 2). Here L = 2, so bn = (2/2)∫ x sin(nπx/2) dx from 0 to 2. With k = nπ/2, ∫ x sin kx dx = -x cos kx / k + sin kx / k². At x = 2, kx = nπ, so this is -2(-1)^n / (nπ/2) + 0 = -4(-1)^n/(nπ). At x = 0 it is 0. So bn = 4(-1)^(n+1)/(nπ), and x = (4/π)[sin(πx/2) - sin(πx)/2 + sin(3πx/2)/3 - ...] for 0 ≤ x < 2.

Which half-range series to choose: In physics and engineering, the boundary conditions decide. Every sin(nπx/L) is zero at both x = 0 and x = L. So a sine series is natural for a guitar string tied down at both ends, or a metal rod whose ends are kept at zero temperature. Every cos(nπx/L) has zero slope at x = 0 and x = L, so a cosine series is natural for a rod whose ends are insulated, where no heat flows out. If the question just says 'find the half-range sine series', of course you follow the question.

Real life example 1, the ektara and the guitar: A Baul singer's ektara has a single string fixed at both ends. When plucked, the string can only vibrate in shapes that are zero at the two ends: half a sine wave, a full sine wave, one and a half, and so on. Those are exactly sin(nπx/L). The starting shape of the pluck, a triangle peaking where the finger pulled, is expanded in a half-range sine series. The coefficients tell you how loud each harmonic will be, which is why plucking near the middle sounds warmer and plucking near the end sounds brighter and more twangy.

Real life example 2, a hot iron rod: A blacksmith in a village bazar heats a rod and then puts both ends into water so they stay at roughly the water temperature. How does heat spread along the rod over time? Engineers solve the heat equation, and the solution is a half-range sine series whose terms decay in time, with higher harmonics dying out faster. After a few seconds the rod's temperature curve looks almost like a single half sine wave. This is the same method Fourier invented in the first place, in his work on heat.

Common mistakes: Students often mix up which extension gives which series: even extension gives cosines, odd extension gives sines. Another error is using 1/L instead of 2/L in half-range formulas, or forgetting to replace nx by nπx/L. Some forget that the half-range series only represents f on (0, L); outside it represents the extension. Watch the endpoints too: the half-range sine series always gives 0 at x = 0 and x = L, even if f is not 0 there, because every sine term is zero at those points.

What exams ask: Show that a given function is even or odd and write its Fourier series using the shortcut. Find both the half-range sine and cosine series of f(x) = x, x², or π - x on (0, π) or (0, L). Find the Fourier series of a function with period 2L, often with L = 1 or L = 2. Use the result to sum a numerical series. Explain why a sine series is appropriate for a string fixed at both ends.

Recap: Even functions have mirror symmetry and give pure cosine series; odd functions have point symmetry and give pure sine series. Products follow sign rules, and every function is an even part plus an odd part. A function given only on (0, L) can be extended evenly for a half-range cosine series or oddly for a half-range sine series, both using 2/L times an integral over 0 to L. For any period 2L, replace nx by nπx/L and 1/π by 1/L. Next lesson: writing Fourier series with complex exponentials, Parseval's identity, and measuring the energy in each harmonic.
key_points: Even: f(-x) = f(x), integral over (-a, a) is twice the integral over (0, a). Odd: f(-x) = -f(x), integral over (-a, a) is 0.
Even × even = even, odd × odd = even, even × odd = odd; any f = [f(x)+f(-x)]/2 + [f(x)-f(-x)]/2.
Even f gives a cosine series (bn = 0); odd f gives a sine series (all an = 0).
Half-range on (0, π): cosine series an = (2/π)∫₀^π f cos nx dx; sine series bn = (2/π)∫₀^π f sin nx dx.
Period 2L: f = a0/2 + Σ [an cos(nπx/L) + bn sin(nπx/L)], an = (1/L)∫ f cos(nπx/L), bn = (1/L)∫ f sin(nπx/L) over (-L, L).
Half-range on (0, L) uses 2/L times an integral from 0 to L.
Sine series suit ends fixed at zero (strings, rods at 0 temperature); cosine series suit insulated ends.
lessons.tip: For every Fourier question, write one line at the top: 'f is even / odd / neither, so ...'. This single habit tells you which coefficients are zero and saves at least half of the integration.
lessons.task: Take f(x) = x on (0, π). In Desmos, plot the first three terms of its half-range cosine series and the first three terms of its half-range sine series, both on -2π to 2π. Compare them with y = x on (0, π) and notice which one is closer, and what each looks like outside (0, π).

quiz.q: Which of these functions is odd?
quiz.explain: x³ and sin x are both odd, and the sum of odd functions is odd.

quiz.q: If f is even on (-π, π), which coefficients are always zero?
quiz.explain: f(x) sin nx is even × odd = odd, so its integral over (-π, π) is zero and every bn = 0.

quiz.q: The half-range sine series of f on (0, π) comes from which extension?
quiz.explain: Extending f as an odd function makes all an vanish, leaving a pure sine series.

quiz.q: For a function of period 2L, the argument of the cosines is:
quiz.explain: Substituting t = πx/L turns period 2L into period 2π, giving cos(nπx/L) and sin(nπx/L).

quiz.q: A guitar string fixed at both ends at x = 0 and x = L is best described by:
quiz.explain: Every sin(nπx/L) is zero at x = 0 and x = L, matching the fixed ends.

lessons.title: Complex Fourier Series, Parseval's Identity and Signal Energy
lessons.content:
Carrying a cosine and a sine for every harmonic is like carrying two separate bags to the bazar, one for vegetables and one for fish, when one big bag would do. In the first half of this course you met Euler's formula, e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ. It packs a cosine and a sine into one neat complex number. In this lesson we use it to pack the whole Fourier series into a single, cleaner formula with complex exponentials. Then we meet Parseval's identity, which tells us how the energy or power of a signal is shared among its harmonics, and we learn to draw a line spectrum, the picture engineers use every day.

From sines and cosines to exponentials: Euler's formula gives cos nx = (e^(inx) + e^(-inx))/2 and sin nx = (e^(inx) - e^(-inx))/(2i). Substitute these into an cos nx + bn sin nx. Collect the e^(inx) parts and the e^(-inx) parts. Since 1/i = -i, you get [(an - i bn)/2] e^(inx) + [(an + i bn)/2] e^(-inx). So each pair of real terms turns into two complex exponential terms, one with positive frequency n and one with negative frequency -n.

The complex Fourier series: Putting everything together, a 2π-periodic function can be written as f(x) = Σ cn e^(inx), where the sum runs over all integers n from minus infinity to plus infinity. The links to the real coefficients are: c0 = a0/2; cn = (an - i bn)/2 for n ≥ 1; and c(-n) = (an + i bn)/2. Going backwards, an = cn + c(-n) and bn = i(cn - c(-n)). One formula, one family of coefficients, no separate a and b to juggle.

Negative frequencies: Students often ask, what is a negative frequency? Think of e^(inx) as a point spinning around a circle as x increases. For positive n it spins anticlockwise; for negative n it spins clockwise. A real cosine is the sum of two spinners going in opposite directions at the same speed, whose imaginary parts cancel and leave a real back-and-forth motion. So negative frequencies are not mysterious; they are just the clockwise half of the bookkeeping that makes the complex form work.

Orthogonality, the complex way: The complex exponentials are orthogonal on (-π, π) too, and the rule is even simpler. The integral from -π to π of e^(imx) times e^(-inx) dx is 2π when m = n and 0 when m ≠ n. Why? When m ≠ n, the integrand is e^(i(m-n)x), which spins a whole number of times around the circle and averages to zero. When m = n, the integrand is just 1. Notice we multiply by e^(-inx), the conjugate, not e^(inx). For complex functions the natural 'dot product' uses the complex conjugate of one of them.

The coefficient formula: Multiply f(x) = Σ cm e^(imx) by e^(-inx) and integrate from -π to π. By orthogonality, only the m = n term survives, giving 2π cn. So cn = (1/(2π)) ∫ f(x) e^(-inx) dx from -π to π. One formula covers every n, positive, negative and zero. For n = 0 it gives c0 = (1/(2π))∫ f dx, the average value, which matches a0/2. For a general period T with fundamental angular frequency ω0 = 2π/T, the same idea gives f(t) = Σ cn e^(inω0t) and cn = (1/T)∫ f(t) e^(-inω0t) dt over one period.

Real signals have conjugate symmetry: If f is real-valued, then c(-n) is the complex conjugate of cn. You can see it from the formulas: cn = (an - i bn)/2 and c(-n) = (an + i bn)/2. So for real signals, the negative-frequency coefficients carry no new information; they mirror the positive ones. This also means |c(-n)| = |cn|, so the magnitude spectrum of a real signal is symmetric about n = 0. Even real functions have real cn, and odd real functions have purely imaginary cn.

Worked example 1, the square wave: Take f = -1 on (-π, 0) and 1 on (0, π). Then cn = (1/(2π))[-∫ e^(-inx) dx over (-π, 0) + ∫ e^(-inx) dx over (0, π)]. For n ≠ 0, the integral over (0, π) is (1 - (-1)^n)/(in), and the one over (-π, 0) is ((-1)^n - 1)/(in). Combining, cn = (1 - (-1)^n)/(iπn). For even n this is 0; for odd n it is 2/(iπn) = -2i/(πn). Also c0 = 0. Check with Lesson 16, where bn = 4/(nπ) for odd n: cn = (an - i bn)/2 = -i(2/(nπ)). It matches, and cn is purely imaginary because the square wave is odd.

Worked example 2, e^x on (-π, π): This one is much easier in complex form than in real form. cn = (1/(2π)) ∫ e^x e^(-inx) dx = (1/(2π)) ∫ e^((1 - in)x) dx from -π to π = (1/(2π)) [e^((1-in)π) - e^(-(1-in)π)]/(1 - in). Since e^(-inπ) = e^(inπ) = (-1)^n, this simplifies to cn = (-1)^n (e^π - e^(-π))/(2π(1 - in)) = (-1)^n sinh π / (π(1 - in)). One integral, no integration by parts twice. That is the practical power of the complex form.

Line spectrum: Because a periodic signal contains only the frequencies nω0, its spectrum is a set of separate vertical lines, not a smooth curve. The amplitude (or magnitude) spectrum plots |cn| against n or against frequency nω0. The phase spectrum plots the angle of cn. For the square wave, |cn| = 2/(π|n|) at odd n and 0 at even n, so you see lines at ±1, ±3, ±5 that get shorter like 1/n. Using real coefficients instead, the one-sided amplitude of harmonic n is sqrt(an² + bn²), which equals 2|cn| for n ≥ 1.

Parseval's identity, real form: Here is the star result. For a 2π-periodic function with Fourier coefficients an and bn, (1/π) ∫ f(x)² dx from -π to π = a0²/2 + Σ (an² + bn²), summing from n = 1 to infinity. The proof uses orthogonality: square the series, integrate, and all the cross terms vanish, leaving only the squares of each coefficient times π (and 2π for the constant). It is like Pythagoras' theorem for functions: the total 'length squared' equals the sum of the squares of the components along perpendicular directions.

Parseval's identity, complex form: In complex form it looks even nicer: (1/(2π)) ∫ |f(x)|² dx from -π to π = Σ |cn|², over all integers n. The left side is the average of |f|² over one period. The right side adds up the squared size of every harmonic. You can check that the two forms agree using c0 = a0/2 and |cn|² + |c(-n)|² = (an² + bn²)/2.

Parseval example 1, Σ 1/n² again: For f(x) = x on (-π, π), we know an = 0 and bn = 2(-1)^(n+1)/n, so bn² = 4/n². The left side is (1/π)∫ x² dx = (1/π)(2π³/3) = 2π²/3. Parseval gives 2π²/3 = Σ 4/n², so Σ 1/n² = π²/6. Same answer as Lesson 15, from a completely different route. Exams love asking you to get a series sum both ways.

Parseval example 2, the square wave: Here f² = 1 everywhere, so the left side is (1/π)(2π) = 2. The right side is Σ over odd n of (4/(nπ))² = (16/π²)(1 + 1/9 + 1/25 + ...). So 1 + 1/9 + 1/25 + ... = 2π²/16 = π²/8, matching Lesson 16. And with real f(x) = x², Parseval gives Σ 1/n⁴ = π⁴/90, another famous result you can derive on one page using the coefficients 4(-1)^n/n² from Lesson 15.

Power and energy of a signal: In signal language, if f(t) is a voltage across a 1 ohm resistor, then f(t)² is the instantaneous power. The average power of a periodic signal is P = (1/T)∫ |f(t)|² dt over one period, and Parseval says P = Σ |cn|². The energy in one period is T times that. Each harmonic contributes its own share: for n ≥ 1 the power at frequency nω0 is |cn|² + |c(-n)|² = 2|cn|² = (an² + bn²)/2. Periodic signals go on forever, so their total energy is infinite; that is why we talk about power for them. Signals that die out, like a single pulse, have finite total energy and are called energy signals, and they are handled by the Fourier transform in the next lesson.

How the power is shared in a square wave: A square wave of height 1 has average power 1, since f² = 1. The fundamental alone has power b1²/2 = (4/π)²/2 = 8/π², which is about 0.81. So roughly 81 percent of the power is in the first harmonic. Adding the third harmonic, with power (4/(3π))²/2 = 8/(9π²), about 0.09, brings the total to about 90 percent. This is why a low-pass filter that keeps just the first few harmonics still captures most of the square wave's power, even though the sharp corners need the rest.

Real life example 1, music and equalizers: When you play a song on your phone, the equalizer display shows bars for bass, mid and treble. Each bar is basically showing how much power sits in a band of frequencies, which is Parseval's idea in action: the total power is the sum of the power in each band. When you boost the bass, the app multiplies the low-frequency coefficients by a bigger number. A pure flute note has most of its power in the fundamental; a harmonium note spreads more power into the harmonics.

Real life example 2, power quality in factories: Garment factories around Gazipur and Savar run hundreds of sewing machines with motor drives, plus lights and computers, which can draw distorted current. Engineers measure total harmonic distortion, THD, which compares the power in the harmonics with the power in the 50 Hz fundamental. Using Parseval, THD is computed from the harmonic amplitudes as the square root of (sum of squares of harmonic amplitudes) divided by the fundamental amplitude. High THD means wasted energy and overheating, so factories install filters to cut it down.

Common mistakes: The most common slip is using 1/π instead of 1/(2π) in the formula for cn, or forgetting the minus sign in e^(-inx). Another is summing n only from 1 upwards in the complex series; it must run over all integers, including negative ones. In Parseval, students often forget the a0²/2 term, or write a0² instead of a0²/2, or forget to square the coefficients. Finally, remember that for real f, c(-n) is the conjugate of cn, not equal to cn.

What exams ask: Derive the complex form of the Fourier series from the real form and state the relations between cn and an, bn. Find the complex Fourier series of e^x, e^(ax), or a square wave on (-π, π). State and prove Parseval's identity. Use Parseval to show Σ 1/n² = π²/6, Σ 1/(2n-1)² = π²/8, or Σ 1/n⁴ = π⁴/90. Sketch the amplitude line spectrum of a given periodic signal. Find what fraction of the power is in the fundamental.

Recap: Euler's formula turns a Fourier series into f(x) = Σ cn e^(inx) over all integers n, with cn = (1/(2π))∫ f e^(-inx) dx. The links are c0 = a0/2, cn = (an - i bn)/2, c(-n) = (an + i bn)/2, and for real f the negative coefficients are conjugates of the positive ones. Plotting |cn| against frequency gives a line spectrum. Parseval's identity, (1/π)∫ f² = a0²/2 + Σ(an² + bn²) or (1/(2π))∫|f|² = Σ|cn|², says the average power equals the sum of the powers of the harmonics. Next lesson, we let the period grow to infinity and the lines melt into the continuous Fourier transform.
key_points: Complex Fourier series: f(x) = Σ cn e^(inx) over all integers n, with cn = (1/(2π))∫ f(x) e^(-inx) dx over (-π, π).
Links: c0 = a0/2, cn = (an - i bn)/2, c(-n) = (an + i bn)/2; for real f, c(-n) is the conjugate of cn.
Orthogonality: ∫ e^(imx) e^(-inx) dx over (-π, π) is 2π if m = n and 0 otherwise.
For period T: cn = (1/T)∫ f(t) e^(-inω0t) dt with ω0 = 2π/T.
A line spectrum plots |cn| (amplitude) and arg cn (phase) at the discrete frequencies nω0.
Parseval: (1/π)∫ f² = a0²/2 + Σ(an² + bn²), or (1/(2π))∫ |f|² = Σ |cn|².
Average power of a periodic signal equals the sum of harmonic powers; about 81% of a square wave's power is in its fundamental.
lessons.tip: Memorise only the complex formula cn = (1/(2π))∫ f e^(-inx) dx and the three links to an and bn. You can rebuild every other formula in this lesson from those in a minute, which is safer than memorising many.
lessons.task: With a calculator, add up (16/π²)(1 + 1/9 + 1/25 + 1/49 + 1/81) and halve it to get the power in the first five odd harmonics of a unit square wave. Compare with the total power 1. What percentage did five harmonics capture?

quiz.q: In the complex Fourier series on (-π, π), cn equals:
quiz.explain: Multiplying by e^(-inx) and using orthogonality (integral 2π when m = n) gives cn = (1/(2π))∫ f e^(-inx) dx.

quiz.q: For n ≥ 1, how is cn related to an and bn?
quiz.explain: Substituting Euler's formula into an cos nx + bn sin nx gives the e^(inx) coefficient (an - i bn)/2.

quiz.q: For a real-valued f, how is c(-n) related to cn?
options: It is the complex conjugate of cn
quiz.explain: From cn = (an - i bn)/2 and c(-n) = (an + i bn)/2 with real an, bn, c(-n) is the conjugate of cn.

quiz.q: Parseval's identity (real form) states that (1/π)∫ f² dx over (-π, π) equals:
quiz.explain: Orthogonality kills all cross terms, leaving a0²/2 + Σ(an² + bn²).

quiz.q: Roughly what fraction of a unit square wave's power is in its fundamental?
quiz.explain: Power in the fundamental is b1²/2 = (4/π)²/2 = 8/π² ≈ 0.81, out of a total power of 1.

lessons.title: From Series to Transform: The Fourier Integral and Fourier Transform
lessons.content:
Think about the tea stall near your school. Every morning the owner hears the same song on the radio at the same time. That song repeats, so a Fourier series can describe it with a neat list of notes: one base frequency and its whole-number multiples. But what about a single knock on the door? A single clap? A single lightning flash during Kalbaishakhi? These things happen once and never repeat. A Fourier series needs a period, and a one-time event has no period. So how do we find the "notes" hidden inside a single clap? The answer is the Fourier transform, and in this lesson we build it step by step, starting from the Fourier series you already know.

The big idea in one line: Make the period longer and longer until it becomes infinite. A function that repeats every 2L, with L going to infinity, is just a function that never repeats. As L grows, the allowed frequencies get packed closer and closer together, and the sum over separate frequencies turns into an integral over all frequencies. That integral is the Fourier integral, and the "recipe" it uses is the Fourier transform.

Step 1, the series with period 2L: From the earlier lessons, a function with period 2L can be written as f(x) = a0 + sum over n of [an cos(nπx/L) + bn sin(nπx/L)]. The frequencies used are ω_n = nπ/L. The gap between two neighbouring frequencies is Δω = π/L. Notice what happens when L = 10: the gap is about 0.31. When L = 1000 the gap is about 0.003. The frequencies are almost touching each other. That is the key observation.

Step 2, let L go to infinity: Put the formulas for an and bn into the series and write 1/L as Δω/π. Each term now looks like (Δω/π) times something that depends on ω_n. A sum of "something times Δω" is exactly a Riemann sum, the thing you used in school calculus to define an integral. As L goes to infinity, Δω goes to 0, and the sum becomes an integral over ω from 0 to infinity. The constant a0 is (1/2L) times the integral of f, and if the total area under |f| is finite, this goes to 0. It simply disappears.

The Fourier integral: The result is f(x) = integral from 0 to ∞ of [A(ω) cos ωx + B(ω) sin ωx] dω, where A(ω) = (1/π) ∫ f(v) cos ωv dv and B(ω) = (1/π) ∫ f(v) sin ωv dv, both integrals taken over the whole real line. Compare with the series: an and bn were numbers for separate n, now A(ω) and B(ω) are smooth functions of a continuous frequency ω. Instead of a list of notes, we now have a continuous spectrum, like a rainbow instead of a few coloured dots.

When does it work: The usual textbook conditions are: f is piecewise continuous on every finite interval, has left and right derivatives at every point (piecewise smooth), and is absolutely integrable, meaning the integral of |f(x)| over the whole line is finite. Under these conditions the Fourier integral equals f(x) wherever f is continuous. At a jump it gives the average of the left and right limits, exactly like Fourier series did at a jump. Same rule, new setting.

Worked example, the rectangular pulse: Let f(x) = 1 for |x| < 1 and f(x) = 0 for |x| > 1. Think of a torch switched on for exactly 2 seconds. f is even, so B(ω) = 0 because sin is odd. A(ω) = (1/π) ∫ from -1 to 1 of cos ωv dv = (1/π)(2 sin ω/ω) = 2 sin ω/(πω). So f(x) = (2/π) ∫ from 0 to ∞ of (sin ω cos ωx / ω) dω.

A free bonus integral: Look at that result at x = 0. Since f(0) = 1, we get 1 = (2/π) ∫ from 0 to ∞ of (sin ω/ω) dω. So ∫ from 0 to ∞ of sin ω/ω dω = π/2. This is the famous Dirichlet integral, and it is very hard to do with ordinary first-year calculus tricks. At x = 1, which is a jump, the integral gives the average (1 + 0)/2 = 1/2. For |x| > 1 it gives 0. Exams love asking "evaluate this integral using the Fourier integral of a suitable function" and this is the classic answer.

The complex form: Just like Fourier series had a neat complex form with e^(inx), the Fourier integral can be written with e^(iωx). Using cos ωx = (e^(iωx) + e^(-iωx))/2, the two real integrals combine into one integral over ω from -∞ to ∞. This leads straight to the transform pair, which is the version engineers and computer scientists actually use every day.

The Fourier transform and its inverse: In this course we use F(ω) = ∫ from -∞ to ∞ of f(x) e^(-iωx) dx, and the inverse f(x) = (1/2π) ∫ from -∞ to ∞ of F(ω) e^(iωx) dω. Read it like this: F(ω) answers "how much of frequency ω is inside f?" and the inverse rebuilds f by adding up all frequencies with those amounts. The minus sign in the forward exponent and the 1/2π in the inverse are a convention. Some books put 1/sqrt(2π) in front of both; physics books sometimes use e^(-2πi ξx) with no constant at all. All are correct as long as you stay with one choice. In an exam, always write down which convention you are using.

Example, pulse again: With f(x) = 1 for |x| < a and 0 otherwise, F(ω) = ∫ from -a to a of e^(-iωx) dx = (e^(iωa) - e^(-iωa))/(iω) = 2 sin(aω)/ω. At ω = 0 we take the limit, which is 2a, the area of the pulse. Notice something important: a narrow pulse (small a) gives a wide spread of frequencies, because sin(aω)/ω first hits zero at ω = π/a. A short clap has many frequencies. A long hum has few. Short in time means wide in frequency, and that is a deep rule of signals.

Example, two-sided exponential: Let f(x) = e^(-a|x|) with a > 0. Split the integral at 0. From 0 to ∞: ∫ e^(-ax) e^(-iωx) dx = 1/(a + iω). From -∞ to 0: ∫ e^(ax) e^(-iωx) dx = 1/(a - iω). Add them: (a - iω + a + iω)/(a² + ω²) = 2a/(a² + ω²). A real, even function gave a real, even transform. That is not luck: if f is real and even, F is real and even too.

Example, the Gaussian bell: The bell curve e^(-x²/2) has transform sqrt(2π) e^(-ω²/2). A Gaussian turns into another Gaussian. That is why bell-shaped pulses are loved in communication and in image blurring: they behave nicely in both time and frequency. You do not need to derive this one in most exams, but you should recognise it.

Fourier cosine and sine transforms: Many real problems live only on x ≥ 0, like heat flowing along a long rod from one end, or a signal that starts at time 0. For such f we can pretend f is extended as even or as odd. The even extension leads to the Fourier cosine transform: Fc(ω) = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of f(x) cos ωx dx, with inverse f(x) = (2/π) ∫ from 0 to ∞ of Fc(ω) cos ωx dω. The odd extension gives the Fourier sine transform: Fs(ω) = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of f(x) sin ωx dx, with inverse f(x) = (2/π) ∫ from 0 to ∞ of Fs(ω) sin ωx dω. Again, some books use sqrt(2/π) on both sides instead.

Worked example, cosine and sine transforms of e^(-ax): For f(x) = e^(-ax), a > 0, x ≥ 0, the standard results are Fc(ω) = a/(a² + ω²) and Fs(ω) = ω/(a² + ω²). Quick check: compute ∫ e^(-ax) e^(-iωx) dx from 0 to ∞ = 1/(a + iω) = (a - iω)/(a² + ω²). The real part is the cosine integral, a/(a² + ω²), and minus the imaginary part is the sine integral, ω/(a² + ω²). One complex integral, two answers. That is the kind of shortcut that saves ten minutes in an exam.

Which one to choose: Use the cosine transform when the problem tells you the slope f'(0) at the boundary, and the sine transform when it tells you the value f(0). This is because the cosine transform of f'' brings in f'(0), while the sine transform of f'' brings in f(0). You will meet this again in partial differential equations, so just remember the pairing for now.

Real life example 1, a mobile phone call in Dhaka: When you call your friend from Mirpur to Chattogram, your voice is a messy pressure wave that never exactly repeats. Inside the phone, the sound is turned into numbers, and the system thinks about it in terms of frequencies, which is exactly the Fourier transform idea. Human speech mostly lives roughly between 300 Hz and 3400 Hz for a classic phone line, so the network can throw away frequencies outside that band and save space. The transform tells engineers which part to keep.

Real life example 2, the cricket ball and the stump mic: In a match at Mirpur Sher-e-Bangla stadium, the stump microphone catches the tiny "tick" when the ball touches the bat edge. A tick is a very short pulse in time. From the pulse example you know a short pulse has a wide spread of frequencies. Tools like UltraEdge look at the sound signal (along with video) for that sudden spike. The math of "short in time, wide in frequency" is why a nick stands out from the smooth background noise of the crowd.

Common mistakes: First, mixing conventions: using the 1/2π in the forward transform and also in the inverse, which puts an extra factor in your answer. Pick one pair and stick to it. Second, forgetting that the function must be absolutely integrable: sin x or a constant 1 does not have an ordinary Fourier transform (they need delta functions, which come in the next lesson). Third, at a jump, writing the function value instead of the average. Fourth, mixing up which transform needs f(0) and which needs f'(0).

What exams ask: Typical questions are: derive the Fourier integral representation of a given pulse; use it to evaluate an integral such as ∫ sin ω cos ωx / ω dω; find the Fourier transform of e^(-a|x|) or a rectangular pulse; find the Fourier sine or cosine transform of e^(-ax); and state the inversion formula with conditions. Write the formula first, then the limits, then the integral. Neat steps earn marks even if a small sign slips.

Recap: A Fourier series handles periodic signals with separate frequencies. Let the period go to infinity and the frequencies merge into a continuous spectrum, giving the Fourier integral. Written with complex exponentials, it becomes the Fourier transform F(ω) = ∫ f(x) e^(-iωx) dx and its inverse with 1/2π. For half-line problems, the cosine and sine transforms do the job. Next lesson, we learn the properties that make this transform so powerful, including the famous convolution theorem.
key_points: A Fourier transform handles signals that never repeat by letting the period 2L go to infinity.
Fourier integral: f(x) = ∫0^∞ [A(ω) cos ωx + B(ω) sin ωx] dω with A, B = (1/π) ∫ f(v) cos/sin ωv dv.
Conditions: piecewise smooth and absolutely integrable; at a jump the integral gives the average.
Transform pair: F(ω) = ∫ f(x) e^(-iωx) dx and f(x) = (1/2π) ∫ F(ω) e^(iωx) dω; other conventions exist.
Pulse of half-width a gives 2 sin(aω)/ω; e^(-a|x|) gives 2a/(a² + ω²); short in time means wide in frequency.
Cosine and sine transforms work on x ≥ 0; for e^(-ax) they give a/(a² + ω²) and ω/(a² + ω²).
The pulse example yields the Dirichlet integral ∫0^∞ sin ω/ω dω = π/2.
lessons.tip: Write your chosen convention (where the minus sign and the 1/2π go) at the top of every answer. Most lost marks in this topic come from mixing two conventions in one solution.
lessons.task: On paper, compute the Fourier transform of the pulse f(x) = 1 for |x| < 2, 0 otherwise. Then use a phone calculator to find F(ω) at ω = 0.5, 1, 1.5 and 3 and sketch the curve. Repeat with |x| < 0.5 and see how the curve gets wider.

quiz.q: Why does a Fourier series not work directly for a single clap?
quiz.explain: A Fourier series needs a repeating (periodic) function; a one-time event has no period, so we let the period go to infinity.

quiz.q: With F(ω) = ∫ f(x) e^(-iωx) dx, what is the inverse formula?
quiz.explain: With this convention the inverse has a plus sign in the exponent and a factor 1/2π.

quiz.q: What is the Fourier transform of e^(-a|x|), a > 0?
quiz.explain: The two halves give 1/(a + iω) and 1/(a - iω); their sum is 2a/(a² + ω²).

quiz.q: At a jump of f, the Fourier integral gives:
options: the average of left and right limits
quiz.explain: Just like Fourier series, the integral converges to the midpoint of the jump.

quiz.q: What is the Fourier sine transform of e^(-ax), x ≥ 0?
quiz.explain: 1/(a + iω) = (a - iω)/(a² + ω²); minus the imaginary part gives the sine integral ω/(a² + ω²).

lessons.title: Fourier Transform Properties and the Convolution Theorem
lessons.content:
Imagine you have a big box of Lego. You could build every new model from loose bricks, or you could learn a few tricks: "this piece always clicks onto that one", "turning the base turns the whole house". Once you know the tricks, building gets fast. The Fourier transform is the same. Computing F(ω) = ∫ f(x) e^(-iωx) dx from scratch every time is slow and painful. Instead, we learn a handful of properties and a small table of standard pairs, and then most transforms can be written down in a few lines. This lesson is that toolbox. We keep the convention from the last lesson: F(ω) = ∫ f(x) e^(-iωx) dx and f(x) = (1/2π) ∫ F(ω) e^(iωx) dω, all integrals over the whole real line.

Notation: We write F{f} or F(ω) for the transform of f, and f ↔ F to say "f and F are a transform pair". So e^(-a|x|) ↔ 2a/(a² + ω²) from the last lesson. Read the arrow as "turns into".

Linearity: The transform of a sum is the sum of the transforms, and constants come out: a f + b g ↔ a F + b G. This is simply because an integral is linear. Example: 3e^(-|x|) + 5e^(-2|x|) ↔ 3·2/(1 + ω²) + 5·4/(4 + ω²) = 6/(1 + ω²) + 20/(4 + ω²). No new integral needed.

Time shifting: If you delay a signal by a, its transform gets multiplied by a phase factor: f(x - a) ↔ e^(-iωa) F(ω). Proof in one line: put u = x - a in the integral, and e^(-iωx) becomes e^(-iωa) e^(-iωu). Notice that |e^(-iωa)| = 1, so the size of each frequency does not change at all; only its phase (its timing) changes. That makes sense: a song played 5 seconds later has the same notes, just started later.

Frequency shifting: The mirror image of the last rule: multiplying by a complex exponential slides the spectrum. e^(iω0 x) f(x) ↔ F(ω - ω0). The whole spectrum moves right by ω0. This tiny formula is the heart of radio. Your voice lives at low frequencies; a radio station slides it up to a high carrier frequency so it can travel through the air.

Modulation: Real radios multiply by cos, not by a complex exponential. Since cos ω0x = (e^(iω0x) + e^(-iω0x))/2, frequency shifting gives f(x) cos ω0x ↔ (1/2)[F(ω - ω0) + F(ω + ω0)]. So the original spectrum is copied twice, half height, centred at +ω0 and -ω0. This is the modulation theorem and it explains AM radio. Similarly f(x) sin ω0x ↔ (1/2i)[F(ω - ω0) - F(ω + ω0)].

Scaling: If you squeeze a signal in time, its spectrum stretches: f(ax) ↔ (1/|a|) F(ω/a) for a ≠ 0. Example: if a = 2, the signal plays twice as fast (like a cassette in fast forward). Then F(ω/2) is stretched to twice as wide in frequency, and the height halves. This is why a fast-forwarded voice sounds squeaky: all frequencies are doubled. It is also the precise form of the rule "short in time, wide in frequency" from last lesson. Special case a = -1: f(-x) ↔ F(-ω).

Differentiation: Taking a derivative in x becomes multiplying by iω: f'(x) ↔ iω F(ω), provided f goes to 0 at ±∞. Proof: integrate by parts; the boundary term vanishes and the derivative of e^(-iωx) brings down -iω, and the minus signs cancel. Repeating, f''(x) ↔ (iω)² F(ω) = -ω² F(ω), and the nth derivative ↔ (iω)^n F(ω). This is the magic trick that turns differential equations into algebra. There is a twin rule: x f(x) ↔ i dF/dω.

Small example, using differentiation: Take the equation y'' - k² y = g(x) on the whole line, with y going to 0 far away. Transforming y'' - k² y = g gives (-ω² - k²) Y = G, so Y = -G/(ω² + k²). A calculus problem became a division. Laplace transforms in the coming lessons use the same trick with initial values built in.

Convolution: The convolution of f and g is (f * g)(x) = ∫ f(t) g(x - t) dt. Think of it as a sliding weighted average: flip g, slide it along, and at each position multiply and add. A blurry photo is the sharp photo convolved with a small blob. An echo in a big hall is your voice convolved with the hall's response. Convolution is slow to compute directly, because for every output point you do a whole integral.

The convolution theorem: Here is the star of the lesson: f * g ↔ F(ω) G(ω). Convolution in time becomes plain multiplication in frequency. The reverse also holds: f(x) g(x) ↔ (1/2π) (F * G)(ω). Proof sketch: write the transform of f * g as a double integral, swap the order, substitute u = x - t, and the double integral splits into ∫ f(t) e^(-iωt) dt times ∫ g(u) e^(-iωu) du. That is all.

Worked example with convolution: Let r(x) = 1 for |x| < 1/2 and 0 otherwise. Its transform is R(ω) = 2 sin(ω/2)/ω. The convolution r * r is a triangle: height 1 at x = 0, falling linearly to 0 at x = ±1. Without doing any new integral, the theorem tells us the triangle's transform is R(ω)² = 4 sin²(ω/2)/ω². That is a standard pair you can now produce in one line.

Duality: The transform and its inverse look almost the same, so pairs come in twins. If f(x) ↔ F(ω), then F(x) ↔ 2π f(-ω). Example: we know e^(-|x|) ↔ 2/(1 + ω²). Duality gives 2/(1 + x²) ↔ 2π e^(-|ω|), so 1/(1 + x²) ↔ π e^(-|ω|). We got the transform of 1/(1 + x²) without contour integration. (You could also check it with residues from lesson 14; it matches.)

Parseval and Plancherel: The energy of a signal is the same whether you measure it in time or in frequency: ∫ |f(x)|² dx = (1/2π) ∫ |F(ω)|² dω. This is the transform version of Parseval's identity for series. Engineers use |F(ω)|² as the energy spectrum: it shows which frequencies carry the energy.

Worked example, checking Parseval: Take f(x) = e^(-a|x|), a > 0. In time, ∫ |f|² dx = ∫ e^(-2a|x|) dx = 2 · 1/(2a) = 1/a. In frequency, F(ω) = 2a/(a² + ω²), so (1/2π) ∫ 4a²/(a² + ω²)² dω. The standard integral ∫ dω/(a² + ω²)² over the whole line equals π/(2a³) (you can get it with residues from lesson 14). So we get (1/2π) · 4a² · π/(2a³) = 1/a. Both sides agree, exactly as Parseval promises. Exams often ask you to verify the identity for this very function, so it is worth doing once by hand. Turned around, the same identity lets you evaluate a hard integral in ω by doing an easy one in x.

Delta function and standard pairs: The Dirac delta δ(x) is an idealised spike: zero everywhere except at 0, with total area 1, and ∫ δ(x) g(x) dx = g(0).
