Then δ(x) ↔ 1: a perfect click contains every frequency equally. By duality, 1 ↔ 2π δ(ω): a constant signal has only frequency zero. Also e^(iω0x) ↔ 2π δ(ω - ω0) and cos ω0x ↔ π[δ(ω - ω0) + δ(ω + ω0)]. These are how sin and cos, which are not absolutely integrable, get "transforms" after all.

A short table to remember: rectangular pulse of half-width a ↔ 2 sin(aω)/ω; e^(-a|x|) ↔ 2a/(a² + ω²); e^(-ax) for x > 0 (0 for x < 0) ↔ 1/(a + iω); e^(-x²/2) ↔ sqrt(2π) e^(-ω²/2); δ(x) ↔ 1; 1 ↔ 2π δ(ω); cos ω0x ↔ π[δ(ω - ω0) + δ(ω + ω0)]. With linearity, shifting, scaling and modulation, these few pairs build hundreds of others.

Example combining rules: Find the transform of e^(-|x - 3|) cos 10x. Start with e^(-|x|) ↔ 2/(1 + ω²). Shift by 3: e^(-|x - 3|) ↔ e^(-3iω) · 2/(1 + ω²). Call this G(ω). Modulate by cos 10x: the answer is (1/2)[G(ω - 10) + G(ω + 10)] = e^(-3i(ω - 10))/(1 + (ω - 10)²) + e^(-3i(ω + 10))/(1 + (ω + 10)²). Three rules, no integration.

From continuous to the computer, DFT and FFT: A computer cannot hold a function on the whole real line; it holds N samples x0, x1, ..., x(N-1). The Discrete Fourier Transform is X_k = sum from n = 0 to N - 1 of x_n e^(-2πikn/N), for k = 0, ..., N - 1. Doing this directly costs about N² multiplications. The Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), made famous by Cooley and Tukey in 1965, splits the problem into even and odd halves again and again, and needs only about N log2 N operations. For N = 1024 that is roughly 1,048,576 versus 10,240, about a hundred times faster. And the convolution theorem means fast convolution: FFT both, multiply, inverse FFT. You will meet the details in a signals or algorithms course.

Real life example 1, FM and AM radio in Bangladesh: When you tune to an FM station around 88 to 108 MHz on a bus in Dhaka, each station sits on its own carrier frequency. Modulation shifts the audio spectrum up near the carrier, so many stations share the air without mixing, each in its own frequency slot. Your radio's tuner picks one slot and shifts it back down. That whole idea is the modulation theorem, (1/2)[F(ω - ω0) + F(ω + ω0)].

Real life example 2, photos on your phone: When you share a photo on Facebook or Messenger, it is usually compressed as JPEG. JPEG uses the discrete cosine transform, a close cousin of the Fourier transform, on 8×8 blocks of pixels. Most of the picture's energy sits in low frequencies, so high-frequency details that your eye barely notices can be stored roughly or dropped. Blurring a photo in an editing app is convolution, and big blurs are often done fast through FFTs and the convolution theorem.

Common mistakes: Getting the sign wrong in the shift: f(x - a) gives e^(-iωa), not e^(+iωa). Forgetting the 1/|a| in scaling, or writing F(aω) instead of F(ω/a). Forgetting the 1/2 in modulation. Writing the convolution theorem backwards: it is convolution in time that becomes multiplication in frequency, and the reverse needs the 1/2π (in our convention). Mixing up convolution with ordinary multiplication: f * g is an integral, not f times g.

What exams ask: State and prove the shifting or modulation theorem; prove the convolution theorem; find the transform of a shifted or modulated pulse using properties; verify Parseval for e^(-a|x|); use duality to find the transform of 1/(a² + x²). Proofs are usually short substitutions, so practise writing them cleanly.

Recap: Linearity, time shift (multiply by e^(-iωa)), frequency shift and modulation (slide the spectrum), scaling (squeeze time, stretch frequency), differentiation (multiply by iω), convolution theorem (convolution becomes multiplication), duality and Parseval. Add a small table of pairs and the delta function, and you can handle almost any transform. On computers, the DFT and the FFT do this with samples. Next we switch to a cousin built for initial value problems: the Laplace transform.
key_points: Linearity: a f + b g ↔ a F + b G.
Time shift f(x - a) ↔ e^(-iωa) F(ω); frequency shift e^(iω0x) f(x) ↔ F(ω - ω0).
Modulation: f(x) cos ω0x ↔ (1/2)[F(ω - ω0) + F(ω + ω0)], the basis of radio.
Scaling: f(ax) ↔ (1/|a|) F(ω/a); squeezing time stretches frequency.
Derivative: f' ↔ iω F, so differential equations turn into algebra.
Convolution theorem: f * g ↔ F G; duality and Parseval complete the toolbox.
Standard pairs: δ ↔ 1, 1 ↔ 2πδ(ω), e^(-a|x|) ↔ 2a/(a² + ω²); the FFT computes the DFT in about N log2 N steps.
lessons.tip: Make one page with the property table and five standard pairs, and practise building new transforms only from that page. If you need a fresh integral, first ask which property you forgot.
lessons.task: Draw the rectangle r(x) = 1 for |x| < 1/2 on paper. Slide a second copy across it and plot the overlap area at x = -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1. You should get a triangle; then write its transform 4 sin²(ω/2)/ω² using the convolution theorem.

quiz.q: Using F(ω) = ∫ f(x) e^(-iωx) dx, what is the transform of f(x - a)?
quiz.explain: Substituting u = x - a pulls out e^(-iωa); the size of each frequency stays the same.

quiz.q: The convolution theorem says the transform of f * g is:
quiz.explain: Convolution in time becomes ordinary multiplication in frequency.

quiz.q: What is the transform of f(2x)?
quiz.explain: Scaling rule: f(ax) ↔ (1/|a|) F(ω/a); squeezing in time stretches the spectrum.

quiz.q: f(x) cos ω0x has transform:
quiz.explain: Modulation theorem: cos splits into two exponentials, each sliding a half-height copy of the spectrum.

quiz.q: Roughly how many operations does an FFT need for N samples?
quiz.explain: The FFT splits the DFT into halves repeatedly, cutting N² down to about N log2 N.

lessons.title: The Laplace Transform: Definition, Existence and Basic Table
lessons.content:
Imagine you are stuck in a Dhaka traffic jam and need to solve a hard maths problem in your head. A clever friend says: "Translate it into English, solve the easy English version, then translate the answer back to Bangla." The translation step feels like extra work, but the middle step becomes so easy that the whole trip is faster. The Laplace transform is exactly that kind of translator. It takes a function of time t, turns it into a function of a new variable s, and in the s-world, derivatives become multiplication and differential equations become simple algebra. Then we translate back. Engineers have used this trick for over a century to analyse circuits, motors, and control systems.

Why not just use Fourier: The Fourier transform needs functions that die away at both ends, so e^(2t), t², or even a constant switched on at t = 0 and left on forever cause trouble. Also, in real problems we usually know what happens from a starting moment t = 0 onwards: "the switch was flipped at t = 0, the spring was released at t = 0". The Laplace transform is built for exactly this: it only looks at t ≥ 0, and it multiplies by a decaying factor e^(-st) that tames functions that grow.

The definition: For a function f(t) defined for t ≥ 0, the Laplace transform is F(s) = L{f(t)} = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(-st) f(t) dt. The integral is improper, so it means the limit as T goes to infinity of ∫ from 0 to T. If this limit exists for some values of s, those values give F(s). We usually take s real for computing tables, but s can be complex, s = σ + iω. If you put σ = 0 and only keep t ≥ 0, the kernel e^(-iωt) is the Fourier one; so Laplace is like a Fourier transform with an extra damping factor e^(-σt).

Notation habit: Lower-case letters for time functions, capital letters for their transforms: f ↔ F, y ↔ Y, i(t) ↔ I(s). The inverse transform is written L⁻¹{F(s)} = f(t). We will study how to compute inverses in lesson 23; for now, just use the table backwards.

First transform, the constant 1: L{1} = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(-st) dt = [-e^(-st)/s] from 0 to ∞. If s > 0, e^(-st) goes to 0 as t grows, so the answer is 0 - (-1/s) = 1/s. If s ≤ 0, the integral blows up. So L{1} = 1/s, valid for s > 0. Notice the condition. Every transform comes with a region where it exists.

Second transform, e^(at): L{e^(at)} = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(-(s - a)t) dt = 1/(s - a), valid for s > a. This one is the master key; many others come from it. With a = 0 we get back 1/s. With a = -3, L{e^(-3t)} = 1/(s + 3) for s > -3.

Third transform, t: By parts with u = t and dv = e^(-st) dt: ∫ t e^(-st) dt = [-t e^(-st)/s] + (1/s) ∫ e^(-st) dt. The boundary term is 0 at both ends when s > 0 (exponential beats t), and the rest is (1/s)(1/s). So L{t} = 1/s². Repeating the same argument gives L{t^n} = n!/s^(n+1) for n = 0, 1, 2, .... For example L{t³} = 6/s⁴.

Sine and cosine in one shot: Use the master key with a = i·a (complex!): L{e^(iat)} = 1/(s - ia) = (s + ia)/(s² + a²). Since e^(iat) = cos at + i sin at, split real and imaginary parts: L{cos at} = s/(s² + a²) and L{sin at} = a/(s² + a²), both for s > 0. Check with a = 2: L{sin 2t} = 2/(s² + 4). This complex trick is a nice reminder of why we studied complex numbers at the start of the course.

Hyperbolic functions: Since cosh at = (e^(at) + e^(-at))/2 and sinh at = (e^(at) - e^(-at))/2, linearity gives L{cosh at} = (1/2)(1/(s - a) + 1/(s + a)) = s/(s² - a²) and L{sinh at} = a/(s² - a²), both for s > |a|. Notice how similar they look to cos and sin, with a minus instead of a plus. Students often swap them, so look closely at the sign.

Linearity, briefly: Because integrals are linear, L{a f + b g} = a F + b G. So L{3 + 2t - 5e^(4t)} = 3/s + 2/s² - 5/(s - 4), valid for s > 4 (the strictest of the conditions). We will collect all the other properties in the next lesson.

Worked example, a piecewise function from the definition: Let f(t) = 2 for 0 ≤ t < 3 and f(t) = 0 for t ≥ 3, like a fan running for 3 seconds and then switched off. The definition gives F(s) = ∫ from 0 to 3 of 2e^(-st) dt = 2[-e^(-st)/s] from 0 to 3 = (2/s)(1 - e^(-3s)). The factor e^(-3s) is the fingerprint of something happening at t = 3. In the next lesson the unit step function will give this same answer in one line, but it is good to see it come straight from the integral first.

Worked examples using identities: Many functions are not in the table directly but can be rewritten. sin² t = (1 - cos 2t)/2, so L{sin² t} = (1/2)(1/s - s/(s² + 4)) = 2/(s(s² + 4)) after simplifying. Next, (t + 1)² = t² + 2t + 1, so L{(t + 1)²} = 2/s³ + 2/s² + 1/s. And sin 3t cos 3t = (1/2) sin 6t, so its transform is (1/2)(6/(s² + 36)) = 3/(s² + 36). The pattern is always: use algebra or trig identities to turn the function into a sum of table entries, then apply linearity. Never try to transform a product by multiplying transforms.

A feel for the s-world: Large s means the factor e^(-st) dies very fast, so F(s) for large s mostly "sees" f near t = 0. Small s lets the transform look far into the future. This is the intuition behind the initial and final value theorems you will meet in lesson 23. Also, places where F(s) blows up, such as s = a for 1/(s - a), are linked to how f grows: e^(at) grows like e^(at), and the trouble spot sits exactly at s = a. Engineers call these points poles, and the word is the same one you met with residues.

The Gamma function and fractional powers: For non-integer powers we need Γ(x) = ∫ from 0 to ∞ of t^(x-1) e^(-t) dt, which satisfies Γ(n + 1) = n! for whole numbers n. Then L{t^a} = Γ(a + 1)/s^(a+1) for a > -1, s > 0. Since Γ(1/2) = sqrt(π), we get L{t^(-1/2)} = sqrt(π/s), and L{t^(1/2)} = Γ(3/2)/s^(3/2) = (sqrt(π)/2)/s^(3/2).

When does the transform exist: Two conditions together are enough. First, f is piecewise continuous on every finite interval [0, T]: it may have finitely many jumps there, but no infinite spikes. Second, f is of exponential order: there are constants M, c and T0 such that |f(t)| ≤ M e^(ct) for all t ≥ T0. In words, f does not grow faster than some exponential. Then L{f} exists for every s > c.

Examples of exponential order: t^10 is of exponential order (any c > 0 works, because e^(ct) eventually beats any power). sin t and cos t are bounded, so c = 0 works. e^(5t) is of order with c = 5. But e^(t²) is not of exponential order, because t² eventually beats ct for every c, so e^(t²)/e^(ct) goes to infinity. Its Laplace transform does not exist.

Sufficient, not necessary: The two conditions guarantee existence, but a function can fail them and still have a transform. The classic example is t^(-1/2): it blows up at t = 0, so it is not piecewise continuous on [0, T], yet its transform sqrt(π/s) exists because the spike is integrable. Exams sometimes ask exactly this: "Are the conditions necessary?" Answer: no, give t^(-1/2).

Two facts about F(s): If f satisfies the conditions, then F(s) goes to 0 as s goes to infinity. So a function like s/(s + 1) or the constant 1 cannot be the Laplace transform of an ordinary function (it needs an impulse, coming in lesson 22). Also, uniqueness (Lerch's theorem): two continuous functions with the same Laplace transform are equal. That is why we can trust the table backwards when we invert.

The basic table: 1 ↔ 1/s; t^n ↔ n!/s^(n+1); e^(at) ↔ 1/(s - a); sin at ↔ a/(s² + a²); cos at ↔ s/(s² + a²); sinh at ↔ a/(s² - a²); cosh at ↔ s/(s² - a²); t^a ↔ Γ(a + 1)/s^(a+1). Learn these by heart; almost every Laplace problem starts here.

Real life example 1, charging a phone: When you plug your phone in at home during load-shedding recovery, think of a simple RC circuit charging up. The capacitor voltage often looks like v(t) = V(1 - e^(-t/RC)). Its transform is V(1/s - 1/(s + 1/RC)). Engineers prefer working with this algebraic form in s, because when the circuit gets more parts, combining them in the s-world is just adding and multiplying fractions.

Real life example 2, a rickshaw on a bumpy road: The seat spring of a rickshaw gets a sudden push when the wheel hits a pothole. The bounce afterwards looks like a decaying sine, something like e^(-2t) sin 5t. With the table and the shifting rule from the next lesson, its transform is 5/((s + 2)² + 25). The numbers in the denominator directly show the decay rate 2 and the bounce frequency 5. Reading behaviour off the s-form is a big reason the Laplace transform is loved in control engineering.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the region of existence (s > a). Mixing up sin and cos: sin has a on top, cos has s on top. Mixing up sin with sinh: plus sign versus minus sign. Writing L{t^n} = n!/s^n instead of n!/s^(n+1). And assuming L{f g} = F G; that is false, the transform of a product is not the product of transforms.

What exams ask: Define the Laplace transform and state sufficient conditions for existence; show whether a function is of exponential order; derive L{1}, L{e^(at)}, L{t^n}, L{sin at}, L{cos at} from the definition; use linearity on a sum such as 4 - 3t² + 2 cos 3t; and show that the conditions are not necessary using t^(-1/2).

Recap: The Laplace transform F(s) = ∫ from 0 to ∞ e^(-st) f(t) dt turns time functions into functions of s. It exists for piecewise continuous functions of exponential order, for s large enough. A short table of transforms, derived from 1, e^(at) and t^n, covers most needs. Next lesson we add the powerful properties: shifting, derivatives, integrals, unit steps, impulses and periodic functions.
key_points: Definition: F(s) = L{f} = ∫0^∞ e^(-st) f(t) dt, an improper integral that exists only for some s.
Laplace looks only at t ≥ 0 and its damping factor e^(-st) tames growing functions, unlike Fourier.
Sufficient conditions: piecewise continuous on every [0, T] and of exponential order |f| ≤ M e^(ct); then F exists for s > c.
Basic pairs: 1 ↔ 1/s, t^n ↔ n!/s^(n+1), e^(at) ↔ 1/(s - a).
sin at ↔ a/(s² + a²), cos at ↔ s/(s² + a²); sinh and cosh use s² - a².
t^a ↔ Γ(a + 1)/s^(a+1); t^(-1/2) ↔ sqrt(π/s) shows the conditions are not necessary.
e^(t²) has no Laplace transform; F(s) → 0 as s → ∞; Lerch's theorem makes the inverse unique.
lessons.tip: Derive the table yourself once: 1, e^(at), t, then sin and cos from e^(iat). After deriving, you will remember which one has s on top and which has a.
lessons.task: Without looking at the lesson, write the eight table entries on a card. Then use a phone calculator to check L{e^(-t)} at s = 1 numerically: add e^(-2t) × 0.1 for t = 0, 0.1, ..., 5 and compare with 1/(s + 1) = 0.5.

quiz.q: What is L{e^(at)}?
quiz.explain: ∫0^∞ e^(-(s-a)t) dt = 1/(s - a), which converges only when s > a.

quiz.q: Which is the Laplace transform of cos 3t?
quiz.explain: cos at ↔ s/(s² + a²); with a = 3 that is s/(s² + 9).

quiz.q: L{t^4} equals:
quiz.explain: L{t^n} = n!/s^(n+1); 4! = 24 and the power of s is 5.

quiz.q: Which function is NOT of exponential order?
quiz.explain: e^(t²) eventually outgrows M e^(ct) for every c, so its Laplace transform does not exist.

quiz.q: t^(-1/2) has Laplace transform sqrt(π/s) although it is not piecewise continuous at 0. This shows the existence conditions are:
quiz.explain: The conditions guarantee existence, but a function can fail them and still have a transform.

lessons.title: Laplace Transform Properties: Shifting, Derivatives, Steps, Impulses and Periodic Functions
lessons.content:
Think of a good kitchen in a Bangladeshi home. Ammu does not cook every dish from zero. She has ready ginger-garlic paste, fried onions, a box of mixed spices. With these few prepared things, she can make bhuna, korma, or bhaji in minutes. Last lesson we made our "ready paste": the basic table of Laplace transforms. This lesson gives us the "cooking moves": properties that turn those few basic transforms into hundreds of new ones, and that handle switches, sudden kicks and repeating signals. These properties are exactly what make the Laplace transform a powerful tool for solving differential equations.

Linearity: L{a f + b g} = a F(s) + b G(s). We met this already. It lets us transform sums term by term. Example: L{2 sin 3t - 4t²} = 6/(s² + 9) - 8/s³.

First shifting theorem (s-shifting): Multiplying by an exponential shifts the transform: L{e^(at) f(t)} = F(s - a). Proof: ∫ e^(-st) e^(at) f(t) dt = ∫ e^(-(s - a)t) f(t) dt, which is F evaluated at s - a. Example: L{e^(2t) sin 3t}. Since L{sin 3t} = 3/(s² + 9), replace s by s - 2: 3/((s - 2)² + 9). Another: L{t³ e^(-t)} = 6/(s + 1)⁴. Notice: e^(-t) means a = -1, so s - a = s + 1. Sign errors here are the most common mistake in the whole topic.

Multiplication by t: L{t f(t)} = -F'(s), and more generally L{t^n f(t)} = (-1)^n F^(n)(s), the nth derivative with respect to s. Reason: differentiate F(s) = ∫ e^(-st) f(t) dt with respect to s, and the s-derivative of e^(-st) brings down -t. Example: L{t sin at}. F(s) = a/(s² + a²), F'(s) = -2as/(s² + a²)², so L{t sin at} = 2as/(s² + a²)². Similarly L{t cos at} = (s² - a²)/(s² + a²)².

Division by t: If the limit of f(t)/t as t goes to 0 from the right exists, then L{f(t)/t} = ∫ from s to ∞ of F(u) du. Example: L{sin t/t} = ∫ from s to ∞ of 1/(u² + 1) du = π/2 - arctan s = arctan(1/s) for s > 0. Now let s go to 0: ∫ from 0 to ∞ of sin t/t dt = π/2. This is the same Dirichlet integral we got from the Fourier integral in lesson 19, now in two lines. Many university exams ask "evaluate ∫ e^(-t) sin t/t dt": that is just the transform at s = 1, which is arctan 1 = π/4.

Worked example, another division by t: Find L{(1 - cos t)/t}. First, (1 - cos t)/t goes to 0 as t goes to 0, so the rule applies. L{1 - cos t} = 1/s - s/(s² + 1). Integrate from s to ∞: ∫ (1/u - u/(u² + 1)) du = [ln u - (1/2) ln(u² + 1)] = [ln(u/sqrt(u² + 1))] from s to ∞. At infinity, u/sqrt(u² + 1) goes to 1 and ln 1 = 0. So the answer is -ln(s/sqrt(s² + 1)) = (1/2) ln(1 + 1/s²). Logarithms appearing in a Laplace answer are a sign that division by t was used.

Worked example, evaluating a real integral: Find ∫ from 0 to ∞ of t e^(-2t) sin t dt. Look closely: it is exactly the definition of L{t sin t} with s = 2. From the multiplication-by-t rule, L{t sin t} = 2s/(s² + 1)². Put s = 2: 4/25 = 0.16. No integration by parts twice, no long working. This trick, "spot a Laplace transform hiding inside a definite integral", is a favourite exam question.

Transform of a derivative: This is the property that makes Laplace famous. L{f'(t)} = s F(s) - f(0). Proof by parts: ∫ e^(-st) f'(t) dt = [e^(-st) f(t)] from 0 to ∞ + s ∫ e^(-st) f(t) dt = -f(0) + s F(s), as long as f is of exponential order so the upper boundary term vanishes. Apply it twice: L{f''} = s² F(s) - s f(0) - f'(0). In general L{f^(n)} = s^n F - s^(n-1) f(0) - ... - f^(n-1)(0). The initial values appear automatically. Compare with the Fourier rule f' ↔ iωF: Laplace keeps the starting values, which is exactly what initial value problems need.

Quick check of the derivative rule: Take f = sin at, so f' = a cos at and f(0) = 0. The rule says L{a cos at} = s · a/(s² + a²) - 0 = as/(s² + a²). Dividing by a gives L{cos at} = s/(s² + a²). Correct. You can use this kind of check to rebuild a forgotten table entry in an exam.

Transform of an integral: L{∫ from 0 to t of f(τ) dτ} = F(s)/s. Integrating in time is dividing by s, just as differentiating is (roughly) multiplying by s. Example: L{∫ from 0 to t of sin 2τ dτ} = 2/(s(s² + 4)). Check: the integral equals (1 - cos 2t)/2 = sin² t, and in lesson 21 we found L{sin² t} = 2/(s(s² + 4)). It matches.

The unit step function: The Heaviside unit step u(t - a), also written H(t - a), is 0 for t < a and 1 for t ≥ a. It is a switch that turns on at time a. Its transform is L{u(t - a)} = ∫ from a to ∞ of e^(-st) dt = e^(-as)/s for a ≥ 0. Steps let us write piecewise functions as one formula. A function that is g1 before a and g2 after a is g1 + (g2 - g1) u(t - a). A window that is on between a and b is u(t - a) - u(t - b).

Second shifting theorem (t-shifting): If you delay f by a and switch it on at a, the transform gets a factor e^(-as): L{f(t - a) u(t - a)} = e^(-as) F(s). The key is that the function inside must be written in terms of t - a. Example: L{(t - 2)² u(t - 2)} = e^(-2s) · 2/s³. But for L{t u(t - 2)}, first rewrite t = (t - 2) + 2, so it is [(t - 2) + 2] u(t - 2), and the transform is e^(-2s)(1/s² + 2/s). A handy equivalent form: L{g(t) u(t - a)} = e^(-as) L{g(t + a)}. Here g(t + 2) = t + 2, whose transform is 1/s² + 2/s. Same answer.

Worked example, a piecewise signal: Let f(t) = 2 for 0 ≤ t < 3 and f(t) = 5 for t ≥ 3. Write f = 2 + 3u(t - 3). Then F(s) = 2/s + 3e^(-3s)/s. Another: the fan from last lesson, 2 for 0 ≤ t < 3 then 0, is 2 - 2u(t - 3), giving (2/s)(1 - e^(-3s)), the same answer as the long integral. Much faster.

The Dirac delta (unit impulse): δ(t - a) models a very strong, very short kick at time a, like a hammer hit or a cricket bat striking the ball. It is zero except at t = a, has total area 1, and ∫ δ(t - a) g(t) dt = g(a). Its transform is L{δ(t - a)} = e^(-as), and L{δ(t)} = 1. This explains the puzzle from lesson 21: a constant like 1 is not the transform of any ordinary function, but it is the transform of an impulse. The delta is also the derivative of the unit step, in a generalised sense, and s · e^(-as)/s = e^(-as) agrees with the derivative rule.

Periodic functions: If f(t + T) = f(t) for all t ≥ 0, we only need one period: L{f} = (1/(1 - e^(-sT))) ∫ from 0 to T of e^(-st) f(t) dt. Reason: the integral over [0, ∞) is the sum of integrals over [0, T], [T, 2T], ..., and each later one is e^(-sT) times the previous, a geometric series with sum 1/(1 - e^(-sT)).

Worked example, a square wave: Let f = 1 for 0 < t < a and -1 for a < t < 2a, repeating with period 2a. One period gives ∫ from 0 to a of e^(-st) dt - ∫ from a to 2a of e^(-st) dt = (1 - e^(-as))/s - (e^(-as) - e^(-2as))/s = (1 - e^(-as))²/s. Divide by 1 - e^(-2as) = (1 - e^(-as))(1 + e^(-as)): F(s) = (1 - e^(-as))/(s(1 + e^(-as))) = (1/s) tanh(as/2). A neat closed form for a signal that computers produce all the time as a clock.

Convolution, a pointer: The Laplace convolution is (f * g)(t) = ∫ from 0 to t of f(τ) g(t - τ) dτ, and L{f * g} = F(s) G(s). We will use it in lesson 23 to find inverse transforms of products.

Real life example 1, a water pump switched on by a timer: In many Dhaka buildings, a pump is switched on at a set time to fill the roof tank. Suppose the pump pushes water at a steady rate r starting at t = 5 minutes. The inflow is r u(t - 5), with transform r e^(-5s)/s. If the tank also leaks a little, the tank equation becomes a first order ODE, and with the derivative rule and the step rule, the whole thing becomes simple algebra in s. The delay of 5 minutes just shows up as a factor e^(-5s).

Real life example 2, a cricket bat hitting the ball: The force of the bat on the ball lasts only around a millisecond, so we model it as an impulse P δ(t - t0), where P is the total push (impulse). In the s-world this is just P e^(-s t0). Engineers model sudden loads the same way: a car hitting a speed breaker, a door slamming, a voltage spike when lightning strikes near a power line. One simple formula handles all these "kicks".

Common mistakes: Mixing the two shifts: e^(at) f(t) shifts s (F(s - a)), while f(t - a)u(t - a) multiplies by e^(-as). Forgetting to rewrite the function in terms of t - a before using the second shift. Writing L{f'} = sF without the - f(0). Forgetting the minus sign in L{t f} = -F'(s). In the periodic formula, integrating over all of [0, ∞) instead of one period.

What exams ask: Find L{e^(-3t) cos 4t}, L{t² sin t}, L{(1 - cos t)/t}; express a piecewise function with unit steps and find its transform; prove L{f'} = sF - f(0); find the transform of a square, sawtooth or half-wave rectified sine wave; evaluate an integral like ∫ t e^(-2t) sin t dt using transforms.

Recap: s-shifting: e^(at) f ↔ F(s - a). t-shifting: f(t - a)u(t - a) ↔ e^(-as)F. Multiply by t: -F'(s). Divide by t: ∫ from s to ∞ F. Derivative: sF - f(0). Integral: F/s. Step: e^(-as)/s. Impulse: e^(-as). Periodic: one period divided by 1 - e^(-sT). With these moves, you can transform almost anything you meet in circuits and mechanics. Next lesson we go backwards: the inverse Laplace transform.
key_points: First shift: L{e^(at) f(t)} = F(s - a); watch the sign of a.
Multiply by t: L{t f} = -F'(s); divide by t: L{f/t} = ∫s^∞ F(u) du.
Derivatives: L{f'} = sF - f(0), L{f''} = s²F - s f(0) - f'(0); initial values come in automatically.
Integral: L{∫0^t f dτ} = F(s)/s.
Unit step u(t - a) ↔ e^(-as)/s; second shift f(t - a)u(t - a) ↔ e^(-as)F(s).
Impulse δ(t - a) ↔ e^(-as), so δ(t) ↔ 1.
Periodic f with period T: L{f} = (1/(1 - e^(-sT))) ∫0^T e^(-st) f dt; a square wave gives (1/s) tanh(as/2).
lessons.tip: Keep the two shifts on one line of your notes: 'multiply by e^(at) moves s; delay by a multiplies by e^(-as)'. Before any second-shift problem, rewrite the function in terms of t - a.
lessons.task: On paper, sketch f(t) = 0 for t < 1, t for 1 ≤ t < 2, and 0 for t ≥ 2. Write it with unit steps as t[u(t - 1) - u(t - 2)], rewrite each piece in terms of t - 1 and t - 2, and find its Laplace transform.

quiz.explain: First shifting: replace s by s + 3 everywhere in s/(s² + 16).

quiz.q: L{f'(t)} equals:
quiz.explain: Integration by parts gives s F(s) - f(0); the initial value enters automatically.

quiz.q: What is L{u(t - 4)}?
quiz.explain: The step is 1 from t = 4 on: ∫4^∞ e^(-st) dt = e^(-4s)/s.

quiz.q: L{t sin at} equals:
quiz.explain: Multiplication by t gives -F'(s); with F = a/(s² + a²) this is 2as/(s² + a²)².

quiz.q: For f with period T, L{f} is:
options: ∫0^T e^(-st) f dt divided by (1 - e^(-sT))
quiz.explain: Each later period adds e^(-sT) times the previous one, a geometric series summing to 1/(1 - e^(-sT)).

lessons.title: Inverse Laplace Transform: Tables, Partial Fractions and Convolution
lessons.content:
Imagine your cousin in London sends you a letter written in English, and your Nanu, who only reads Bangla, wants to know what it says. You translate it into Bangla, she reads it, then she dictates a reply in Bangla, and you translate it back into English before posting it. The Laplace transform is the first translation: it turns a function of time f(t) into a function of s, F(s). Problems that are hard in the time world (derivatives, integrals, switches) become simple algebra in the s world. But nobody wants an answer in the s world forever. In the end we must translate back to time. That return trip is the inverse Laplace transform, and this lesson is all about doing it quickly and correctly.

What it is: If L{f(t)} = F(s), then we write f(t) = L^{-1}{F(s)} and call f the inverse Laplace transform of F. For example, since L{e^{3t}} = 1/(s - 3), we have L^{-1}{1/(s - 3)} = e^{3t}. A natural worry is: could two different functions have the same transform? Lerch's theorem says that if two continuous functions have the same Laplace transform, they are the same function. (Functions can differ at a few isolated jump points, but that never matters in practice.) So the inverse is well defined, and we can trust our tables in both directions.

Linearity works backwards too: Because L is linear, so is L^{-1}: L^{-1}{aF + bG} = a L^{-1}{F} + b L^{-1}{G}. This is the most used rule of the whole lesson. Almost every inverse problem is solved by breaking a messy F(s) into a sum of simple pieces that we recognise from the table, inverting each piece, and adding the answers. The two big tools for breaking things up are partial fractions and completing the square. The big tool for gluing products together is the convolution theorem. We will meet all three.

The table read backwards: Keep these pairs in your head. 1/s gives 1. 1/s² gives t. n!/s^{n+1} gives t^n, so 1/s^{n+1} gives t^n/n!. 1/(s - a) gives e^{at}. ω/(s² + ω²) gives sin ωt. s/(s² + ω²) gives cos ωt. a/(s² - a²) gives sinh at. s/(s² - a²) gives cosh at. Notice the pattern: when s is on top, you get the 'cos' type function; when a plain constant is on top, you get the 'sin' type. Also notice that the sine pair needs the exact ω on top. That small detail is where many marks are lost.

Fixing the constants: Suppose F(s) = 5/(s² + 9). Here ω² = 9, so ω = 3. The table wants 3/(s² + 9), but we have 5 on top. Write 5/(s² + 9) = (5/3) · 3/(s² + 9). Now invert: f(t) = (5/3) sin 3t. Another one: F(s) = 1/s⁴. The table says 3!/s⁴ = 6/s⁴ gives t³, so 1/s⁴ gives t³/6. Always ask: 'What exact form does the table want, and what number must I multiply and divide by to get there?'

Splitting a numerator: Take F(s) = (3s + 4)/(s² + 4). Split it into two fractions: 3 · s/(s² + 4) + 4/(s² + 4). The first piece is 3 cos 2t. The second piece needs a 2 on top, so write 4/(s² + 4) = 2 · 2/(s² + 4), which gives 2 sin 2t. Final answer: f(t) = 3 cos 2t + 2 sin 2t. You can check it quickly at t = 0: f(0) = 3. We will soon see a theorem that predicts f(0) straight from F(s), and it also gives 3 here.

First shifting theorem, backwards: Forward, we learned L{e^{at} f(t)} = F(s - a). Backwards it reads: if you see s replaced by s - a, the answer gets multiplied by e^{at}. Example: F(s) = 1/(s - 2)³. Without the shift, 1/s³ gives t²/2. The shift s → s - 2 multiplies by e^{2t}, so f(t) = (t²/2) e^{2t}. Careful with signs: (s + 1) in the formula means a = -1, which gives e^{-t}. A shift to the right in s means growth e^{+at}; a shift to the left means decay.

Partial fractions, the main idea: Most F(s) that come from real problems are rational: a polynomial P(s) divided by a polynomial Q(s). If the degree of P is less than the degree of Q, we can split P/Q into a sum of simple fractions, one for each factor of Q. (If the top degree is not smaller, do polynomial long division first.) There are three kinds of factors: distinct linear factors like (s + 1), repeated linear factors like (s + 1)², and quadratic factors that do not factor over real numbers, like s² + 2s + 5. Each kind has its own recipe.

Distinct linear factors and the cover-up trick: Take F(s) = (s + 5)/((s + 1)(s + 2)). Write it as A/(s + 1) + B/(s + 2). To find A, cover the factor (s + 1) with your thumb and put s = -1 into what is left: A = (-1 + 5)/(-1 + 2) = 4/1 = 4. To find B, cover (s + 2) and put s = -2: B = (-2 + 5)/(-2 + 1) = 3/(-1) = -3. Quick check: 4(s + 2) - 3(s + 1) = s + 5. Correct! So f(t) = 4e^{-t} - 3e^{-2t}. This cover-up method (Heaviside's method) only works directly for simple, non-repeated factors.

Repeated linear factors: Take F(s) = 1/(s²(s + 1)). Here s appears twice, so we need A/s + B/s² + C/(s + 1). Cover-up still gives the top power and the simple factor: B = 1/(0 + 1) = 1 and C = 1/(-1)² = 1. For A, multiply out: 1 = A s(s + 1) + B(s + 1) + C s². Compare the s² coefficients: 0 = A + C, so A = -1. Now invert: -1 + t + e^{-t}. Check at t = 0: -1 + 0 + 1 = 0. That matches what we expect, because F(s) falls off like 1/s³, which means f starts at zero.

Quadratic factors and completing the square: Take F(s) = (s + 3)/(s² + 2s + 5). The bottom has no real roots (discriminant 4 - 20 < 0), so do not try to factor it. Complete the square: s² + 2s + 5 = (s + 1)² + 4. Now rewrite the top in terms of (s + 1): s + 3 = (s + 1) + 2. So F(s) = (s + 1)/((s + 1)² + 4) + 2/((s + 1)² + 4). Without the shift these are cos 2t and sin 2t, and the shift s → s + 1 multiplies by e^{-t}. Answer: f(t) = e^{-t}(cos 2t + sin 2t). This is a damped oscillation, like a swing slowly stopping.

A mixed example: F(s) = 1/((s + 1)(s² + 1)). Write A/(s + 1) + (Bs + C)/(s² + 1). Cover-up gives A = 1/((-1)² + 1) = 1/2. Multiply out: 1 = A(s² + 1) + (Bs + C)(s + 1). Comparing s²: 0 = A + B, so B = -1/2. Comparing constants: 1 = A + C, so C = 1/2. So F(s) = (1/2)/(s + 1) - (1/2) s/(s² + 1) + (1/2)/(s² + 1), and f(t) = (1/2)e^{-t} - (1/2)cos t + (1/2)sin t. Notice the two parts: e^{-t} dies out, while the sine and cosine keep going forever. Engineers call these the transient and the steady-state parts.

Second shifting theorem, backwards: Forward, a function that switches on at time a, f(t - a)u(t - a), has transform e^{-as}F(s). So whenever you see an exponential e^{-as} multiplying something, it means 'delay by a'. Recipe: ignore e^{-as}, invert the rest to get f(t), then replace t by t - a and multiply by the unit step u(t - a). Example: e^{-2s}/s². Without the exponential, 1/s² gives t. So the answer is (t - 2)u(t - 2): zero until t = 2, then a ramp that starts climbing from there.

The convolution theorem: Sometimes F(s) is a product F(s)G(s) of two things whose inverses we know, f(t) and g(t). The inverse of the product is not f(t)g(t). It is the convolution (f * g)(t) = ∫ from 0 to t of f(τ) g(t - τ) dτ. Example: 1/(s(s + 1)). Take f = 1 (from 1/s) and g = e^{-t} (from 1/(s + 1)). Then (f * g)(t) = ∫ from 0 to t of e^{-(t - τ)} dτ = 1 - e^{-t}. Partial fractions gives 1/s - 1/(s + 1), the same answer, which is a nice check.

Where convolution really helps: Some products are painful with partial fractions. A classic is F(s) = 1/(s² + 1)², which is (1/(s² + 1)) times (1/(s² + 1)). Each factor inverts to sin t, so f = sin t * sin t = ∫ from 0 to t of sin τ sin(t - τ) dτ. Using the product-to-sum formula and integrating, you get f(t) = (1/2)(sin t - t cos t). That t cos t term grows with time; we will see in the next lesson that it describes resonance, like pushing a swing at exactly its natural rhythm.

Initial value theorem: You can predict where f starts without inverting at all: f(0+) = lim as s → ∞ of sF(s). For F(s) = (s + 5)/((s + 1)(s + 2)), sF(s) = (s² + 5s)/(s² + 3s + 2), which tends to 1 as s grows. And indeed f(t) = 4e^{-t} - 3e^{-2t} gives f(0) = 4 - 3 = 1. For (3s + 4)/(s² + 4), sF(s) tends to 3, matching f(0) = 3 from before. This is a fast way to catch arithmetic mistakes in a long partial fraction calculation.

Final value theorem: Similarly, lim as t → ∞ of f(t) = lim as s → 0 of sF(s), but only if f really settles down. The safe rule: all poles of sF(s) must have negative real part (strictly in the left half of the s-plane). Example: F(s) = 1/(s(s + 1)). Then sF(s) = 1/(s + 1), whose only pole is -1, so the theorem applies: the limit is 1. Check: f(t) = 1 - e^{-t} → 1. Warning example: F(s) = 1/(s² + 1). Blindly, sF(s) → 0 as s → 0, but f(t) = sin t never settles. The poles ±i are on the imaginary axis, so the theorem is not allowed here.

A peek at the official formula: There is an integral formula for the inverse, the Bromwich integral: f(t) = (1/2πi) ∫ from γ - i∞ to γ + i∞ of e^{st} F(s) ds, along a vertical line to the right of all poles. You rarely compute it directly, but closing the path with a big curve and using the residue theorem from Lesson 13 gives a neat result: f(t) is the sum of the residues of e^{st}F(s) at the poles of F. For a simple pole at s = a of F = P/Q, that residue is (P(a)/Q'(a)) e^{at}, which is exactly what the cover-up trick computes. So partial fractions is secretly complex analysis.

Real-life example 1, a cup of cha cooling: You pour tea at 90 °C in a room at 30 °C, in a Dhaka tea stall. Newton's law of cooling says T' = -k(T - 30). Taking Laplace with T(0) = 90 gives sT(s) - 90 = -kT(s) + 30k/s, so T(s) = (90s + 30k)/(s(s + k)). Cover-up: at s = 0, A = 30k/k = 30; at s = -k, B = (-90k + 30k)/(-k) = 60. So T(t) = 30 + 60e^{-kt}. The final value theorem confirms it: sT(s) → 30 as s → 0. The tea ends at room temperature, exactly as your tongue already knew.

Real-life example 2, a delayed switch: A water pump in a building turns on 2 seconds after you press the button, and the water level in a pipe behaves like a first-order system. Its output transform might be e^{-2s}/(s(s + 1)). Ignore e^{-2s} first: 1/(s(s + 1)) gives 1 - e^{-t}. Then delay it: y(t) = (1 - e^{-(t - 2)}) u(t - 2). Nothing happens for 2 seconds, then the level rises smoothly toward 1. Control engineers and game physics programmers use exactly this kind of delay reasoning.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the ω on top of the sine pair (5/(s² + 9) is not 5 sin 3t). Getting the shift sign wrong (1/(s + 2) is e^{-2t}, not e^{2t}). Using cover-up on a repeated factor for every coefficient (it only gives the highest power). Not doing long division when the top degree is too big. Trying to factor s² + 2s + 5 into ugly complex roots instead of completing the square. Applying the final value theorem when there are poles on the imaginary axis or in the right half-plane. And writing f(t)g(t) instead of the convolution for a product.

What exams ask: Find inverse transforms using partial fractions (distinct, repeated and quadratic factors). Use completing the square to get e^{at} sin and cos terms. Use the second shifting theorem with e^{-as}. Use the convolution theorem to find something like L^{-1}{1/(s(s² + 1))} or 1/(s² + a²)². State and use the initial and final value theorems, and explain when the final value theorem fails. Show your partial fraction constants clearly; examiners give method marks even if the arithmetic slips.

Recap: The inverse Laplace transform takes us home from the s world to the time world. Linearity lets us invert piece by piece. Partial fractions breaks rational functions into table pieces, completing the square handles quadratic factors, the first shifting theorem turns s - a into e^{at}, the second shifting theorem turns e^{-as} into a delay, and convolution handles products. The initial and final value theorems let you check answers without full inversion. In the next lesson we put the whole machine to work on differential equations, circuits and springs.
key_points: L^{-1}{F(s)} = f(t) means L{f(t)} = F(s); by Lerch's theorem continuous inverses are unique.
Inversion is linear: split F(s) into table pieces, invert each, add.
Fix constants: 5/(s² + 9) = (5/3)·3/(s² + 9) gives (5/3) sin 3t.
First shift backwards: F(s - a) gives e^{at} f(t); second shift: e^{-as}F(s) gives f(t - a)u(t - a).
Partial fractions: cover-up for distinct linear factors, compare coefficients for repeated ones, complete the square for quadratics.
Convolution: L^{-1}{FG} = ∫ from 0 to t of f(τ)g(t - τ) dτ, e.g. 1/(s² + 1)² gives (1/2)(sin t - t cos t).
Initial value: f(0+) = lim s→∞ sF(s). Final value: lim t→∞ f(t) = lim s→0 sF(s), only if poles of sF(s) are in the left half-plane.
lessons.tip: After every partial fraction split, add the pieces back over a common denominator or use the initial value theorem as a 20-second check. It catches most sign slips.
lessons.task: On paper, find the inverse Laplace transform of (2s + 1)/(s(s + 1)) by cover-up, then check f(0) with the initial value theorem and the limit as t → ∞ with the final value theorem.

quiz.explain: ω = 3 and the sine pair needs 3 on top, so 5/(s² + 9) = (5/3)·3/(s² + 9), which gives (5/3) sin 3t.
1/s³ gives t²/2, and the shift s → s - 2 multiplies by e^{2t}.

quiz.q: For which F(s) is the final value theorem NOT allowed?
quiz.explain: 1/(s² + 1) has poles ±i on the imaginary axis; f(t) = sin t never settles, so the theorem does not apply.

quiz.q: The convolution theorem says L^{-1}{F(s)G(s)} equals:
options: ∫ from 0 to t of f(τ)g(t - τ) dτ
quiz.explain: The inverse of a product is the convolution integral, not the product of the inverses.
Initial value theorem: sF(s) → 1 as s → ∞. Also f(t) = 4e^{-t} - 3e^{-2t} gives f(0) = 1.

lessons.title: Solving ODEs with Laplace: IVPs, Systems, Circuits and Springs
lessons.content:
Imagine a juice machine at a shop in New Market. You drop in whole oranges, the machine does all the hard work inside, and out comes juice. You never have to squeeze anything by hand. The Laplace transform is a machine like that for differential equations. You drop in a hard calculus problem (an equation with y, y' and y''), the transform turns it into an easy algebra problem in s, you solve for Y(s) like a class 8 equation, and then the inverse transform from the last lesson pours out the answer y(t). Even better, the starting values y(0) and y'(0) go into the machine at the very beginning, so you never have to find arbitrary constants at the end.

The two key formulas: Everything rests on how derivatives transform. If L{y(t)} = Y(s), then L{y'} = sY(s) - y(0) and L{y''} = s²Y(s) - s y(0) - y'(0). In general, the nth derivative gives s^n Y minus a tail of initial values. Look at what happened: differentiation in time became multiplication by s, and the initial conditions appeared automatically. That is the whole magic. A differential equation becomes an algebraic equation in Y(s).

The four-step recipe: Step 1, take the Laplace transform of both sides of the equation, using the derivative formulas and the table for the right-hand side. Step 2, put in the initial values. Step 3, solve the algebra for Y(s). Step 4, invert Y(s) using partial fractions, completing the square, shifting or convolution. A fifth, optional but very wise step: put your answer back into the original equation and the initial conditions to check it.

A first-order example: Solve y' + 2y = 4 with y(0) = 1. Transform: (sY - 1) + 2Y = 4/s. Collect: (s + 2)Y = 4/s + 1 = (s + 4)/s. So Y = (s + 4)/(s(s + 2)). Cover-up: at s = 0, A = 4/2 = 2; at s = -2, B = (-2 + 4)/(-2) = -1. So y(t) = 2 - e^{-2t}. Check: y' = 2e^{-2t}, so y' + 2y = 2e^{-2t} + 4 - 2e^{-2t} = 4, and y(0) = 2 - 1 = 1. Both conditions satisfied. The solution starts at 1 and settles at 2, which is 4 divided by 2.

A second-order example: Solve y'' + 3y' + 2y = 0 with y(0) = 1 and y'(0) = 0. Transform: (s²Y - s·1 - 0) + 3(sY - 1) + 2Y = 0. Collect: (s² + 3s + 2)Y = s + 3. So Y = (s + 3)/((s + 1)(s + 2)). Cover-up: A = (-1 + 3)/(-1 + 2) = 2 and B = (-2 + 3)/(-2 + 1) = -1. So y(t) = 2e^{-t} - e^{-2t}. Check: y(0) = 2 - 1 = 1 and y'(t) = -2e^{-t} + 2e^{-2t}, so y'(0) = 0. Notice that the denominator s² + 3s + 2 is exactly the characteristic polynomial you met in the ODE course. Laplace just finds it for you.

Exponential forcing: Solve y'' - 3y' + 2y = 4e^{3t} with y(0) = 0 and y'(0) = 0. With zero initial values the left side becomes (s² - 3s + 2)Y = (s - 1)(s - 2)Y, and the right side is 4/(s - 3). So Y = 4/((s - 1)(s - 2)(s - 3)). Cover-up three times: at s = 1, 4/((-1)(-2)) = 2; at s = 2, 4/((1)(-1)) = -4; at s = 3, 4/((2)(1)) = 2. So y(t) = 2e^t - 4e^{2t} + 2e^{3t}. Check: y(0) = 2 - 4 + 2 = 0 and y'(0) = 2 - 8 + 6 = 0. No guessing of a particular solution was needed at all.

Resonance: Solve y'' + y = 2 sin t with y(0) = 0 and y'(0) = 0. Transform: (s² + 1)Y = 2/(s² + 1), so Y = 2/(s² + 1)². From the last lesson, 1/(s² + 1)² inverts to (1/2)(sin t - t cos t) by convolution. So y(t) = sin t - t cos t. The t cos t term grows bigger and bigger. Why? The system's natural frequency (from s² + 1, so ω = 1) equals the forcing frequency. Pushing a swing at exactly its own rhythm makes it go higher every time. That is resonance, and it is why soldiers break step when crossing a bridge.

Step inputs, switching things on: Real inputs often switch on suddenly. Solve y' + y = u(t - 1), y(0) = 0, where u(t - 1) is a unit step that turns on at t = 1. Transform: (s + 1)Y = e^{-s}/s. So Y = e^{-s} · 1/(s(s + 1)). Ignore e^{-s}: 1/(s(s + 1)) = 1/s - 1/(s + 1) gives 1 - e^{-t}. Delay by 1: y(t) = (1 - e^{-(t - 1)}) u(t - 1). Classical methods would need you to solve two separate pieces and glue them at t = 1. Laplace does it in one go.

Impulses, a sudden hit: The Dirac delta δ(t - a) models a very short, very strong kick at time a, like a cricket bat hitting the ball. Its transform is e^{-as}. Solve y'' + y = δ(t - 2) with y(0) = 0 and y'(0) = 0. Transform: (s² + 1)Y = e^{-2s}, so Y = e^{-2s}/(s² + 1). Invert: y(t) = sin(t - 2) u(t - 2). The system sits still until t = 2, gets hit, and then swings forever (there is no damping). The function you get from an impulse at t = 0 is called the impulse response, and it describes the whole system. We will use that idea in the final lesson.

Systems of ODEs: Laplace also handles several unknowns at once. Picture two connected water tanks. Let x(t) and y(t) be the amounts in each, with x' = -x + y and y' = x - y, starting with x(0) = 1 and y(0) = 0. Transform: sX - 1 = -X + Y and sY = X - Y. The second gives Y = X/(s + 1). Put it in the first: (s + 1)X - 1 = X/(s + 1). Multiply by (s + 1): X((s + 1)² - 1) = s + 1, so X = (s + 1)/(s(s + 2)). Cover-up gives 1/2 and 1/2, so x(t) = 1/2 + (1/2)e^{-2t}. Then Y = 1/(s(s + 2)) gives y(t) = 1/2 - (1/2)e^{-2t}.

Reading the tank answer: Check that it makes sense. At t = 0, x = 1 and y = 0. As t grows, both approach 1/2, so the water shares itself equally. And x + y = 1 at every moment, which is right because water flows between the tanks but is never lost. Systems like this appear in chemical mixing, in population models, and in compartment models used for medicine dosage. The method is always the same: transform each equation, solve the small algebraic system (Cramer's rule works nicely), then invert.

Electrical circuits, RL: A series circuit with inductor L, resistor R and battery E obeys L i' + R i = E. Take L = 1 henry, R = 10 ohms, E = 20 volts, switched on at t = 0 with i(0) = 0. Transform: (s + 10)I = 20/s, so I = 20/(s(s + 10)). Cover-up: A = 20/10 = 2 and B = 20/(-10) = -2. So i(t) = 2(1 - e^{-10t}) amperes. The current rises from 0 and settles at 2 A, which is exactly E/R by Ohm's law. The number 1/10 second, L/R, is the time constant: after one time constant the current reaches about 63 percent of its final value.

Electrical circuits, RLC: For a series RLC circuit, the charge q on the capacitor obeys L q'' + R q' + q/C = E(t). Take L = 1, R = 2, C = 1/5 (so 1/C = 5), E = 0, q(0) = 1 and q'(0) = 0. Transform: (s² + 2s + 5)Q = s + 2. Complete the square: s² + 2s + 5 = (s + 1)² + 4, and s + 2 = (s + 1) + 1. So Q = (s + 1)/((s + 1)² + 4) + (1/2)·2/((s + 1)² + 4), and q(t) = e^{-t}(cos 2t + (1/2) sin 2t). The charge sloshes back and forth while dying out. Check: q'(0) = -1 + 1 = 0.

Spring-mass systems: A mass m on a spring with stiffness k and a damper c obeys m x'' + c x' + k x = F(t). This is the same equation shape as the RLC circuit, with mass like inductance, damping like resistance and stiffness like 1/C. Undamped example: x'' + 4x = 0, x(0) = 0, x'(0) = 2. Then (s² + 4)X = 2, so X = 2/(s² + 4) and x(t) = sin 2t. The mass bounces forever with angular frequency 2, since sqrt(k/m) = sqrt(4) = 2.

Three kinds of damping, read from the poles: The roots of ms² + cs + k decide everything. Two different real negative roots: overdamped, the mass creeps back without swinging, like y'' + 3y' + 2y = 0 earlier. A repeated real root: critically damped, the fastest return without overshoot. Complex roots with negative real part: underdamped, it swings with shrinking size, like the RLC example. Critical example: x'' + 2x' + x = 0, x(0) = 1, x'(0) = 0. Then (s + 1)²X = s + 2, so X = 1/(s + 1) + 1/(s + 1)², and x(t) = e^{-t}(1 + t). Check x'(0): -1 + 1 = 0.

Why engineers love this method: Initial conditions go in at the start, so no constants to find later. Discontinuous inputs (steps, switches, pulses) and impulses are handled smoothly with u(t - a) and δ(t - a). Systems of equations become ordinary algebra. And the denominator of Y(s) shows the system's poles, which tell you straight away whether the solution decays, oscillates or blows up. The main limitation: the method is designed for linear equations with constant coefficients. For nonlinear equations you need other tools.

Real-life example 1, a bus over a speed breaker: A BRTC bus in Dhaka hits a speed breaker. The seat's suspension is a spring-damper, and the bump is close to an impulse. With m x'' + c x' + k x = P δ(t), the solution is (P/m) times the impulse response. Designers choose c so the poles are complex with a decent negative real part: a little bounce, but it dies quickly. Too little damping and passengers keep bouncing; too much (overdamped and very stiff) and every bump feels like a hard jolt.

Real-life example 2, load shedding and an IPS: When the power cuts, an IPS switches on and the voltage across the fan's circuit rises like a step input. A simple RC model gives RC v' + v = V u(t), so V(s) = V/(s(RCs + 1)) and v(t) = V(1 - e^{-t/(RC)}). The fan speeds up in a similar first-order way: J ω' + b ω = T gives ω(t) = (T/b)(1 - e^{-bt/J}). Same maths, different devices. That is the beauty: once you know the shape of the equation, you know the shape of the answer.

Common mistakes: Writing L{y''} = s²Y and forgetting -s y(0) - y'(0). Mixing up the order: the term with y(0) is multiplied by s, not the term with y'(0). Sign slips when moving initial values to the right side. Forgetting the 1/s when transforming a constant input (4 becomes 4/s, not 4). Doing the delay wrong: e^{-s}/(s(s + 1)) needs t replaced by t - 1 everywhere, plus the step. And skipping the final check, which takes one minute and saves many marks.

What exams ask: Solve a second-order initial value problem with constant coefficients, often with a right-hand side like e^{at}, sin ωt or t. Solve one with a unit step or Dirac delta input. Solve a pair of first-order linear ODEs. Find the current or charge in an RL, RC or RLC circuit. Model a spring-mass system and say whether it is over, under or critically damped. Sometimes: use the convolution theorem to write the answer as an integral for a general input f(t).

Recap: Laplace turns a linear ODE into algebra by using L{y'} = sY - y(0) and L{y''} = s²Y - s y(0) - y'(0). Solve for Y(s), invert, and check. It handles constant, exponential and sinusoidal forcing, resonance, steps, impulses and systems. Circuits and springs share the same equation shape, and the poles of the denominator tell you whether the response is overdamped, critically damped, underdamped or growing. In the final lesson we will turn this point of view into the language that signal processing and control engineers speak every day.
key_points: L{y'} = sY - y(0) and L{y''} = s²Y - s y(0) - y'(0): derivatives become multiplication by s, initial values come in for free.
Recipe: transform, insert initial values, solve for Y(s), invert, then check.
Steps u(t - a) and impulses δ(t - a) are handled in one go through e^{-as}.
Forcing at the natural frequency gives resonance terms like t cos t.
Systems of ODEs become small algebraic systems in X(s), Y(s).
RLC circuits and spring-mass systems share the same equation shape: L q'' + R q' + q/C = E and m x'' + c x' + k x = F.
Roots of the denominator decide behaviour: distinct real (overdamped), repeated (critical), complex (underdamped).
lessons.tip: Always finish by plugging y(0), y'(0) and the equation back in. If y(0) does not come out right, the mistake is almost always a sign when you moved the initial values across.
lessons.task: Solve y'' + 4y = 0 with y(0) = 1 and y'(0) = 0 using Laplace, then change the equation to y'' + 4y' + 4y = 0 with the same starting values. Sketch both answers on paper and label which is undamped and which is critically damped.

quiz.q: What is L{y''}?
quiz.explain: Applying L{y'} = sY - y(0) twice gives s²Y - s y(0) - y'(0).

quiz.q: The solution of y' + 2y = 4 with y(0) = 1 is:
The system x'' + 2x' + x = 0 is:
quiz.explain: s² + 2s + 1 = (s + 1)² has a repeated real root, which means critical damping.

quiz.q: With zero initial conditions, y'' + y = δ(t - 2) gives y(t) =
quiz.explain: Y = e^{-2s}/(s² + 1); 1/(s² + 1) gives sin t and e^{-2s} delays it by 2.

quiz.q: In L i' + R i = E with L = 1 H, R = 10 Ω, E = 20 V, i(0) = 0, the current settles at:
quiz.explain: i(t) = 2(1 - e^{-10t}) → 2 A, which equals E/R.

lessons.title: Putting It Together for CSE: Signals, Systems, Stability and Filters
lessons.content:
You have climbed a long hill: complex numbers, analytic functions, contour integrals, residues, Fourier series, Fourier and Laplace transforms. Now stand at the top and look around. Why does a computer science student need all this? Because almost everything a computer touches in the real world is a signal: your voice in a WhatsApp call, the photo on your phone, the Wi-Fi radio waves, the readings from a temperature sensor, even the vibration data from a smartwatch. And almost every program that processes those signals is a system. This last lesson connects the maths you learned to the language of signals, systems, transfer functions, stability and filters, the language of DSP, control and communication courses.

Signals: A signal is just a quantity that changes over time (or space). A continuous-time signal x(t) has a value at every instant, like the voltage from a microphone. A discrete-time signal x[n] has values only at whole-number steps n = 0, 1, 2, ..., like audio samples stored in an MP3 or the daily closing price of a share on the Dhaka Stock Exchange. Computers can only store discrete signals, so real-world continuous signals are sampled. A picture is a two-dimensional signal: pixel brightness as a function of row and column.

Systems: A system takes an input signal and produces an output signal. A mobile phone's noise remover, a car's cruise control, the bass knob on a speaker and a smoothing function in your code are all systems. Two properties make systems easy to analyse. Linear: if input x1 gives y1 and x2 gives y2, then a·x1 + b·x2 gives a·y1 + b·y2. Time-invariant: if you delay the input by T, the output is delayed by T and otherwise unchanged. Systems with both properties are called LTI systems, and they are exactly the ones Laplace and Fourier handle perfectly.

Impulse response and convolution: Hit an LTI system with an impulse δ(t) and record the output h(t). That one function, the impulse response, tells you everything. Why? Any input can be thought of as a long row of tiny impulses, each scaled and delayed. By linearity and time-invariance, the output is the matching row of scaled, delayed copies of h, added up. That sum is the convolution y(t) = (x * h)(t) = ∫ x(τ) h(t - τ) dτ. In discrete time it is y[n] = Σ x[k] h[n - k]. This is the same convolution you used with Laplace in Lesson 23.

Transfer function: Convolution in time is hard; Laplace makes it a product: Y(s) = H(s) X(s). The function H(s) = Y(s)/X(s), computed with all initial conditions set to zero, is the transfer function, and it equals the Laplace transform of h(t). Example: the system y' + 2y = x. Transform with zero initial value: (s + 2)Y = X, so H(s) = 1/(s + 2), and h(t) = e^{-2t}. For the RLC circuit with input voltage and output capacitor voltage, H(s) = 1/(LCs² + RCs + 1). A transfer function is like the system's ID card.

Frequency response: Put s = iω into H(s) and you get H(iω), the frequency response. If the input is a sine wave of angular frequency ω, a stable LTI system outputs a sine wave of the same frequency, with its amplitude multiplied by |H(iω)| and its phase shifted by arg H(iω). Using H(s) = 1/(s + 2): |H(iω)| = 1/sqrt(ω² + 4). At ω = 0 the gain is 1/2, at ω = 2 it is 1/(2·sqrt 2) ≈ 0.354, and at ω = 20 it is about 0.05. Low frequencies pass, high frequencies are squashed. This is the link between Laplace (s anywhere) and Fourier (s on the imaginary axis) that you saw in the transform lessons.

Poles and zeros: Write H(s) = N(s)/D(s). The roots of N are zeros (where the output vanishes) and the roots of D are poles (where H blows up). Plot them on the complex plane, the same Argand plane from Lesson 1. Example: H(s) = (s + 1)/(s² + 4s + 13). The zero is at -1. The poles solve s² + 4s + 13 = 0, so s = -2 ± 3i. Each pole p contributes a term like e^{pt} to the impulse response. For p = -2 ± 3i, that is e^{-2t} times a sine or cosine of 3t: an oscillation of frequency 3 that dies away at rate 2.

Stability: A system is BIBO stable (bounded input, bounded output) if every bounded input gives a bounded output. For a causal LTI system with a rational transfer function, the test is beautifully simple: all poles must have negative real part, that is, lie strictly in the left half of the s-plane. Then every e^{pt} decays. 1/(s + 2) is stable. 1/(s - 1) has a pole at +1, so h(t) = e^t explodes: unstable. 1/(s² + 1) has poles ±i on the imaginary axis: h(t) = sin t never dies, and the bounded input sin t produces t-growing resonance, so it is not BIBO stable either. Engineers call that case marginal.

Filters: A filter is a system designed to keep some frequencies and remove others. The simplest is the RC low-pass filter: H(s) = 1/(1 + sRC). Its cutoff angular frequency is ω_c = 1/(RC), where the gain falls to 1/sqrt 2 ≈ 0.707 (that is, -3 dB). Example: R = 1 kΩ and C = 1 µF give RC = 0.001 s, so ω_c = 1000 rad/s and f_c = 1000/(2π) ≈ 159 Hz. Swap the parts around and you get a high-pass filter, H(s) = sRC/(1 + sRC), which blocks slow changes and passes fast ones. Combine both and you get a band-pass filter, like a radio tuning in one station.

Spectrum thinking: Fourier analysis says any reasonable signal is a mixture of sine waves. That is how an equalizer app shows bass, mid and treble bars, and how a doctor's ECG machine filters out 50 Hz mains hum (Bangladesh's grid runs at 50 Hz). Compression also uses it: MP3 throws away sound components your ears are unlikely to notice, and JPEG uses the discrete cosine transform, a close cousin of the Fourier transform, to keep the important low-frequency parts of each 8 by 8 block of pixels and drop fine detail. The FFT, which computes the DFT in about N log N steps instead of N², is what makes all this fast enough for phones.

Sampling: To turn a continuous signal into numbers, a computer samples it every T seconds. The sampling theorem (Nyquist-Shannon) says that if a signal has no frequencies above f_max, you can rebuild it perfectly from samples taken at a rate greater than 2·f_max. Human hearing goes up to about 20 kHz, which is why audio CDs use 44.1 kHz. If you sample too slowly, high frequencies disguise themselves as low ones. That is aliasing, and it is why a spinning wheel in a video can seem to turn backwards.

The Z-transform, Laplace for computers: For discrete signals, the cousin of Laplace is the Z-transform: X(z) = Σ from n = 0 to ∞ of x[n] z^{-n}. A delay by one step becomes multiplication by z^{-1}, just as differentiation became multiplication by s. Sampling with period T links the two through z = e^{sT}. This map sends the left half of the s-plane into the inside of the unit circle |z| < 1. So the stability rule for discrete systems becomes: all poles must lie strictly inside the unit circle. You will study it properly in a Signals and Systems or DSP course.

A digital filter in three lines: Take y[n] = 0.5·y[n - 1] + x[n]. Z-transform: Y = 0.5 z^{-1} Y + X, so H(z) = 1/(1 - 0.5 z^{-1}) = z/(z - 0.5). The pole is at z = 0.5, inside the unit circle, so it is stable. Its impulse response is h[n] = 0.5^n, which fades away. In code, a popular smoothing filter is: y = y + a·(x - y) for each new sample x, with a between 0 and 1. That is y[n] = (1 - a) y[n - 1] + a x[n], a pole at 1 - a, stable for 0 < a < 1. Phone step counters and game cameras use exactly this trick to smooth jittery sensor data.

Where complex analysis itself shows up: Inverse Laplace and Z-transforms are really residue calculations, as you saw in Lesson 23. The Nyquist stability criterion, a classic control engineering tool, is built on the argument principle: it counts how many times a contour's image winds around a point to count unstable poles. Conformal maps from Lesson 8 are used in fluid flow around wings (the Joukowski map turns a circle into a wing-like shape) and in image warping. Harmonic functions from Lesson 7 describe steady heat and electrostatic potentials, which is useful in chip design.

Real-life example 1, a phone call on a noisy bus: You are calling home from a crowded Dhaka bus. The phone's microphone picks up your voice plus engine rumble. First, an anti-aliasing low-pass filter and sampling turn the sound into numbers. Digital filters, designed using poles and zeros inside the unit circle, cut the low rumble. Noise suppression works on short frames of sound in the frequency domain using the FFT. The voice codec compresses it, and on 4G the data travels using OFDM, a scheme in which the FFT and inverse FFT do the heavy lifting. Every step uses ideas from this course.

Real-life example 2, a line-following robot: At a university robotics contest, your robot must follow a black line. A sensor measures how far the robot drifts, and a PID controller sets the motor speeds: output = Kp·e + Ki·∫e dt + Kd·e'. In Laplace language, the controller is C(s) = Kp + Ki/s + Kd·s. Combine it with the motor's transfer function and you get a closed-loop transfer function. If its poles are in the left half-plane with a decent negative real part, the robot settles smoothly. If Kp is too big, poles may move toward the right and the robot wiggles wildly or flies off the track. Tuning a PID is pole placement in disguise.

The whole course on one page: Lessons 1 to 4 built complex numbers and functions. Lessons 5 to 8 showed what it means to be analytic: Cauchy-Riemann, harmonic functions and conformal maps. Lessons 9 to 14 were integration: Cauchy's theorem and formula, series, singularities, residues and real integrals. Lessons 15 to 20 were Fourier: series, half-range series, complex form, Parseval and the Fourier transform. Lessons 21 to 24 were Laplace: definition, properties, inversion and solving ODEs. Today tied it together as signals and systems.

Common confusions and what exams ask: Stability in the s-plane means left half-plane; in the z-plane it means inside the unit circle. Do not mix them up. A transfer function is defined with zero initial conditions. The magnitude at cutoff is 1/sqrt 2 of the passband value, not one half. The Fourier transform is the Laplace transform on the imaginary axis only when the region of convergence includes that axis. Exam-style questions: find H(s) from a differential equation, find its poles and decide stability, compute |H(iω)| at a few frequencies, find the impulse or step response, or explain the sampling theorem.

What to learn next: Signals and Systems (a full course on LTI systems, convolution and all the transforms), Digital Signal Processing (Z-transform, FIR and IIR filter design, FFT), Control Systems (feedback, root locus, Bode and Nyquist plots), Communication Engineering (modulation, OFDM), Image Processing and Computer Vision (2D Fourier, convolution kernels), and Machine Learning, where convolutional neural networks are built on the same convolution idea. Python with NumPy and SciPy (numpy.fft, scipy.signal) lets you try all of these on your laptop.

Recap: Signals are functions; systems turn input signals into output signals. LTI systems are fully described by their impulse response h, and the output is the convolution x * h. Laplace turns that into Y = H X, where H(s) is the transfer function. Poles in the left half-plane mean stability; s = iω gives the frequency response and tells you what a filter keeps or removes. Sampling must be faster than twice the highest frequency. The Z-transform is the discrete twin of Laplace, with the unit circle as the stability boundary. Well done for finishing Math III: you now speak the mathematical language behind sound, images, radios and robots.
key_points: Signals are functions of time (x(t)) or steps (x[n]); systems turn input signals into output signals.
An LTI system is fully described by its impulse response h, and output = convolution x * h.
Transfer function H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) with zero initial conditions = L{h}; e.g. y' + 2y = x gives 1/(s + 2).
Frequency response H(iω): a sine input comes out scaled by |H(iω)| and phase-shifted by arg H(iω).
Continuous-time stability: all poles in the left half-plane; discrete-time: all poles inside the unit circle.
RC low-pass: H = 1/(1 + sRC), cutoff ω_c = 1/(RC) with gain 1/sqrt 2 (-3 dB).
Sample faster than 2·f_max (Nyquist) to avoid aliasing; the Z-transform is the discrete twin of Laplace via z = e^{sT}.
lessons.tip: For any system in a later course, ask the same three questions: what is H(s) or H(z), where are the poles, and what does |H| do at low and high frequencies. Those three answers explain most of its behaviour.
lessons.task: Take H(s) = 1/(s + 2). On paper compute |H(iω)| for ω = 0, 1, 2, 5 and 20, then sketch gain against ω. Mark the frequency where the gain drops to 1/sqrt 2 of its starting value (it is ω = 2) and explain why this is a low-pass filter.

quiz.q: A causal LTI system with a rational transfer function is BIBO stable when all its poles:
quiz.explain: Each pole p adds e^{pt} to the impulse response; it decays only if Re(p) < 0.

quiz.q: What is the transfer function of y' + 2y = x (zero initial conditions)?
A discrete-time LTI system is stable when all poles of H(z) lie:
quiz.explain: z = e^{sT} maps the left half s-plane to |z| < 1, so stable poles lie inside the unit circle.

quiz.q: An RC low-pass filter has R = 1 kΩ and C = 1 µF. Its cutoff angular frequency is:
quiz.explain: ω_c = 1/(RC) = 1/0.001 = 1000 rad/s (that is about 159 Hz).

quiz.q: By the sampling theorem, a signal with highest frequency f_max must be sampled at a rate:
quiz.explain: Nyquist-Shannon: sample faster than twice the highest frequency to avoid aliasing.
